title: Collective behavior and emergent risks in a model of human- and autonomously-driven vehicles
evidence: "Our approach reveals a model-independent role for percolation in interpreting the results." (Abstract)
method: Active-matter force model of mixed human and autonomous traffic with MOBIL lane changes; a mass hack halts a subset of autonomous vehicles and no-flow probability is explained by geometric percolation.
evaluation: Python simulation, 1 km periodic road, 3 lanes, plus webcam and NGSIM flux data; all-human vs mixed vs all-autonomous. Peak flux drops near 60% after hack. No inference, no latency, hardware not reported.
contribution: Models mixed human and autonomous traffic as active matter and shows that a simultaneous disabling of connected vehicles stops flow through a percolation transition at roughly 10-20% disabled.
flag: timing is the contribution: no; application is safety-relevant (traffic collapse after a hack) but there is no learned model and no inference timing at all - the response times are driver reaction parameters of a physics model. Not Pillar 4 material. If anything it is an emergent multi-vehicle risk model, but it measures flux loss, not a hazard rate of a safety mechanism, so it does not meet (c) either.

title: SurveilEdge: Real-time Video Query based on Collaborative Cloud-Edge Deep Learning
evidence: The threshold update is triggered when classification latency exceeds the query sampling interval, and each image is sent to the edge node minimising queue length times estimated inference time (scheduling section, paraphrase).
method: Cloud fine-tunes a query-specific MobileNet-v2 per camera cluster; edge classifies, uncertain frames between two confidence thresholds go to cloud ResNet-152; load-adaptive thresholds and latency-estimating task allocation.
evaluation: No stated deadline (implicit 1 s sampling interval). 14 cameras, query moped; vs fixed-threshold, edge-only, cloud-only. Avg latency 1.02-10.3 s vs cloud 14.8-37.4 s; 3 Core i7-6700 edge nodes plus Tesla P4 cloud.
contribution: A cloud-edge video query system that fine-tunes camera-specific classifiers and balances load across edge nodes, cutting average query latency several-fold against cloud-only at 87-91% of cloud accuracy.
flag: timing is the contribution: partly; application is surveillance video query, not safety-relevant. Borderline: accuracy is traded against latency and thresholds adapt when latency exceeds the 1 s sampling interval, but no deadline or budget is stated as a requirement and only AVERAGE latency is reported (no miss rate, percentile or bound; lower variance is claimed without percentiles) - hence E1 under the average-latency rule; maintainer may prefer E2 or include. Abstract numbers not found in body tables as summarised to me: 7x less bandwidth (tables show 2.9-3.3x), 5.4x faster than cloud (tables 3.62x, 5.48x, 14.56x - 5.48x is the homogeneous case), 43.9% accuracy gain over edge-only (tables show about 19-27 points). Single-edge and heterogeneous tests use Docker containers on a server, only the homogeneous test uses three real desktop-class edge nodes.

title: Sponge Examples: Energy-Latency Attacks on Neural Networks
evidence: "the system will need to be designed for worst-case performance, and if need be a fallback driving mechanism should be provided." (Sec. 7.2)
method: Sponge examples: inputs crafted by genetic algorithm (white-box or black-box on measured latency/energy) or L-BFGS to maximise inference energy and latency; proposes an untested worst-case cut-off defence.
evaluation: No stated deadline. Transformers and ImageNet CNNs on Xeon CPU, 1080 Ti GPU, 45nm ASIC simulator, Azure Translator; vs natural and random inputs. GPU time up to 26.5x, energy up to 30.6x; Azure 1 ms to 6 s.
contribution: Shows that crafted inputs can drive neural-network inference to its worst case, raising language-model latency and energy up to about 30x, and argues time-critical systems need worst-case design.
flag: timing is the contribution: yes for worst-case inference latency (adversarially induced), but partly for Pillar 4 scope - application framing is safety-relevant (autonomous-vehicle perception with tight latency constraints, fallback to driver) yet that is argument only. Check before including: (1) NOT edge - hardware is a server CPU, desktop GPU, a simulated ASIC and a cloud API, so condition 2 (edge/on-device inference) is met only by motivation; if the maintainer reads condition 2 strictly this is exclude-E1. (2) No deadline or budget is stated, so no latency/jitter cell. (3) The large effect is on NLP/translation models; on vision models (the ones relevant to edge perception) the increase is only about 1-3% ASIC energy. (4) The cut-off defence is proposed, not evaluated. (5) Body reports white-box up to about 35.6x ASIC energy and 43x time on WMT16 while abstract says up to 30x - check tables. I read characters 0-100000 of about 114500 (appendix tail not read). Abstract numbers 30x and 6000x on Azure were found in the body.

title: ApproxDet: Content and Contention-Aware Approximate Object Detection for Mobiles
evidence: "ApproxDet is the first system that accounts for the joint adaptation to video content and resource contention" (Sec. 1); scheduler picks the most accurate branch whose predicted latency is under the requirement.
method: Multi-branch Faster R-CNN plus tracker with five approximation knobs; learned latency and accuracy predictors and a contention sensor let a scheduler pick the most accurate branch meeting the latency requirement.
evaluation: Budgets 80-300 ms (95th percentile SLA) on Jetson TX2, ImageNet VID; vs FRCNN, FRCNN+MedianFlow, AdaScale, YOLOv3. Under 50% GPU contention violations within 5% vs 8-100%; +11.8% accuracy at 80 ms.
contribution: An adaptive video object detector for mobile GPUs that senses resource contention and content, then selects the most accurate configuration meeting a stated latency budget, holding 95th-percentile latency under contention.
flag: timing is the contribution: yes (accuracy traded against stated latency budgets, P95 latency and violation rate measured on real Jetson TX2 under contention); application not safety-relevant in the paper (generic video object detection). Check: latency SLA is soft and P95, not worst case; violation rates and P95 values are mostly read from figures 7-10, I only have the text figures quoted; budgets start at 80 ms, far above the 15 ms target of RQ1. Contention is mostly synthetic (one real background app, where ApproxDet shows a larger onset spike than the baseline). Abstract says 52% lower latency than YOLOv3, conclusion says 52.9% - minor inconsistency; 11.1% higher accuracy is consistent. non-generative inference cell is my reading (discriminative detector), drop if the cell is meant more narrowly.

title: Scheduling Real-time Deep Learning Services as Imprecise Computations
evidence: "we are the first to consider a deep neural network model that offers mandatory and optional parts." (Sec. I)
method: DNN requests as imprecise computations: mandatory early stages plus optional later stages with per-stage exits; stage-level EDF with a dynamic program assigning depths to maximise predicted confidence under deadlines, (1-eps) approximation.
evaluation: Relative deadlines 0.01-0.3 s (CIFAR-10), 0.01-0.8 s (ImageNet), 20 clients; 3-stage ResNet on i7-4770 plus TITAN X; vs EDF, LCF, round-robin, oracle. Accuracy +10-20%, near-zero misses, within 2% of oracle.
contribution: Schedules multi-exit neural network requests as imprecise computations, shedding the least useful optional stages so that nearly all deadlines are met while accuracy improves 10-20% over standard real-time schedulers.
flag: timing is the contribution: yes (deadline-constrained scheduling of anytime/early-exit DNN inference with a proved (1-eps) reward bound and deadline-miss results); application not safety-relevant (image classification service, IoT motivation). Check: hardware is a desktop with a TITAN X GPU, not edge hardware, so no edge-deployment cell; workload is synthetic clients with uniformly random deadlines. The exact accuracy and miss-rate values against EDF/LCF/RR are in figures 3-13 only - the text gives just 10-20% and large margin, and the abstract does not name the baseline for 10-20%; (nearly) no deadline misses should be verified in the figures. Stage worst-case times are a 99% confidence upper bound from profiling, not a hard WCET. Theorem 1 is a quantisation bound; the FPTAS claim goes a little beyond the proof shown. Scheduler overhead 0.5-6%.

title: Multi-Exit Semantic Segmentation Networks
evidence: Sec 6.1: 'we deploy MESS instances on a high-end (Nvidia GTX1080Ti; 250W TDP) and an edge (Nvidia Jetson AGX Xavier; 30W TDP)'; Eq 5-6 pose exit search as accuracy under a cost limit or cost under an accuracy limit.
method: Multi-exit segmentation: early-exit heads on a CNN backbone, image-level confidence exit policy, exit-aware pre-training, distillation and a search for exits under latency or accuracy constraints.
evaluation: COCO, VOC vs backbones, Layer Cascade, AutoDeepLab. No numeric deadline; budget is relative. DRN-50 39.96 to 17.92 ms (GTX 1080 Ti); MobileNetV2 67.04 to 40.97 ms (Jetson AGX Xavier).
contribution: Shows multi-exit segmentation networks searched under a latency or accuracy constraint cut mean latency about 2.2x at near-equal mIoU, with MobileNetV2 results measured on a Jetson AGX Xavier.
flag: timing is the contribution: partly; application not safety-relevant in the paper (generic segmentation). Accuracy is traded against a cost constraint in the search (Eq 5-6) and anytime and budgeted modes are defined, but no absolute deadline in ms is stated and only mean latency is reported - no tail, worst-case or miss rate. If the ruling needs a numeric budget this drops to exclude-E1. Only the MobileNetV2 rows are on the Jetson; ResNet-50 rows are desktop GPU. Abstract 2.83x latency gain not located in a table row from my reading. Latency/jitter cell withheld for lack of a stated budget.

title: CANS: Communication Limited Camera Network Self-Configuration for Intelligent Industrial Surveillance
evidence: Sec III: per-stream latency is bounded by L_i (constraint 2) with L_max set to 80 ms in Sec IV; Abstract: 'achieves low end-to-end latency (13 ms on average) with high accuracy (92% on average)'.
method: Heuristic that picks each camera stream's resolution and detector CNN under a shared bandwidth limit and per-stream latency bound, reconfiguring when bandwidth shifts by over 10%.
evaluation: MOT20, SSD detectors, simulated. Budget L_max 80 ms, 20-100 Mbps. CANS 13 ms mean and 92% F1 vs delay-chronic 33 ms and 48%, accuracy-optimal about 95%. Profiling on Jetson Xavier NX.
contribution: Configures resolution and detector model per camera stream under a shared bandwidth limit and an 80 ms latency bound, reaching 13 ms mean latency at 92% accuracy in simulation.
flag: timing is the contribution: partly (joint latency-accuracy objective with a hard per-stream latency bound; bandwidth allocation is the framing); application is industrial surveillance, weakly safety-relevant. Check: system-level results are simulated, only detector profiling ran on the Jetson Xavier NX, so no edge-deployment cell. Latency is mean only - no tail, jitter or miss rate - and the 13 ms figure sits far below the 80 ms bound, so the bound may never bind. Accuracy is F1 against the most expensive configuration, not ground truth. Baselines are the authors' own strawmen. Weak include; a maintainer wanting tail or miss evidence should exclude-E1.

title: Fluid Batching: Exit-Aware Preemptive Serving of Early-Exit Neural Networks on Edge NPUs
evidence: Sec III-B: 'We introduce an SLO-aware preemption criterion that aims to minimise SLO violations.'
method: NPU with per-layer fluid batching and stackable processing elements, plus a scheduler that preempts batches only at early-exit points when estimated overhead fits the remaining SLO slack.
evaluation: 4-exit ResNet-50 and Inception-v3, Poisson arrivals, on Xilinx ZC706 and ZCU104. p99 SLO 400 and 200 ms. Vs LazyBatching: 1.43-2.5x lower mean latency, 13.2 and 27.1 points fewer SLO violations.
contribution: Serves early-exit networks on an edge NPU with exit-aware preemptive batching, cutting mean latency 1.43-2.5x and tail-latency SLO violations by 13-27 points against LazyBatching on FPGA boards.
flag: timing is the contribution: yes (p99 tail-latency SLOs and violation rates are the measured outcome); application not safety-relevant (generic image classification serving). Check: abstract headline numbers (1.97x average latency, 6.7x SLO satisfaction) could not be traced to body values in my reading - the body gives a 1.89x geometric mean vs LazyBatching; most latency values are in figures only. The NPU is an FPGA prototype (Z7045, ZU7EV) measured with hardware counters, not a commercial NPU. The SLO values used for the LazyBatching comparison were in a table I could not read cleanly. Scheduler preempts inference batches, not actions, so interceptor is no.

title: PerfSAGE: Generalized Inference Performance Predictor for Arbitrary Deep Learning Models on Edge Devices
evidence: Abstract: 'predicts inference latency, energy, and memory footprint on an arbitrary DNN TFlite graph'; Sec 3.4: 'All the measurements that we have taken are average results from several inference runs'.
method: Graph neural network over a TFLite operator graph with per-operator-type weights that predicts mean latency, energy and memory of arbitrary networks on edge CPU, NPU and TPU targets.
evaluation: EdgeDLPerf, 134,912 models, vs Eagle and nn-Meter. No deadline. MAPE under 4.73% specialised, under 5.90% generalised; Eagle 15-97%. Cortex-A57 (TX2), Coral Edge TPU measured; Ethos-U via Vela simulator.
contribution: Predicts mean inference latency, energy and memory of arbitrary TFLite networks on edge CPU, NPU and TPU with a graph neural network, at under 6% mean absolute percentage error.
flag: timing is the contribution: yes in the sense that predicting inference latency is the paper (alongside energy and memory); application not safety-relevant. BORDERLINE, same call as MAPLE-Edge: mean latency only, batch size one, no deadline, budget, bound, tail or jitter; the only quantitative result is MAPE, which is not one of the result types in the evaluation floor, hence E2 (E1 equally defensible). If mean-latency predictors are in scope, flip to include with d. Abstract says under 5% MAPE across all targets, but Table 6 generalised model reaches 5.847%, 6.390%, 5.115% on KWS and 5.901% on ViT energy. Paper is inconsistent on whether NPU figures are simulated (Vela) or measured, and names both Ethos-U and Ethos-N. Models have random untrained weights.

title: Utility-Aware Load Shedding for Real-time Video Analytics at the Edge
evidence: "The objective of the control loop is to keep the end-to-end latency under a query-specific bound." (Sec. I, contribution 2)
method: Load shedder ahead of a DNN video-analytics backend drops low-utility frames; utility learned from HSV colour features; control loop sets drop rate and queue size to hold an end-to-end latency bound.
evaluation: VisualRoad/CARLA videos at 10 fps; bound is query-specific, value only in figures; Azure NC6 (Tesla K80) backend with efficientdet-d4, Jetson TX1 camera side (<35 ms median overhead); one latency violation in stress scenario; QoR vs random shedding.
contribution: A utility-aware load shedder that drops low-value video frames before DNN analytics so that end-to-end latency stays under a per-query bound while preserving quality of result.
flag: timing is the contribution: partly - the control loop exists to hold a latency bound, but the headline results are QoR against drop rate; application (camera object queries) not safety-relevant. Check: the numeric latency bound and latency traces are only in figures I could not read (text says "one latency violation" and "always less than the required end-to-end latency"); the timing result has no baseline of its own - the random-shedding baseline is compared on QoR, so the evaluation floor is met only weakly and E2 is arguable. The learned part of the shedder is a colour-histogram utility function, not a neural network; the DNN (efficientdet-d4) is the backend on a cloud VM, and only overhead was measured on the Jetson TX1, so I did not claim the edge deployment cell. Runtime interceptor is yes only in the sense of dropping frames, not vetoing an action.

title: A3D: Adaptive, Accurate, and Autonomous Navigation for Edge-Assisted Drones
evidence: "We should emphasize that optimizing QoN does not imply minimizing the end-to-end latency directly" (Sec. III-A)
method: A2C scheduler picks input resolution, local or edge execution and JPEG compression per decision for a DroNet navigation model with SPP; network-aware edge CPU allocation across drones.
evaluation: No latency deadline; SLO is steering error threshold. PX4 Vision drone (UP core) plus Xeon edge; AirSim with Jetson Nano. Local 588-709 ms; latency -28.06% vs Dynamic; QoN +4-12%, up to +21.97%; scheduler 4.35-6.35 ms.
contribution: An edge-assisted drone navigation framework whose learned scheduler adapts resolution, offloading and compression to network conditions to keep steering decisions within an error threshold.
flag: timing is the contribution: partly - latency is a hidden factor behind a decision-quality metric (QoN), not a constraint; the paper says it does not optimise latency directly and states no deadline, budget, bound or tail figure; application (drone navigation) is safety-relevant. BORDERLINE: Sec. II-B and III-A do study how latency degrades the steering decision (yaw-off at 0.9 s, QoN vs latency), which the scope ruling lists; if the maintainer counts that as the contribution this becomes include with criteria d, though the only timing results are average-latency reductions. Check: Sec. III-A gives QoN 80.7% at 0.5 s but Fig. 6 reportedly shows 86.7%. Edge hardware is real (prototype drone, Jetson Nano in the simulation loop).

title: Learning for Semantic Knowledge Base-Guided Online Feature Transmission in Dynamic Channels
evidence: "The semantic loss optimization is subject to a constraint on the average transmission latency" (Sec. III)
method: Soft actor-critic policy chooses online which of four feature levels (visual, intermediate, semantic, class label) a device transmits to a receiver, minimising semantic loss under an average latency threshold.
evaluation: Simulation only (AwA dataset, PC with TITAN RTX); budget tau = 3 ms default, swept 3-28 ms; vs loss-first and latency-first greedy; DRL latency stays below tau with higher accuracy; values only in Fig. 3.
contribution: A reinforcement-learning policy that selects which level of learned feature to transmit over a varying channel so that device-edge classification accuracy is maximised under an average transmission-latency budget.
flag: timing is the contribution: partly - accuracy is traded against a stated latency budget, but the budget is a long-run AVERAGE transmission latency, not a per-inference deadline, and there is no tail or miss-rate analysis; application (zero-shot image classification) not safety-relevant. Check: every result is in Fig. 3 and I could not read a single number, the text gives trends only; the fetched text appeared to skip part of Sec. IV, so the method description relies on what was returned; simulation only, latency is a modelled transmission delay; baselines are two greedy heuristics. If average-latency constraints do not count as a budget under the scope ruling, this is exclude-E1.

title: PAAM: A Framework for Coordinated and Priority-Driven Accelerator Management in ROS 2
evidence: "The goal of the proposed framework is to provide predictable and analyzable real-time support for accelerators" (Sec. I)
method: ROS 2 accelerator server executor: callbacks request GPU/TPU through priority buckets mapped to CUDA stream priorities, with a chain response-time bound extending the PiCAS analysis.
evaluation: Jetson AGX Xavier and Coral Edge TPU; periods 100-360 ms, no numeric deadlines; vs ROS 2 default and PiCAS; hot path 510/163/79 ms; critical chain 917 to 83 ms; overhead 198-391 us; preemption delay max 129 us.
contribution: A ROS 2 framework that manages GPU and TPU access by chain priority and provides an analysable end-to-end response-time bound for accelerator-using callback chains.
flag: timing is the contribution: yes - worst-case response-time bound and observed maxima are the results; application (Autoware reference system) is safety-relevant. BORDERLINE on the learned-model condition: accelerator workloads are synthetic 10 ms GPU segments and kernel benchmarks (MatMul, Reduction, VectorAdd, Histogram); the only inference is an unnamed TPU inference workload on one callback in Case Study 2, and no DNN is named or evaluated. I read this as timing work with no learned model in it; if the maintainer accepts accelerator scheduling as inference timing by proxy it would be include with criteria d and cells latency/jitter aware;edge deployment. Check: deadlines are assumed constrained (D <= T) but none is stated numerically; no deadline-miss counts; Case Study 1 values are only in figures.

title: Optimization of Layer Skipping and Frequency Scaling for Convolutional Neural Networks under Latency Constraint
evidence: "We propose an approach involving Proportional Layer Skipping (PLS) and Frequency Scaling (FS)." (Abstract)
method: Skips a fixed proportion of layers per ResNet group without retraining, then selects the DVFS frequency meeting a latency bound d_max while minimising energy-delay product.
evaluation: Budget symbolic only (d_max, no value). Jetson Orin, ResNet-152, CIFAR-10. GPU about 13 ms full vs 4.5 ms at 20% layers (612 MHz); accuracy 87.64% to 55.65%; energy 35 to 11 mJ per frame. Baseline: full model.
contribution: Combines proportional layer skipping with processor frequency scaling to trade CNN accuracy and energy against a latency bound on a Jetson Orin, cutting GPU energy per frame by up to 69%.
flag: timing is the contribution: partly (the optimisation is formulated under a latency constraint tau(f) <= d_max, but no numeric deadline is ever set and no constraint satisfaction, miss rate or tail latency is reported; results are accuracy, parameters, energy and a few mean inference times); application safety-relevant: no. Recommend E2 because the evaluation floor (latency against a stated budget) is not met; if the maintainer reads it as plain speed/energy/accuracy reporting, E1 fits equally. No CPU latency values given; no comparison with SkipNet, BranchyNet or other dynamic-inference methods. Latency figures are approximate values described from plots.

title: LA-IMR: Latency-Aware, Predictive In-Memory Routing and Proactive Autoscaling for Tail-Latency-Sensitive Cloud Robotics
evidence: "LA-IMR is an event-driven, in-memory controller that predicts imminent P99 breaches" (Sec. I, contribution 2)
method: Closed-form latency model (utilisation power law, network RTT, M/M/c queueing) drives per-request routing or offload to a faster tier and proactive replica scaling via a custom Kubernetes HPA metric.
evaluation: Budget 1.8 s (2.25 x 0.8 s inference). 32 Raspberry Pi 4B Kubernetes cluster plus cloud; YOLOv5m. P99 1.989-5.435 s vs 2.012-6.855 s for latency-based autoscaler at 1-6 req/s (up to 20.7% lower).
contribution: LA-IMR predicts tail-latency breaches for robot vision inference and reroutes or scales before they occur, cutting P99 latency by up to 20.7% against a reactive latency-based autoscaler on a Raspberry Pi edge cluster.
flag: timing is the contribution: yes (P99 tail latency of model serving against a stated latency budget); application safety-relevant: partly (cloud-robotics perception; no safety outcome measured). Doubts: reported P99 exceeds the 1.8 s budget at every load for both systems (1.989 s at 1 req/s), so the SLO is not met and no breach or miss rate is given; budget is seconds-scale, far from RQ1's 15 ms. P95 is slightly worse than baseline at 2 and 4 req/s, contradicting the text's 'lower or equal' claim, and the text's 14% P95 figure does not match the table (16.4%). Single baseline; no measured CPU-HPA comparison and no ablation of routing vs scaling. 'Millisecond-scale' decision claims are not measured. Offloading a request is routing, not an action veto, hence runtime_interceptor no. Preprint, not peer reviewed as far as the arXiv copy shows.

title: Black-Box Edge AI Model Selection with Conformal Latency and Accuracy Guarantees
evidence: "must be completed before the end of the frame" (Sec. II System Model); deadline-violation probability is bounded by beta via conformal calibration (Props. 1-2).
method: Conformal risk control picks a WebP encoder plus EfficientNetV2 classifier pair, fixed or re-selected per uplink rate, so expected loss stays under alpha and deadline-violation probability under beta.
evaluation: ImageNet val, Rayleigh uplink simulation; deadline T=150 ms, alpha=beta=0.01; Small/Large fixed baselines; Large exceeds beta, proposed meets it except very low SNR. Hardware none: compute times assumed 24-98 ms.
contribution: Calibrates black-box encoder and classifier selection at an edge server so that prediction-set loss and the probability of missing a 150 ms frame deadline are both bounded distribution-free.
flag: timing is the contribution: yes; application not safety-relevant (ImageNet classification). Check: all timing is simulated - classifier times are constants taken from the EfficientNetV2 paper, channel is a Rayleigh model, no hardware; violation rates are only plotted, no numeric values in text; guarantee fails at very low SNR where no pair meets the deadline. Maintainer to judge if a proved bound plus simulated violation curves meets the evaluation floor.

title: Rethink 3D Object Detection from Physical World
evidence: "we measure how accurate the detection is at the moment the inference is completed" (Sec. 3.1 Latency-aware Average Precision).
method: Latency-aware AP extrapolates ground truth forward by measured inference time; planning-aware AP weights planner-relevant errors; latency-aware hyperparameter search (L-HPO) over CenterPoint maximises L-mAP.
evaluation: nuScenes val and nuPlan closed loop; no deadline stated; RTX 3090 and 4060 Ti; L-HPO 45 ms, L-mAP 55.1 vs CenterPoint 80 ms, 46.7; injected 500 ms latency cuts nuPlan score 0.9277 to 0.8978.
contribution: Shows that 3D detectors ranked by standard mAP reorder once inference latency is charged against accuracy, and quantifies how injected perception latency degrades closed-loop planning on nuPlan.
flag: timing is the contribution: partly (latency-aware metric and a latency-degradation study; half the paper is the planning-aware metric); application safety-relevant (autonomous driving perception). Check: NO deadline, budget, bound or tail analysis is stated - only mean latency folded into a metric - so it rests solely on the 'study of how latency degrades a time-critical decision' clause; borderline with exclude-E1. Hardware is desktop GPUs, not edge; the only budget in the paper is monetary (USD 60k for 10 systems); nuPlan latency is injected, not measured.

title: DeDelayed: Deleting Remote Inference Delay via On-Device Correction
evidence: "The remote model provides accurate outputs, and yet delivers them with delay." (Sec. 4 Method); remote model is conditioned on the delay and predicts features for arrival time.
method: Split video segmentation: delay-conditioned remote video model sends predicted future features that a light local model fuses with the current frame; falls back to local-only if features are stale or missing.
evaluation: BDD100K 30 fps, pseudo-labels; simulated delays 0-167 ms; 33 ms per-frame budget; local, remote image/video/predictive baselines; at 167 ms mIoU 0.641 vs local 0.588, remote 0.596; local 9.3 ms M3 Pro CPU, remote 24.4 ms H100.
contribution: Compensates round-trip delay in device-edge split inference by having the remote model predict features for the moment they arrive, keeping segmentation accuracy nearly flat up to 167 ms of delay.
flag: timing is the contribution: yes (how network delay degrades remote inference and how to cancel it); application safety-relevant only by motivation (driving video segmentation, no control loop). Check: delays are known, fixed and simulated - no real wireless link, no jitter or tail measurement despite the high-tail motivation; no explicit deadline beyond the 33 ms frame budget, so the latency/jitter cell is generous; local device is an Apple M3 Pro laptop CPU, not edge hardware, hence no edge cell; labels are pseudo-labels from other models. Abstract's 9.8 mIoU gain over remote at 100 ms is only in a figure; Sec. 7 text says 6.7 points over local at 5 frames but Table 3 gives about 5.3. Non-generative cell: predicts latent features, not pixels - drop if you read the cell more narrowly.

title: SLICE: SLO-Driven Scheduling for LLM Inference on Edge Computing Devices
evidence: "the duration of each cycle strictly limited to within 1000 milliseconds" (Sec. IV-D Rate Allocation); real-time tasks carry a 1.5 s deadline and at least 20 tokens/s.
method: SLICE: utility-rate greedy task selection plus a decode-mask matrix that gives each LLM task a per-cycle token rate matching its TPOT SLO; online rescheduling on arrival and completion.
evaluation: ChatGLM2-6B-INT4 on RTX 4060 Ti, Poisson arrivals; SLOs TPOT 100/120/250 ms, 1.5 s deadline; vs Orca, FastServe; SLO attainment 83.33% vs 31.25%; real-time 85.29% vs about 26%.
contribution: Schedules concurrent LLM decoding on one edge GPU so each task receives the token rate its SLO needs, raising deadline and SLO attainment for real-time tasks about threefold over Orca and FastServe.
flag: timing is the contribution: yes (SLO- and deadline-driven scheduling of LLM inference); application not safety-relevant as evaluated (robot and vehicle control only as motivation, synthetic Poisson workloads). Check: 'edge' hardware is a desktop RTX 4060 Ti with a Xeon host, so no edge cell; about 15% of real-time tasks still miss their SLO; TTFT SLO has no numeric value; non-real-time attainment 78.15% in text vs 78.5% in caption; deadline-miss rate is my inversion of the attainment figure, not reported directly. Scheduler defers and preempts tasks but not actions, so interceptor is no.

title: Uncertainty Makes It Stable: Curiosity-Driven Quantized Mixture-of-Experts
evidence: Sec. 6 Discussion: "the primary value lies in stability, not raw accuracy"; Abstract: "curiosity-driven routing reduces MoE latency variance by 82% (p=0.008, Levene's test)"
method: Quantised mixture-of-experts (BitNet ternary, 1-16 bit BitLinear, 8-bit PTQ experts) with an MC-dropout uncertainty router; a KL curiosity term reweights routing to stabilise inference latency.
evaluation: ESC-50, Quinn, UrbanSound8K audio; 5-fold CV; Apple M3 Max CPU. No deadline. Latency std 230 ms uniform MoE vs 29 ms curiosity (means 1335 vs 1278 ms); Levene variance cut 82%; F1 0.83-0.85.
contribution: Shows that uncertainty-driven routing across quantised experts cuts the run-to-run latency spread of audio classification from 230 ms to 29 ms std at roughly equal F1, on a laptop-class CPU.
flag: timing is the contribution: partly (latency variance/stability is the headline claim, alongside accuracy and energy); application (environmental sound classification) not safety-relevant. BORDERLINE on the evaluation floor: no deadline or budget is stated (only a '<1200 ms latency-critical' category in recommendations), no p99 or worst-case, jitter is run-to-run std only, tested with Levene's test against uniform-routing MoE and single-model baselines. Hardware is an Apple M3 Max CPU (36 GB), not an edge device, despite the edge framing; latencies are ~1.1-1.3 s per inference. Inconsistencies: abstract ties the 82% variance reduction to the 230->29 ms change, but 82% (p=0.008) belongs to a different model variant and 230->29 ms std is ~87% as std; text claims 4-bit saves 41% energy vs 8-bit while Table 2 implies ~29%. Curiosity strength value not given. If the maintainer requires a stated deadline, this becomes exclude-E2.

title: HiDVFS: Hierarchical Multi-Agent DVFS for Real-Time OpenMP DAG Workloads
evidence: Sec 4.8 (Feasibility gate and safety shield): the action "executes only if" the conformal upper bound on response time is within the deadline; "On rejection the runtime falls back to a safe action, the performance governor or a reserved core."
method: Hierarchical multi-agent RL (D3QN) for DVFS and core allocation of OpenMP DAG workloads, with a schedulability gate and a conformal response-time/temperature shield that substitutes a safe action.
evaluation: Jetson TX2, Orin NX, RubikPi; BOTS/PolyBench; baselines zTT, GearDVFS, DynaQ, PlanGAN, SARB, MAMB, MAMF. Makespan 4.16 s vs 11.79 s, energy -32.9%; shield PICP 89.3-98.2%; 2 ms decision cycle.
contribution: Hierarchical multi-agent RL frequency scaling for real-time OpenMP DAG workloads on Jetson boards, with a conformal response-time shield that is calibrated offline but not evaluated in closed loop.
flag: neither. The shield is a genuine runtime veto with fallback, but it is a minor component: headline claims are makespan, speedup and energy; no ablation removes the shield, no veto or intervention rate is reported, and the conclusion lists "closed-loop evaluation of the shield under the learned policy" as future work. Only shield evidence is offline calibration coverage (Table 7), described by the authors as "a calibrated empirical prediction interval, not a hard guarantee". "Multi-agent" here means several cooperating RL agents controlling one board, not hazards among agents, so (c) does not apply. If the maintainer judged the shield central it would still fail the evaluation floor (E2). Read characters 0-100000 of about 149000; the unread remainder is presumably appendix and was not checked.

title: Pareto-Optimal Model Selection for Low-Cost, Single-Lead EMG Control in Embedded Systems
evidence: Abstract: "balancing classification accuracy with strict latency (<100ms) and memory (<320KB) constraints"; Sec. 4.4: "ResNet50: Rejected. Inference time (> 100ms) exceeds human perception limits [12]."
method: Benchmarks 18 classifiers (heuristics, classical ML, 1D CNN, CRNN, transfer learning, ensemble) for 3-class single-lead EMG on an ESP32, filtering by a 100 ms latency and 320 KB memory limit.
evaluation: One subject, ~1300 one-second windows, test N=268. Budget 100 ms, 320 KB (ESP32 NodeMCU-32S). Random Forest 74.25% at 0.01 ms; 1D CNN 78.36% at 0.83 ms; MaxCRNN 83.21% at 0.15 ms on A100. No tail latency.
contribution: A single-subject comparison of 18 EMG gesture classifiers that picks a Random Forest as the Pareto choice for an ESP32 under 100 ms latency and 320 KB memory limits.
flag: timing is the contribution: partly at best (a stated <100 ms budget is used as a static pass/fail filter in a model-selection table; no adaptive, anytime or deadline-aware mechanism); application (prosthetic/assistive EMG control) only weakly safety-relevant. BORDERLINE against the 'accuracy traded against a stated latency budget' clause - I recommend exclude because the timing evidence does not hold up: it is unclear which latencies were measured on the ESP32 (0.01 ms for a Random Forest is implausible on a 240 MHz MCU; MaxCRNN was timed on an A100 GPU and its ESP32 figure of >500 ms is an estimate), ResNet50 is '>100 ms' in Table 2 but 15.26 ms in App. D.12, and the budget rejects only one model. Other inconsistencies: MaxCRNN called highest at 83.21% while a CRNN baseline reports 86.94%; '1000x' latency reduction only holds against the estimated figure. The 100 ms budget is justified by a mouse-interaction perception reference. Single subject (the author), no on-device closed-loop test. If the maintainer reads the clause literally this could be include; if so do NOT tick edge deployment without confirming on-device measurement.

title: Hierarchical Online-Scheduling for Energy-Efficient Split Inference with Progressive Transmission
evidence: Sec. III-C: "The transmission process for device n is terminated if the uncertainty condition Hth is met"; Sec. IV-B.3: "achieves a remarkable 43.12% accuracy gain over benchmarks at the stringent 100 ms deadline"
method: ENACHI: Lyapunov two-tier scheduler for device-edge split inference; per frame picks split point, bandwidth and power, per 1 ms slot adapts power; progressive feature transmission stops on low entropy or at the deadline.
evaluation: Simulation only: ResNet-50/ImageNet, multi-user FDMA, hard deadline swept 100-500 ms, 0.25 J energy budget. Baselines EFFECT-DNN, SC-CAO, fixed-split, edge-only, device-only. Accuracy ~72.5% at 100 ms, 80.1% at 300 ms; energy up to 62% lower.
contribution: An online scheduler for split device-edge inference that trades accuracy against a hard per-task deadline by progressively sending features until uncertainty is low or time runs out, under a long-term energy budget.
flag: timing is the contribution: yes (deadline-constrained split inference with accuracy explicitly traded against a 100-500 ms hard deadline over a fading wireless uplink); application not safety-relevant (ImageNet classification). Check: everything is simulated - no real device, edge server or radio (2 GHz device CPU, 20 GHz edge, FDMA channel model), and the accuracy-vs-transmitted-ratio curve is a fitted surrogate validated at four split layers, so accuracy figures are model-derived. The deadline is not an explicit constraint in problem P1; it is met by construction (transmission window = T minus compute time, forced termination at the batch deadline), so there is no deadline-miss rate - baselines are instead reported as infeasible (fixed-split and device-only below 275 ms; edge-only below 2.5 MHz). The evaluation floor is met via accuracy and energy against the stated deadline versus five baselines. The stop-on-low-entropy rule ends transmission early; it is an early-exit, not a safety veto, hence runtime_interceptor no. Gains (43.12% accuracy at 100 ms, 62.13% energy) are best-case points versus the weakest baseline. No latency distribution or jitter figures.

title: Motion-to-Response Content Generation via Multi-Agent AI System with Real-Time Safety Verification
evidence: Sec 3.5.2: if verification fails, "the Filtering Unit triggers content regeneration with adjusted constraints", repeated "until verification passes or a maximum iteration count is reached"; Algorithm 1 then outputs "default safe content".
method: Four-stage pipeline (emotion recognition, response policy, content parameter generation, safety verification) from speech; a rule-based verifier gates each output and forces regeneration or a default safe output.
evaluation: IEMOCAP, RAVDESS, AIHub, synthetic TTS; internal ablations only. Safety 100% vs 87.3% without the safety agent; regeneration 1.6%; latency 12.3 ms GPU, 89.7 ms mean and 112.5 ms P99 on Raspberry Pi 4.
contribution: A speech-emotion-to-response pipeline whose rule-based output verifier forces regeneration of unsafe content parameters, raising rule compliance from 87.3% to 100% at about 90 ms on a Raspberry Pi 4.
flag: Pillar 1 route considered, but this is a single-output rule filter on one generated content-parameter vector: the "multi-agent system" is a fixed four-module pipeline, with no hazard among agents, no sequential decision and no handoff, so E4. If the maintainer treats the reported latency table as a latency aspect it becomes a weak (a) candidate, but the safety result is near-tautological: 100% compliance is measured after the filter against the filter's own rules; thresholds, the iteration cap K and the fallback rate are not reported. No external baseline. "Formal guarantees" are claimed (Sec 5.1) without proof. Title says motion-to-response but the input is audio. "Real-time on all platforms" (<100 ms) fails at P99 on Raspberry Pi 4 (112.5 ms). No human takeover.

title: Self-Supervised Path Planning in Unstructured Environments via Global-Guided Differentiable Hard Constraint Projection
evidence: Abstract: "deployment verification on an NVIDIA Jetson Orin NX confirms an inference latency of 94 ms, showing real-time feasibility"; Sec. 3.2.3: "Enforcing a strict iteration cap guarantees deterministic worst-case execution time."
method: MLP path planner trained self-supervised from a global-guided potential field, with a differentiable Newton-Raphson projection layer (capped iterations) that pushes output waypoints onto collision, curvature and spacing constraints.
evaluation: Random 40x20 m obstacle maps, CARLA closed loop; baselines Hybrid A*, Informed RRT*, NMPC, IL, soft-penalty. Success 88.75% vs soft 55.22%, Hybrid A* 98.80%. Jetson Orin NX mean 94 ms (43/94/136 ms at 20/50/100 iterations); no deadline.
contribution: A self-supervised neural path planner whose differentiable projection layer enforces collision and curvature constraints on its own output, reaching 88.75% success at 94 ms on a Jetson Orin NX.
flag: timing is the contribution: no (a planning-method paper that reports mean inference time; no stated deadline or control-cycle budget, no p99 or measured worst case); application is safety-relevant (autonomous driving in unstructured terrain). The claim that the iteration cap 'guarantees deterministic worst-case execution time' is asserted, not measured; the iteration-cap ablation (87.01/88.75/89.58/89.84% success at 20/50/80/100 iterations vs 43/94/-/136 ms) is an accuracy-latency trade but against no budget. Inconsistency: Table 5 lists 0.2079 s for the same method that is 0.0939 s elsewhere. The authors call the projection a 'runtime assurance mechanism', but it is a layer inside the planner trained end to end (a constraint inside a planner), cannot halt or defer, and still fails ~11% of scenarios, so I set runtime_interceptor no and (a) not met - maintainer may disagree. Single ego vehicle, no multi-agent. Jetson timing is real hardware but the vehicle is simulated (CARLA); traditional baselines were timed on an i9, so timing comparison is cross-hardware. No collision or violation rate reported separately; 'AFD' column is undefined. Hybrid A* beats it on success rate.

title: Hardware Co-Design Scaling Laws via Roofline Modelling for On-Device LLMs
evidence: "Our approach reduces architecture selection from months to days." (Abstract); Table 2 lists latency targets, e.g. Embodied AI <20 ms decode, Autonomous Driving <100 ms total.
method: Design-time co-design law: a fitted loss scaling law plus roofline latency estimates maps accuracy-latency Pareto frontiers for on-device LLM architectures; no runtime mechanism.
evaluation: Jetson Orin, vLLM; 1,942 architectures modelled, 170 trained; budgets per Table 2 (20 ms to 2 s); vs latency-matched Qwen2.5-0.5B: perplexity 50.88 vs 63.14; no ms figures reported.
contribution: A hardware co-design scaling law that combines a fitted loss law with roofline latency modelling to pick on-device LLM architectures on Jetson Orin, giving 19.42% lower perplexity than Qwen2.5-0.5B at matched latency.
flag: timing is the contribution: partly (accuracy is traded against latency targets, but at design time via architecture search); application safety-relevant: no. Recommended E2 because I found no quantitative timing result: no absolute latency in ms for the co-designed model or the baseline, and the roofline-vs-measured claim ('strong correlation', Sec. 4.2.1, Appendix D) has no error or correlation figure; the only hard result is perplexity at 'matched latency'. Maintainer may prefer E1 or, if matched-latency perplexity is accepted as budgeted accuracy, include. Check figures for ms values I could not see in text. Internal inconsistencies: driving budget <100 ms (Table 2) vs sub-50 ms (Sec. 5.3); fit split 120/17 vs 138/32; no tail, jitter or worst-case analysis; paper admits 10-20% deviation from roofline.

title: EdgeNav-QE: QLoRA Quantization and Dynamic Early Exit for LAM-based Navigation on Edge Devices
evidence: "This substantial latency reduction is directly attributable to the Dynamic Early Exit (DEE) mechanism" (Sec. 4.2.4)
method: 4-bit QLoRA of OpenVLA-7B plus entropy-thresholded early-exit heads at layers 6, 12 and 18 for object-goal navigation; exit is confidence-driven, not deadline-driven.
evaluation: Habitat-Sim/Matterport3D ObjectNav; emulated Jetson Orin AGX; <=100 ms target mentioned (Sec. 4.2); 78 ms vs 450 (FP16), 95 (DeeR-VLA), 120 (static QLoRA); SR 81.8% vs 84.1%; means only.
contribution: EdgeNav-QE combines 4-bit QLoRA with entropy-based early exit on OpenVLA-7B for simulated navigation, reporting 78 ms mean latency against 450 ms for the FP16 baseline at 81.8% success.
flag: timing is the contribution: partly; application safety-relevant: weakly (robot navigation, no collision or safety metric). Borderline: it is early-exit inference and a <=100 ms target is mentioned, but the exit rule is an entropy threshold not tied to any budget or deadline, the target is not enforced, and only mean latency is given (no tail or jitter), so it reads as compression reported as speed and accuracy. If the maintainer counts the 100 ms target as a stated budget, it would meet the floor (78 ms vs 5 baselines). Doubts: Sec. 4.1.2 says Jetson Orin AGX constraints were 'emulated', so latency may not be real-device; many internal inconsistencies (FP16 memory 28 GB vs 16.2 GB; 'DEE 58.3% improvement' vs about 35% from Table 4; episode counts 1,000/5,000/500; 'all p<0.001' vs p=0.08; '8 GB edge' vs 32 GB device). Under load latency rises to 89 ms.

title: How Fast Can I Run My VLA? Demystifying VLA Inference Performance with VLA-Perf
evidence: Sec. 4.2/4.11 test which hardware and placements reach the paper's 10 Hz (acceptable) and 100 Hz (high-performance) control targets; Takeaway 9 (Sec. 4.7): "Server-side inference, even with only consumer GPUs, significantly outperforms on-device".
method: VLA-Perf: analytical roofline model predicting vision-language-action inference latency and control frequency across GPUs, on-device/edge/cloud placement, network links, denoising steps, chunking and sync vs async.
evaluation: Budget 10 Hz/100 Hz; pi0 modelled: Jetson Thor 52.6 ms, RTX 4090 31.1 ms, B100 3.2 ms; 5G sync 35.9 Hz; validated on RTX 4090 only: roofline 14.7/22.5/30.4 ms vs real 20.0/27.3/36.8 ms.
contribution: VLA-Perf is an analytical model of VLA inference latency across hardware, placement and network links, showing which configurations reach 10 Hz or 100 Hz control and that Jetson Thor needs about 5x speed-up for 100 Hz.
flag: timing is the contribution: yes (analysis and prediction of inference timing against stated 10 Hz/100 Hz targets, including the wireless/network path); application safety-relevant: indirectly (robot control rate; no safety outcome studied). Check: nearly all numbers are roofline upper bounds computed from spec sheets, not measurements; the only validation is one external pi0 implementation on an RTX 4090, where real latency is 22-36% above the model (73-83% of roofline). No tail, percentile or jitter analysis; staleness under async inference left to future work. I listed 'latency/jitter aware' because latency is evaluated against a stated budget, but it is modelled not measured - maintainer may wish to drop the cell. No edge-deployment cell (Jetson Thor is modelled only). The effect of latency on task success is not studied. Minor: text says 73.3-82.6%, table shows 82.3%.

title: Low Latency GNN Accelerator for Quantum Error Correction
evidence: "allowing the decoder to reach the submicrosecond threshold with a latency of 988.8 ns" (Sec. V-F); syndrome rounds "can be as fast as 1 us" (Sec. I).
method: Pruned, fixed-point-quantised GNN decoder for surface-code syndromes in a three-stage pipelined VHDL FPGA design, with a max-latency variant (graphs capped at 30 nodes) and an average-latency variant.
evaluation: Deadline 1 us per syndrome round; Alveo U250 (Vivado synthesis/simulation); d=7 worst case 988.8 ns, average model 846 ns; vs MWPM 30.3 us CPU, GNN 291.4 us GPU; LER 1.47e-5 vs 1.69e-5.
contribution: A pruned, quantised GNN decoder for quantum error correction on an FPGA meets the 1 us syndrome-round deadline with a 988.8 ns worst case at distance 7 while beating MWPM logical error rate by 13%.
flag: timing is the contribution: yes (hard 1 us deadline, worst-case-bounded learned inference, accuracy traded for the bound via pruning, quantisation and graph-size capping); application safety-relevant: no (quantum error correction). Check scope fit: this is an FPGA beside a quantum computer, not an edge or mobile device in the usual sense - maintainer to rule whether it counts as 'on a device'. All latency and resource figures come from cycle counts times clock period in Vivado simulation/synthesis, no on-board measurement, so no edge-deployment cell. The worst-case bound holds only because graphs above 30 nodes are discarded (decoder assumes no error; cost included in LER). The average-latency variant has no stated worst case. Abstract '1 us average latency' is 846 ns in body; improvement figures vary (21%/43% Sec. V-B, 41% Sec. V-C, 40% abstract); hardware results only for d=7 though abstract says 'up to distance 7'. Baseline latencies are CPU/GPU software, not other FPGA decoders.

title: Policy-Aware Edge LLM-RAG Framework for Internet of Battlefield Things Mission Orchestration
evidence: "This additional validation layer ensures that generated actions satisfy operational policies before execution." (Sec. IV-G)
method: Edge-hosted LLM with policy retrieval (fuzzy plus Jaccard, top-3) emits JSON plans for simulated drones and UGVs; a JudgeLLM (same LLM, validation prompt) checks plans before and after dispatch.
evaluation: RoboDK simulation, 10 fixed commands, 4 quantised LLMs on a CPU-only Ryzen 7 7800X3D workstation; no baseline or ablation; no deadline; mean end-to-end latency 4.17 s (Gemma-2B) to 6.79 s (Qwen-2.5-7B).
contribution: A policy-retrieval LLM orchestrator with an LLM judge for simulated battlefield IoT assets, reporting 100% task success for Gemma-2B at 4.17 s mean latency on a CPU workstation, without baselines.
flag: timing is the contribution: no; application safety-relevant: yes (military mission orchestration, simulated). 'Low-latency' is claimed with no threshold, deadline, tail or jitter analysis; only mean latency in seconds, so it fails the Pillar 4 scope. Check: the JudgeLLM is a pre-execution gate that might read as criterion (a), but the paper never says what happens on a Failure verdict, the judge is the same LLM and also defines the success metric (circular), and there is no baseline or ablation and no violation or detection rate, so it would be E2 on that route too. Abstract claims 'significantly improves reliability' and 'effectively detects policy-violating commands' have no supporting comparison in the body. Hardware is a desktop workstation, not an edge device. Same paper as queued record doi:10.1109/ais69919.2026.11621620 (preprint of it) - merge.

title: A Delta-Aware Orchestration Framework for Scalable Multi-Agent Edge Computing
evidence: "Reducing orchestration below 10 ms creates the timing headroom that makes caching viable" (Sec. I); per-task deadline constraint L_i <= d_i in the problem formulation, deadline satisfaction reported in Tables V and VIII.
method: DAOEF: tiered candidate-node filtering, LSH feature-level delta caching and a TD3 cross-attention policy that places DNN inference tasks of many agents on heterogeneous edge nodes under per-task deadlines.
evaluation: Simulation 100-250 agents; testbed 20 Raspberry Pi 4B agents with Jetson AGX Orin/NUC/Coral/ZCU104 nodes; vs MADRL, MAPPO, QMIX; testbed 156 vs 285 ms, deadline satisfaction 94% vs 78%; 100 ms deadline in example only.
contribution: A delta-caching reinforcement-learning orchestrator that places multi-agent inference tasks on heterogeneous edge nodes, raising deadline satisfaction from 78% to 94% on a 20-agent hardware testbed.
flag: timing is the contribution: partly - the framing is scalability and mean latency/cost, deadlines are a constraint and a reported metric; application not safety-relevant (generic perception workloads). Check: deadline values are not clearly stated (100 ms appears only in a worked example, yet mean latencies of 156-445 ms give 94-96% satisfaction); no p99 or jitter; abstract claim of 62% reduction (280 vs 735 ms) does not match Table IX (378 vs 1520 ms at 200 agents); testbed called 20-device in abstract, 50-device in conclusion. Timed latency is task end-to-end plus 4.2-8.5 ms orchestrator decision time. Could reasonably be E1 if the maintainer reads it as average-latency minimisation.

title: Characterizing Vision-Language-Action Models across XPUs: Constraints and Acceleration for On-Robot Deployment
evidence: "Pairs below the frequency threshold are infeasible regardless of cost or power efficiency" (Sec. 3.2) - but no threshold is adopted in the body and no deadline, tail or jitter result is reported.
method: Characterisation of VLA models (pi0, pi0.5, OpenVLA, SmolVLA, Gr00t, Diffusion Policy, ACT) across GPUs and NPUs with a cost-energy-time leaderboard, plus two training-free accelerations: DP-Cache and V-AEFusion.
evaluation: Real RTX 4090, Jetson Thor, AGX Orin, Arc B60, Ascend 310P; LIBERO plus Franka and JAKA robots; pi0 102.3/246.0/920.6 ms on 4090/Thor/Orin; DP-Cache 1.89x, V-AEFusion 1.3x; no stated deadline.
contribution: A cross-hardware characterisation of vision-language-action models with two training-free accelerations, reporting mean latency, energy and task success on Jetson, Ascend and desktop GPUs.
flag: timing is the contribution: partly - latency is profiled and used as a feasibility screen, but only mean latency, Hz and speedups are reported, with no adopted control-rate budget, deadline-miss, p99 or jitter; application is robot manipulation, not framed as safety. Check: figures show 1-30 Hz thresholds that the reader could not find stated in the body text; the abstract 6x NPU speedup is DP-Cache plus compilation on Diffusion Policy (Table 6), not a VLA; Franka energy figures only in Figure 12. Read via automated PDF summary, figures not inspected.

title: Bench2Drive-Robust: Benchmarking Closed-Loop Autonomous Driving under Deployment Perturbations
evidence: "Inference latency exposes a strong synchronization failure mode. All methods degrade as delay increases" (Sec 4.2 Results, Latency vulnerability)
method: Closed-loop CARLA benchmark injecting camera-stream failures, ego-state noise and fixed compute-control delay (FIFO action buffer) around unchanged end-to-end driving policies.
evaluation: Bench2Drive 220 routes; TCP-traj, UniAD, VAD, SimLingo vs own clean baseline. No deadline stated; injected delay 100/200/500 ms; no hardware timing. SimLingo DS 85.94 to 28.45/19.47/15.70; avg latency RD 0.25-0.75.
contribution: Benchmark showing injected inference delay of 100-500 ms cuts closed-loop driving score of four end-to-end driving models by 25-75 percent on average, more than most sensor perturbations.
flag: timing is the contribution: partly (latency is one of three perturbation families; the others are camera and GPS/speed noise); application safety-relevant: yes (driving). Check: delay is injected in simulator ticks, not measured - no edge hardware, no deadline or budget, no tail analysis; qualifies only under the 'study of how latency degrades a time-critical decision' clause, so maintainer may prefer E1. No mitigation proposed. A real-time wall-clock latency mode is described but not used in results. The 198 ms in Fig 1 is illustrative only. Read main text and Table 3 in full; appendix skimmed.

title: Beyond aggregate scores: Deployment-aware and non-compensatory benchmarking of vision-based eye-state recognition models for driver monitoring
evidence: "batch-2 P95 latency no greater than 33.333 ms" (Sec. 4.4); "Strong performance elsewhere cannot compensate for a failed gate" (Sec. 3.3).
method: Benchmarking framework for eye-state classifiers in driver monitoring with separate evidence blocks and conjunctive pass/fail gates (numerical parity, P95 latency, safety screen) instead of one weighted score.
evaluation: Six ImageNet-pretrained classifiers on MRL Eye and RT-BENE; Jetson Nano TensorRT FP32 P95 pair latency 12.7-64.1 ms against a 33.333 ms deadline (two models pass); no model passes the safety screen.
contribution: A non-compensatory benchmark for driver-monitoring eye-state classifiers that gates models on a 33.3 ms P95 latency deadline on a Jetson Nano alongside robustness and transfer screens.
flag: timing is the contribution: partly - a stated 33.333 ms P95 deadline is a hard gate measured on a real Jetson Nano, but it is one of five evidence blocks in a paper about benchmarking methodology (robustness, domain transfer, explanation faithfulness); application safety-relevant (driver monitoring). Borderline: a maintainer who counts a hard P95 deadline gate as sufficient could include it, and it clears the evaluation floor (six models against the budget). Check: only the classifier engine is timed, not end-to-end cabin latency; no P99 or jitter; parity tolerance 1e-4 in Sec. 4.4 vs 5e-4 in Supplement S.3.4. All abstract numbers were found in the body.

title: RAMS: Resource-Adaptive and Detection-Conditioned Model Switching for Embedded Edge Perception
evidence: The problem is balancing "latency and detection quality under changing resource pressure" (Abstract); safety policies "prevent downgrade to the NANO tier within a short window after a VRU is observed" (Sec. III-D.4).
method: RAMS: a non-learned runtime controller that switches among three resident YOLOv8 tiers from a CPU/memory/thermal/battery pressure index, with hysteresis, EWMA prediction and a hold-up after vulnerable-road-user detections.
evaluation: KITTI on Raspberry Pi 5 and Jetson Orin (TensorRT FP16) under synthetic CPU stress; vs fixed tiers; heavy-load P95/P99 4.21/4.62 ms vs 4.71/6.12 ms threshold policy; no stated deadline.
contribution: A resource-pressure-driven controller that switches YOLOv8 model tiers on Raspberry Pi 5 and Jetson Orin, holding larger models after vulnerable-road-user detections to protect recall.
flag: timing is the contribution: partly - adaptive inference trades accuracy against latency and P95/P99 are reported under load, but there is no stated latency budget, deadline or fps target and no deadline-miss rate; application safety-relevant (VRU perception for driving). Borderline with include if tail-latency reporting against fixed-tier baselines is judged enough. Check, the paper has several internal inconsistencies: Sec. V-J says safety2 matches FIXED-MEDIUM recall at 24% lower latency but Table X shows 13.7 ms vs 9.1 ms (higher); 74% accuracy-retention figure does not match Sec. V-G (about 93%); Pi 5 idle pressure 0.46 in the intro vs 0.67 in Table II; most accuracy values are COCO mAP50 proxies, not measured on KITTI. The tier hold-up defers a model downgrade, not an action, so runtime_interceptor is no.

title: EagleVLA: Towards Onboard Real-Time Robot Control via Foresight-Aligned Asynchronous Inference
evidence: "We deploy the XR-1 model" on a Jetson Orin where the robot "executes actions at 15 Hz" (Sec. 5.3); Table 3 measures success as inference delay grows from 1 to 9 action steps.
method: EagleVLA: a 40M-parameter future correction module predicts the VLM features at t+delay so the action expert generates delay-aligned actions under asynchronous inference; confidence-gated VLM skipping; llama.cpp runtime optimisations.
evaluation: LIBERO with pi0.5 vs sync, RTC, VLASH: at delay 9 on Spatial 97.0 vs 88.8 vs 30.1; Jetson Orin reaction time 1420.8 to 144.3 ms (0.70 to 6.93 Hz), Thor 97.6 ms; real folding task 15 Hz.
contribution: A foresight-aligned asynchronous inference scheme that keeps a vision-language-action policy near synchronous success rates under nine-step inference delay and cuts Jetson Orin reaction time from 1421 to 144 ms.
flag: timing is the contribution: yes - compensating inference delay and a study of how delay degrades task success; application not framed as safety (manipulation, cloth folding). Check: no explicit latency budget beyond the 15 Hz execution rate, and the achieved policy rate on Orin (6.93 Hz) is below it; no jitter or tail latency; simulated delay uses an estimated action-expert latency, not measured; real-robot text says XR-1 while the rest uses pi0.5; Eq. 1 and Algorithm 1 threshold sign are garbled; text claims 14.8% over VLASH and 3.9% over RTC, Table 3 averages give about 14.4 and 3.5 points; real-robot results are 10 trials per subtask (Figure 7); the confidence gate only schedules VLM calls and cannot veto actions.

title: PRISA: Proactive Infrastructure LiDAR Framework for Intersection Safety Assessment
evidence: "PPET-based assessment operates at 194 ms end-to-end latency over a 2.4-second predictive horizon" (Abstract); no deadline or budget is quantified anywhere in the body.
method: Roadside LiDAR pipeline: PointPillars+AB3DMOT perception, self-labelled FlowChain trajectory prediction, then TTC/PPET surrogate safety metrics against thresholds to raise conflict alerts.
evaluation: R-LiViT and a Chattanooga field site; Jetson AGX Thor; single-value latency 21+143+30=194 ms; no stated deadline, tail or miss rate; ADE/FDE vs CV, CA, MID, Trajectron++.
contribution: An infrastructure-LiDAR framework that predicts road-user trajectories and scores intersection conflicts with TTC and PPET, running end to end in 194 ms on a Jetson AGX Thor.
flag: timing is the contribution: no; application is safety-relevant (intersection conflict alerts). Speed is merely reported: one 194 ms figure, no stated deadline or budget, no p99, no miss rate, no latency baseline. Alerts only, no veto. Note it could be argued under criterion (c) multi-vehicle hazard detection, but conflict counts have no ground truth or baseline (only ADE/FDE do), so it would fail the safety-metric floor. Table VI ablation values were garbled in my extraction; 24.1%/26.2% gaps are as stated.

title: MM-BEV: Enhancing Timeliness by Computing Where and When it Matters
evidence: "The 95th-percentile e2e latency shrinks from 1455 ms to 434 ms" (Sec VI-E End-to-End Pipeline Performance)
method: Splits BEV LiDAR-camera detection into mandatory (braking-distance/TTC-critical) and optional work; temporal-ROI routing, a latency-aware coordinator shedding sweeps/resolution, and freshest-wins asynchronous scheduling.
evaluation: nuScenes in ROS, RTX 3080, vs BEVFusion plus ablations; about 100 ms per-frame target. Inference 202 to 103 ms; e2e mean 1006 to 344 ms, p95 1455 to 434 ms; safety-critical recall 94.9 to 94.7. Jetson AGX Orin on Husky: 91.0 to 43.2 ms.
contribution: Criticality-aware multi-modal BEV perception that prioritises objects within braking distance or short time-to-collision, cutting end-to-end latency 2.93x and p95 from 1455 to 434 ms with 0.2-point safety-critical recall loss.
flag: timing is the contribution: yes (accuracy traded against a per-frame latency budget, with p95 e2e latency); application safety-relevant: yes (AV perception). Check: the budget is stated only loosely ('~100 ms per-frame target') and no deadline-miss rate is reported; e2e 344 ms mean is still well above 100 ms; main results are on a desktop RTX 3080 with replayed nuScenes; the Jetson Orin/Husky run reports mean inference latency only (no accuracy ground truth, no tail). time-to-irreversibility cell given because TTC drives the mandatory set and compute budget - drop if judged too generous. No comparison against RT-BEV or FLEX, only BEVFusion and ablations. Two-column text extraction was interleaved; accuracy-table details partly skimmed.

title: Cross-Platform Benchmark of Neural 3D Reconstruction for Autonomous Laboratory Robots
evidence: "Values below 10 FPS represent unacceptable latency for interactive robotic tasks" (Sec. 3.2.1) is the only threshold; the paper proposes no method and gives averages only.
method: Benchmark of NerfStudio NeRF and 3D Gaussian Splatting training and rendering, plus SAM3D single-image reconstruction, across three GPU platforms for laboratory robot perception.
evaluation: One 40-image scene; Jetson AGX Orin, RTX 2080, A100; render FPS 0.09-24.16 and training 15.6-90 min; PSNR 18.96-24.32; no stated deadline, tail or miss rate.
contribution: A cross-platform benchmark of NeRF, Gaussian splatting and SAM3D reconstruction cost and quality for laboratory robots, arguing for tiered fast and slow reconstruction.
flag: timing is the contribution: no (speed and quality benchmark with an informal 10 FPS threshold); application not safety-relevant. Mostly training time and render FPS, not deadline-bound inference; averages from single runs, one scene, no ablation. Only Alienware-GS (24.16 FPS) clears the paper's own 10 FPS line and the paper does not discuss that. SAM3D accuracy figures are cited from elsewhere, not measured. The tiered design and scientist intervention are future work.

title: Real-Time Plasma State Prediction via FPGA-Accelerated Quantized Recurrent Probabilistic Neural Networks
evidence: "As no physical Alveo U50 card was available to us for direct hardware testing, this achieved-frequency figure is obtained directly from the post-implementation timing simulation by Vivado" (Sec. V.B).
method: GRU-based recurrent probabilistic network for tokamak plasma state prediction, shrunk 94.9% and quantised to 16-bit fixed point with QKeras QAT, synthesised to FPGA via hls4ml.
evaluation: 19,648 DIII-D shots; abstract sub-10 us target, no PCS deadline stated; post-route simulation for Alveo U50: 2.64 us (276 cycles); CPU 608 us, A100 1085 us; MSE +2.8% vs FP32.
contribution: A quantised recurrent probabilistic network for plasma state prediction synthesised to an FPGA with a simulated 2.64 microsecond single-step latency and under 5% accuracy loss.
flag: timing is the contribution: partly (deterministic FPGA latency is the motivation, but it is quantisation reported as speed and accuracy); application is safety-relevant in principle (plasma control) but no control integration. Borderline - check: the sub-10 us figure is the only budget and appears only in the abstract, with no plasma-control-system deadline or cycle time in the body; latency is from Vivado timing simulation, not measured hardware, so no jitter, worst-case or miss data despite the word deterministic; the 240x CPU speed-up is about 230x from Table XII (608/2.64). If the maintainer counts fixed-cycle FPGA latency as timing-predictable inference with a proved bound, this could flip to include, but without edge deployment credit. Closed-loop rollout degrades (EV -0.41 vs +0.10 at t=100).

title: Risk-Aware Online Conformal State Probing
evidence: Sec 3: probes with probability p_t = rho + (1-rho)*1[O_t >= mu_t] when the estimated outage probability of the candidate action exceeds an online-updated threshold; if it probes, the agent takes the optimal action instead of the candidate. Sec 1: "OCSP does not aim to calibrate a predictor [10] or to defer from cloud to edge [5]."
method: OCSP: wrapper around a pre-trained value-based policy that, per step, estimates the outage probability of its candidate action and probes the true state when it exceeds an online conformal threshold.
evaluation: Synthetic MDP (30 states, 4 actions), 1e5 steps, 100 seeds; exact, over- and underconfident beliefs; baseline augment-and-train. Missed query error held at target 0.3 vs up to 0.4; no hardware or latency.
contribution: An online conformal wrapper that decides at each step whether a pre-trained policy should probe the true state before acting, with a distribution-free bound on missed-query error at a minimised probing rate.
flag: Pillar 3, borderline (routes ii sequential and v theory). The gate decides when the agent stops trusting its belief and queries an oracle for the true state, replacing the candidate action; that is structurally a sequential ask-for-help rule, but the paper explicitly says it does NOT aim at deferral, and the target is a state oracle, not a human or safeguard. If the maintainer does not accept probing as deferral this is E1. Evidence is thin: one toy tabular MDP, results mostly in plots (cumulative return, probing rate have no numeric values; rho and eta unstated), and the baseline is described as an upper bound at matched probing rate. Proposition 1 (MQE_T <= alpha + Delta(N_T, delta), with prob. 1-delta) has only a proof sketch, part "omitted due to space constraints". No time-to-irreversibility, latency, multi-agent or human element. The arXiv id carries a 2609 prefix; title matched the record.

title: TrackFlood: Relocating Latency Attacks from NMS-Free Detectors to Real-Time Trackers
evidence: Latency is reported as median, p99 and deadline-miss fraction against "the 33 ms (30 FPS) real-time deadline" (Sec. 4.3).
method: White-box adversarial perturbation floods NMS-free detectors (YOLOv10, YOLO26, RT-DETR) with spread phantom boxes so the downstream tracker's association cost inflates; a bounded-admission cap is the defence.
evaluation: 33 ms deadline; Jetson AGX Orin, TensorRT FP16; KITTI; clean vs attacked: ByteTrack p99 7-21 ms, 0 misses at 8/255; 40 ms, 0.62 misses at 32/255; OC-SORT 109 ms, 1.00 misses.
contribution: A latency attack that moves the slowdown from NMS-free detectors to the tracker, with p99 latency and deadline-miss rates measured on a Jetson AGX Orin against a 33 ms deadline, plus a bounded-admission defence.
flag: timing is the contribution: yes; application is safety-relevant (driving perception) but no driving decision is measured, only argued. Check: at the standard 8/255 budget there are zero deadline misses (end-to-end 1.09-1.47x); misses appear only at 16-32/255, which is a visible perturbation. Detector latency itself is unchanged (0.99-1.01x). Universal attack gives 1.11-1.24x end to end. Defence tested only against a non-adaptive attacker, costs detection retention (0.42 at K=10 on RT-DETR-l) and is not compared with threshold tuning; it filters detections, not actions, so I set runtime_interceptor no. No ablation of the loss terms; four clips, sign test p=0.0625 (authors say so). New tag adversarial-robustness added.

title: Micro Neural Policies for Safe Real-Time Robotic Control
evidence: "The timing is effectively deterministic" (Sec. VI-C)
method: Evolution-strategy search for very small MLP control policies (2x2 to 32x32) verified offline by statistical model checking, optionally residual on a linear controller; compiled to C via onnx2c on Zephyr RTOS.
evaluation: Cartpole and quadrotor at 50/100 Hz (20/10 ms periods); baselines SAC-Lagrangian DRL and residual variants. nRF54L15 Cortex-M33: mean inference 10.10-258.98 us (<2.6% of period), std <24 ns over 1000 runs.
contribution: Synthesises micro neural control policies that pass statistical model checking and run in under 260 microseconds with nanosecond-level variation on a Cortex-M33 microcontroller.
flag: timing is the contribution: partly; application safety-relevant (quadrotor and cartpole control with offline statistical safety verification). BORDERLINE - maintainer should decide: the primary claim is that compact policies stay verifiable (verifiability 5/5 ES vs 0-1/5 DRL on cartpole; ES-Res 5/5 vs DRL 0/5 on quadrotor); timing is one of three listed contributions and is supporting evidence. If timing-predictable inference on an MCU with latency against the 10 ms period counts, this meets the floor (width sweep as ablation) and would be include with criteria d. Doubts: no WCET, p99 or deadline-miss rate, only mean and std; "jitter" is inference-time std, not control-loop jitter; timing benchmark is on nRF54L15 while flights used Pixhawk STM32F427 and Raspberry Pi 4B, and it is unclear which device ran the policy in real tests; text says 2.5% of deadline in Sec. VI-C but 2.6% in contributions; ES-Res crashed on the real quadrotor despite passing verification. Safety is offline only, no runtime filter.

title: FALCON: FPGA-Accelerated Latency-Certifiable Occupancy Networks for Camera-Based Autonomous Driving
evidence: "PL compute is cycle-bounded; inference latency is a measured envelope; delivery is enforced by a watchdog." (Sec. 3.3)
method: FlashOcc-R50 camera occupancy network on an FPGA: INT8 DPU subgraphs plus fixed-trip-count HLS IPs for view-transform gather and resize, with a watchdog that publishes a stale ego-warped output when a frame misses its deadline.
evaluation: Deadline 100 ms (six-inference ResNet-50 proxy). AMD Kria KR260. Median 95.5 ms, miss 0.070% pooled over 3x100k frames, max 169.0 ms; enforced delivery tops at 107.8 ms. Tail ratio vs Orin NX, RTX 4090, A100, L4. mIoU 29.88 vs FP32 32.19.
contribution: Deploys a camera occupancy network on an embedded FPGA with cycle-bounded logic and a deadline watchdog, reporting tail latency and deadline-miss rates over 300,000 frames against GPU platforms.
flag: timing is the contribution: yes; application safety-relevant (autonomous-driving perception). Check: "certifiable" is weaker than the title suggests - only the PL compute term is analytic, and the paper says "measured maxima are reported as envelopes, not bounds". The 100 ms deadline results are for a six-inference ResNet-50 PROXY; the full six-camera FlashOcc pipeline takes about 1.3 s per frame and has no deadline-miss rate. runtime_interceptor set to no: the watchdog overrides a late perception output with a stale one (68 of 88 late frames in one run) but does not veto or halt a vehicle action - maintainer may read this as a deferral mechanism. Discrepancies: abstract says 1.5x KR260 tail, body 1.44x; intro says PL compute 11.6 ms per frame but Table 1 cycle counts sum to about 8.1 ms; the 23.6x L4 figure is in abstract and Fig. 1 caption only. Platform comparison is not precision- or isolation-matched. Board accuracy is weak on safety classes (pedestrian recall 14.8%, falling to 11.6% after one stale step). No on-car validation.

title: DetM-Tracker: Deterministic and Memory-Efficient VIS for Autonomous Industrial Inspection
evidence: "Specifically, the inference latency on the GB10 is approximately 60 ms per frame." (Appendix B Limitations, item 3)
method: Video instance segmentation model for server-rack socket tracking using compact four-scalar instance memory, dynamic instance channels and an entropy-gated skip connection to bound memory and compute.
evaluation: Own industrial dataset; vs SAM 2.1, SAM 3/3.1, Cutie, LiVOS. mIoU 0.697 vs 0.36 best baseline; mean 15.2 ms on A100 vs 291.8 ms Cutie; VRAM 557 MB. GB10 about 60 ms against 125 ms budget, asserted only.
contribution: A memory-bounded video instance segmentation tracker for industrial inspection reporting 15.2 ms mean inference and 557 MB VRAM with higher mIoU than SAM-family baselines.
flag: timing is the contribution: no (despite 'deterministic' in the title, only one mean latency per model is reported; no variance, tail, worst-case or deadline-miss analysis); application safety-relevant: no (inspection). Check: all tabulated timing is on NVIDIA A100, not edge hardware; the GB10 60 ms figure and 125 ms budget appear only in the limitations appendix with no table or baseline; abstract says edge deployment but none is measured. Determinism refers to bounded memory/complexity, not measured timing. Segmentation paper that merely reports speed.

title: VLA-HWBench: Where the Time Goes When VLA Models Run on Edge Hardware
evidence: "Only 10 of the 19 configurations on the Jetson and 9 on the AMD platform keep up with LIBERO's control rate." (Sec 5.1)
method: Measurement benchmark timing 18 open VLA models with a seven-stage per-call breakdown, then adding compilation, specialised backends (FlashRT, TensorRT) and FP8/4-bit weights one at a time, plus roofline bottleneck analysis.
evaluation: Budget 50 ms per action (LIBERO 20 Hz). Jetson AGX Thor and Ryzen AI Max+ PRO 395. p50 77 ms-6.3 s (Jetson), 114 ms-17.9 s (AMD), p5-p95 reported; pi0.5 318 to 44 ms, GR00T N1.7 119 to 46 ms.
contribution: Characterisation of 18 vision-language-action models on two edge platforms: latency spans 82x and follows action-generation iterations, not model size; only about half meet the 50 ms per-action control period.
flag: timing is the contribution: yes (latency characterisation is the whole paper); application safety-relevant: no (robot manipulation benchmark input, no safety decision). Check: it is a profiling study, not a deadline-meeting method; statistics are median with p5-p95, no p99, jitter or miss-rate analysis; the 50 ms budget is per action after dividing by chunk size, so long chunks pass with 400 ms calls; one fixed LIBERO observation, 20-100 timed calls; task success not re-measured after optimisation (only action cosine similarity). Maintainer may judge it E1 as speed reporting. Appendices C-F not read in full.

title: EdgePace: Deadline- and Freshness-Aware LLM Scheduling on Unified-Memory Platforms
evidence: Camera task has a "one-frame deadline of 33.33 ms at 30 Hz" and robot tracking a 40 ms sensing-to-command deadline (Sec. 4.3-4.4, closely paraphrased)
method: Runtime that splits LLM prefill/decode into quanta at sublayer boundaries, monitors PMU memory-contention counters on foreground threads, and chooses Bypass, Admit or Hold per quantum to protect foreground deadlines and LLM freshness.
evaluation: Deadlines 33.33 ms (camera) and 40 ms (robot tracking, MuJoCo). OnePlus 13, Jetson Orin Nano/AGX Orin/Thor. Miss rate vs unmanaged llama.cpp: Nano 18.33->7.67%, OnePlus 66.78->5.83%; AGX VLM 7.53->0.29%; decision P99 7.135 us.
contribution: Schedules on-device LLM inference around memory-bandwidth contention so co-running sensing tasks meet 33-40 ms deadlines, cutting deadline misses by 24-91 percent while retaining 65-98 percent of LLM throughput.
flag: timing is the contribution: yes; application not safety-relevant as evaluated (replayed OpenEQA video and a simulated Panda tracking task, no safety claim). Check: the deadline protected is that of the foreground sensing/control tasks (some not learned models); the learned-model inference (LLM/VLM) is what gets scheduled and its timing is a seconds-scale freshness window with no single stated value - confirm this satisfies condition 2. Abstract claim that all measured LLM outputs arrive within their freshness windows has no reported fraction in the body; foreground p95/p99 said to be measured but no table found. No component ablation (monitor or freshness override removed); only load and quantisation sensitivity. Residual miss rates remain 4-8% in several configs. runtime_interceptor no: Hold defers LLM compute quanta, not an action. Fig. 3 policy comparison gives numbers only for FCFS and SJF. Miss reductions vs TensorRT and MLC-LLM come with lower throughput retention.

title: Ripple: Deadline-Aware CPU-GPU Sharing for Embodied Inference
evidence: "Ripple is the only solution meeting the DMR requirement consistently." (Sec 5.2)
method: CPU-GPU co-scheduler for unified-memory edge devices: splits LLM/VLM inference into pausable layer units and converts each CPU job's deadline slack into a GPU memory-byte budget for admission; adaptive pricing, SM narrowing.
evaluation: DGX Spark (GB10); four mixes of robotic CPU tasks plus Qwen3 LLM/VLM; vs Sereno, SiGAMMA, Pause, Cap-x, unmanaged. Deadlines k x co-run p99 (k 1.1-2.0), VLM 5-10 s, 2% miss limit. Ripple under 2%; native Pause 84.8% DMR; p98 3.4-8.6 ms under deadline.
