contribution: Deadline-aware scheduler that meters LLM/VLM inference memory traffic on a unified-memory edge device so co-running robotic CPU tasks stay under a 2 percent deadline-miss target while VLM deadlines are met.
flag: timing is the contribution: yes (deadline-miss rate is the primary outcome); application safety-relevant: partly (obstacle-avoidance style CPU tasks motivate it, but no safety outcome measured). Check: the protected deadlines belong mainly to non-learned CPU tasks (costmap, KDNN, stereo, control); the learned-model side is VLM frame deadlines of 5-10 s plus best-effort LLM throughput - maintainer should decide whether that satisfies the learned-model-inference condition. Most DMR and tokens/s values are in figures, not text; baselines run untuned; single device; self-described proof of concept. Defers inference work units, not agent actions, so runtime_interceptor is no. Appendices (throughput bound, conformal margin) not read.

title: Where Is VLA Inference Time Spent? Bottlenecks and Optimization Interactions Across GPUs
evidence: "A single-action policy must finish inference within one control period, which is set by the robot motor frequencies." (Sec 2.1, with Eq. 1 setting budget B to the 50 ms control period, or the remaining-chunk window for asynchronous chunked policies)
method: Measurement study of seven inference optimisation families on seven VLA policies across four GPUs, checked against control-period latency budgets; yields VLA-Triage guidelines for stacking optimisations under a budget.
evaluation: Budget 50 ms (20 Hz), 50-1200 ms per model. H100, A10G, RTX 4090, Jetson Thor. Eager baseline; medians of 200+ runs. OFT Thor 180.6 to 109.3 ms (150); CogACT Thor 134.4 to 97.7 ms (50, missed).
contribution: Shows where vision-language-action inference time goes on four GPUs and that optimisation gains do not compose or transfer across hardware, so meeting a control-period budget must be measured per platform.
flag: timing is the contribution: yes (latency against a stated control-period budget is the measured outcome); application is safety-relevant only indirectly (robot manipulation control, no safety decision or hazard studied). Check: (1) all latencies are MEDIANS - no p99, tail, jitter or worst-case figures, so the tail-latency tag was not applied; the only deadline-miss-like metric is an idle-step fraction from a simulated action-queue replay (1% limit, Table 10), and authors say those robot counts are not capacity estimates. (2) No task success or accuracy is measured, so accuracy is not traded against the budget; pruning and quantisation effects on behaviour are left to the user. (3) VLA-Triage is validated by worked examples and a screen audit only, with no before/after count of budgets met. (4) Edge evidence is Jetson Thor only (OFT, CogACT, SmolVLA 308 to 82 ms compiled, GR00T slower when compiled 188 vs 149 ms); the other three platforms are server or desktop GPUs. (5) Read via arxiv v1 PDF, first 100000 of 108593 characters; Appendix H Table 17 not seen. Maintainer may judge this a profiling study rather than deadline-aware inference - borderline between include and exclude-E1.

title: Real-Time Multimodal and Parent-Configured Social Robot for Child-Centered Language Interaction Using Large Language Models
venue: Lecture notes in networks and systems
evidence: "If validation fails, the system replaces the candidate with a safe fallback template or requests regeneration with stricter control tags." (Sec. 4.3 Constraint Enforcement Pipeline)
method: Child-facing social robot on Jetson Xavier: multimodal state plus parent profile feed a local LLM; post-generation rule validator checks hard parental constraints before actuation, substituting a fallback or regenerating.
evaluation: Jetson Xavier AGX; Qwen 2.5 3B 28.1 tok/s, 2.54 s turn latency, validation 0.05 s; policy compliance 98.2% nominal, 90.7% at 20% STT noise. No baseline measured.
contribution: An edge-deployed child-robot dialogue pipeline that validates each LLM reply against parent-set hard constraints before actuation, reporting latency and compliance under noisy input but no comparison against prompt-only control.
flag: neither - the post-generation validator is a real runtime veto (Pillar 1 route a) but the compliance figures (Table 5) have no baseline or ablation: the prompt-only comparison is only a protocol for a future study (Sec. 5.4, Sec. 7), yet Sec. 6.3 and the abstract claim improvement over prompt-only. Also a single-agent single-output text filter, so exclude-E4 is equally defensible. Rules, test-set size and how compliance was scored are not described. 9-page paper inside a 2.6M-char proceedings volume (IntelliSys 2026, pp. 509-517); I read only that paper, not the rest of the file. No deferral to a human.

title: On the Timing Determinism of CUDA and Vulkan SC for Safety-Critical AI Workloads on Integrated SoC GPUs
evidence: "This work compares CUDA and Vulkan SC on the NVIDIA Jetson Orin Nano SoC platform with a focus on timing determinism." (Abstract); "Measured WCET denotes the maximum observed runtime" (Sec. 3.2)
method: Empirical timing study of two GPU APIs (CUDA vs Vulkan SC) on an integrated SoC GPU, decomposing mean, jitter, measured WCET and skew across allocation, transfer and kernel phases for NN primitives and a fused feed-forward NN.
evaluation: No deadline stated. Jetson Orin Nano, 1000 runs, N=1e7. Kernel SAXPY mean/WCET: CUDA 6.66/7.03, Vulkan SC 1.99/2.04; Chain1000 total 3453/3462 vs 4252/4255; kernel MAJ 2.12 vs 0.17; fused-NN kernel jitter CUDA about 10x Vulkan SC.
contribution: A measurement study on a Jetson Orin Nano showing Vulkan SC gives lower kernel-level jitter and measured worst-case time than CUDA for neural-network primitives, while host-device transfers still dominate end-to-end variability.
flag: timing is the contribution: yes; application safety-relevant (avionics certification motivation, SAFECOMP 2026) but no decision or control loop is evaluated. Chapter found inside the SAFECOMP volume (pp. 330-345) and read in full. Check: (1) the learned-model condition is thin - most results are synthetic primitives (SAXPY, ReLU, sigmoid, tanh, softmax, chains); the fused NN is a tiny fixed-weight feed-forward net (380 MACs, 20 ReLU, 4 sigmoid per sample) with no accuracy or task, and its timing is given only in figures plus skew values (CUDA 1.27, Vulkan SC -0.001); (2) no deadline or budget is stated, so 'latency/jitter aware' is not claimed; (3) 'WCET' is the maximum observed over 1000 runs, not a bound, and the paper says it 'does not provide certification evidence'; (4) Tables 4-5 give no time unit in the extracted text (Fig. 3 caption suggests ms); (5) Vulkan SC is slower end-to-end on SAXPY and chains (17-23%). The comparison baseline is CUDA itself.

title: Multimodal AI Architectures for Real-Time Decision-Making in Autonomous Systems
venue: Communications in computer and information science
evidence: "The deadline-miss rate decreases from 22.4 to 3.1, indicating that compute adaptation and early-exit gating substantially improve timing stability." (Sec. 4.1); "represents the deadline (50 ms, based on interview-derived budgets)" (Sec. 3.3)
method: Camera-LiDAR-radar cross-attention transformer with sparsely gated mixture-of-experts and entropy-gated early exits, trained with a deadline-penalty, energy, calibration and CVaR loss, deployed with INT8 on Jetson Orin.
evaluation: Deadline 50 ms, DMR target <=5%. nuScenes on Jetson AGX Orin 30 W: mean latency 64 to 41 ms, DMR 22.4% to 3.1%, jitter 4.2 ms, 1.6 J per decision vs non-adaptive transformer; Waymo 66 to 44 ms, DMR 24.7% to 4.2%; Orin Nano 55 ms vs about 90 ms.
contribution: A multimodal perception transformer with mixture-of-experts routing and adaptive early exits that reports deadline-miss rate, jitter and energy against a 50 ms budget on Jetson AGX Orin and Orin Nano.
flag: timing is the contribution: partly - it is one of three co-equal claims (accuracy, timing, calibration) but deadline-miss rate and jitter against a stated 50 ms budget are measured with baselines and ablations; application safety-relevant (autonomous driving perception). Chapter found inside the SEMIT 2026 volume (pp. 50-71); read through the discussion, not the conclusion or references in detail. Doubts, candidly: (1) essentially every result is in bar-chart figures with no tables, so the figures quoted in the prose cannot be cross-checked; (2) the Orin Nano mean latency of 55 ms is above the 50 ms deadline yet the abstract claims DMR below 5% and the text says only the adaptive design 'preserves' timing budgets - inconsistent, and no Nano DMR is given; (3) the abstract's 'up to 71% 3D mAP' and 'calibration error reduced by more than 50%' are not found as numbers in the body text; (4) the 50 ms deadline and thresholds come from '25 structured expert interviews' and '12 deployment reports' that are not documented; (5) code and logs 'will' be released, none cited; (6) garbled or contradictory sentences (Sec. 4.2 'Unimodal models achieve better performance, although the combined model is weaker'; 'reduced by approximately between'; duplicated phrases) suggest machine-assisted or unreviewed text, and the scale claimed (1.4M + 12M frames, two datasets, two boards, interviews) is large for the detail given. Jitter defined as variance but reported in ms. Abstention is evaluated only as selective-risk statistics, so runtime_interceptor is no; maintainer may consider criterion (a) not met. Treat numbers as low-confidence.

title: A Power-Aware Adaptive FDIR Framework Using Heterogeneous System-on-Chip Modules
evidence: "the goal of the AMS is to maintain a particular QoS deadline (frame rate) while using as little power as possible and always ensuring that a system-wide power constraint is met." (Sec. 6.2.3)
method: FDIR scheme for SRAM FPGAs in space: duplicate-and-compare detects SEU faults, the task migrates to a hard ARM core during scrubbing, and frequency scaling holds a frame-rate QoS within a power cap.
evaluation: Xilinx ZC702 Zynq, injected faults up to 1 per second, K-means on video frames; vs naive stall-and-scrub. Worst-case availability near 100% vs below 0.2; heartrate and power only in figures; no numeric deadline given.
contribution: A fault detection, isolation and recovery framework for FPGA system-on-chip payload processors that migrates a hardware task to a processor core during scrubbing to keep availability near full under injected upsets.
flag: timing is the contribution: partly (availability and a frame-rate QoS under faults), but there is no learned-model inference - the workload is Lloyd's K-means clustering run afresh on each video frame (unsupervised, called 'machine learning' in the text, but nothing trained is deployed) and the controller is a two-state heuristic; a learning-based controller is future work only. Application is spacecraft payload processing, safety-relevant only loosely. Chapter 6 found inside the book 'FPGAs and Parallel Architectures for Aerospace Applications' (pp. 75-89) and read in full. Also a book chapter (possible E3) and results are given only as figures with no numeric deadline or miss rate. The duplicate-and-compare fault trigger is hardware fault recovery, not a safety interceptor on an agent's action.

title: Real-Time Inference Approach Based on Gateway-Centric Edge Computing for Intelligent Services
evidence: "For evaluating the proposed edge computing, we collected the memory usage of the edge gateway." (Sec. 4); "the edge computing architecture reduces the latency to get the control factor" (Abstract)
method: EdgeX-based gateway on a Raspberry Pi 4 hosts a TensorFlow Lite heater-energy model trained in the cloud and exposes it as a microservice triggered by a rules engine for IoT devices.
evaluation: No deadline, no latency figure at all. Raspberry Pi 4 gateway (4 GB), Raspberry Pi 3 IoT device; only result is memory use: 1,499,948 kB of 3,884,376 kB. No baseline, no accuracy, no timing.
contribution: An architecture description of an EdgeX gateway on a Raspberry Pi 4 that serves a cloud-trained TensorFlow Lite heater-control model to IoT devices, evaluated only by memory usage.
flag: timing is the contribution: no - 'real-time' is in the title and the abstract asserts reduced latency, but no latency, deadline, jitter or tail is measured anywhere; application is smart-heater control in a building, not safety-relevant. Chapter found inside the ICISN 2021 volume (pp. 355-361) and read in full. Would equally fail the evaluation floor (E2): the only measurement is gateway memory usage, with no baseline. Seven-page architecture note; edge hardware is real but nothing timing-related was measured on it, so no gap cell is claimed.

title: EcoVLA: Energy-Efficient Device-Edge Co-inference for Vision-Language-Action Models Under Real-Time Constraints
evidence: Evaluation requires "the action output frequency to reach 20 Hz" with "TSLO <= 1 s for models with an action chunk size of 20" (Sec. 7.2); the scheduler picks the most energy-efficient mapping that meets the latency budget (Sec. 6.1).
method: Stage-level DAG of a VLA model; online latency/energy predictor with EWMA calibration picks the device-edge stage placement maximising actions per joule subject to a per-request latency SLO.
evaluation: Budget T_SLO 1 s per 20-action chunk; Jetson AGX Orin 32GB + RTX 4090 edge, tc-shaped bandwidth; pi0.5 712-902 ms; Device-Only misses SLO on 4 of 5 models; vs Device-Only, Edge-Only, Fixed Split.
contribution: A device-edge co-inference scheduler for vision-language-action models that places model stages to maximise actions per joule while holding each request inside a stated latency budget, measured on a Jetson AGX Orin testbed.
flag: timing is the contribution: partly (latency SLO is the constraint, energy is the objective); application not safety-relevant as evaluated (synthetic requests, no robot task, policy accuracy not evaluated). Check: SLO satisfaction is shown only as mean latency against the 1 s budget - no deadline-miss rate, p99 or jitter, and scheduler overhead is only called millisecond-level. The 1 s budget is per 20-action chunk, far from sub-15 ms. No ablation of predictor or calibration. Paper's 35.8% efficiency gain does not match its own figures (3.3 vs 2.45 Actions/J gives about 34.7%). Fig. 3/4 values were partly garbled in extraction; the 0.1 s degraded-network latency I could not reconcile with the other figures. Record is the 2027 Springer chapter; I read the arXiv version, title matches.

title: A Unified Performance Profile and Prediction System of DNN Models On Heterogeneous Devices
venue: Communications in computer and information science
evidence: "It also achieves over 96% ACC10 on various DNN models and devices." (Abstract)
method: Profiling system (converter, profiler, generator) plus device-specific GNN that predicts mean end-to-end DNN inference latency from the computing graph, as mantissa/exponent classification.
evaluation: No deadline or budget stated. 110k generated models; Kirin 9000 NPU, RK3588 NPU, Mali-G78 GPU; ACC10 97.9-99.7% overall; predictor 28 MB vs nn-Meter 501 MB; prediction 2-52 ms vs 720-5686 ms.
contribution: A GNN predictor estimates mean DNN inference latency on phone and board NPUs/GPUs within 10% for over 96% of models, at far lower memory and overhead than kernel-level nn-Meter.
flag: timing is the contribution: partly (predicts MEAN latency for deployment/NAS; no deadline, budget, bound, tail or jitter analysis); application not safety-relevant. Chapter located inside CWSN 2025 proceedings volume (pp 459-472), only that chapter read. Check: nn-Meter is compared only on memory and prediction time, not on prediction accuracy; ground truth is a 120-run mean; operational-mode study (ResNet50 60.5 ms at 315 MHz vs 31.8 ms at 608 MHz) is descriptive. If the maintainer reads 'predicting inference timing' broadly this could flip, but the evaluation floor (tail/worst-case/budget) is still not met.

title: Edge-deployed streaming real-time trajectory prediction
evidence: "our model achieves a real-time inference latency of 97 ms on the Jetson Orin Nano using half-precision (FP16) execution" (Sec 5.3)
method: SEAM: streaming multi-agent trajectory forecaster using previous endpoints as context anchors; fixed agent/lane token caps give static, predictable compute for TensorRT edge compilation.
evaluation: Argoverse 2; budget is 10 Hz stream (100 ms, implicit). Jetson AGX Orin in Orin Nano emulation, 15 W/7 W: 97 ms FP16 vs 590 ms uncapped FP32, minFDE6 1.286 vs 1.250 m; 75 ms variant. V100: 28 ms vs RealMotion 24, DeMo 39.
contribution: A streaming trajectory predictor with capped agent and lane tokens reaches 97 ms per step on a Jetson Orin Nano profile, trading under 4 cm of endpoint error for a sixfold latency cut.
flag: timing is the contribution: partly (main contribution is forecasting accuracy; the edge latency-accuracy Pareto study under token budgets is one of three contributions); application safety-relevant (autonomous driving) but no safety metric. Check: the 100 ms deadline is never stated as a number, only 'exceeding 10 Hz' and the 10 Hz dataset rate, and 97 ms leaves 3 ms margin; latencies are averages, no p99/jitter/deadline-miss figures despite 'deterministic' wording; 'worst-case' means max token counts, not measured WCET; hardware is an AGX Orin emulating Orin Nano; 7 W mode is about 2.48x slower so would miss 10 Hz. Criterion (b) arguably also met (prediction over multi-agent state, baselines on AV2) - not claimed here. Dates odd: journal year 2027 vol 38, received and revised same day. Likely overturn candidate if average-latency-only is judged insufficient.

title: An environment-adaptive multi-modal perception edge-AI for real-time robotic fruit harvesting
evidence: "Remarkably, the system achieved a 0% Deadline-Miss Rate (DMR) across the entire trajectory, even in the presence of stochastic hardware latency jitter on the Jetson Orin Nano." (Sec 7.2.3)
method: M2PE RGB-D YOLOv11-based fruit perception plus LCOS-F2: controller feedback sets per-phase time budgets; a temporal arbiter picks the freshest output from full model or two lightweight fallback heads.
evaluation: Budgets 12/20/50 ms per task phase; Jetson Orin Nano 8 GB 15 W; p50/p99 33.1/37.6, 14.8/16.2, 9.7/10.9 ms; DMR 0% vs static 42.8%, early-exit 18.2%, anytime 4.5%; jitter 0.4 ms; effective mAP 72.4%.
contribution: A deadline-aware output selector on a Jetson Orin Nano picks among a full detector and two fallback heads per control-phase budget, reporting zero deadline misses against 4.5-42.8% for anytime, early-exit and static baselines.
flag: timing is the contribution: yes (one of two contributions, with deadline-miss rate, p99 and jitter against explicit budgets); application weakly safety-relevant (harvesting robot arm, 'safer' claimed but not measured). Check: closed-loop test is a SIMULATED harvesting sequence of task budgets on the Jetson, no physical robot trial; 0% DMR is partly by construction since each head's p99 sits under its assigned budget; baselines are the authors' own re-implementations with few details; M2PE latency given as 21.1 ms in the model comparison but 33.1 ms end-to-end elsewhere; '100% predictable guaranties' is empirical over 500 trials, not a proved bound; arbiter selects outputs but does not veto actions, hence interceptor no. Table 5 'cross-domain' is two fruit datasets, not the review's cross-domain cell.

title: Evaluating virtualization for fog monitoring of real-time applications in mixed-criticality systems
evidence: "we evaluate the ability of each architectural scenario to isolate the non-deterministic nature of AD. In light of this, we do not consider any metric for AD in our experimentation." (Sec 5.1.2)
method: Model-based development process and formal notation for deploying fog monitoring alongside hard real-time control on a virtualized MPSoC (Xen), comparing shared-memory and network-socket monitor placement.
evaluation: ITER plasma control case study; control task period 1000 us; Zynq UltraScale+ ZCU104; control WCET 14 us baseline, 15 us shared memory (+7.14%), 43 us sockets (+207.14%), 69 us with network disturbance; 50 runs.
contribution: On a Xen-virtualized Zynq MPSoC, co-locating an anomaly-detection monitor via hypervisor shared memory raises a 1 kHz control task's worst-case execution time by 7%, against 207% over network sockets.
flag: timing is the contribution: yes, but NOT of learned-model inference - timing is measured for the control task and the data-sampling task only; the anomaly detector is process mining (pattern conformance, no neural or trained-model inference timed) and the authors explicitly report no metric for it. Application is safety-relevant (nuclear fusion plasma control, simulated plant). Check: 'WCET' is the observed maximum over 60000 samples x 50 runs, not a static bound; the monitor detects anomalies but no veto/halt path or detection accuracy is evaluated, so criterion (a) is not met either. Maintainer may want it as background for interference/isolation of monitors on edge hardware.

title: Timing guarantees for inference of AI models in embedded systems
evidence: "We propose the design of deadline-aware scheduling algorithms for multi-DNN workloads, allowing concurrent execution without violating real-time constraints." (Sec 3.1)
method: Short position paper listing challenges (memory, energy, multi-DNN scheduling, heterogeneous accelerators) and planned research directions for timing-guaranteed DNN inference on embedded systems.
evaluation: None. No experiments, hardware, deadline or latency figures; the paper states no datasets were generated or analysed. Only cites prior work (RT-MOT, RT-Swap, LaLaRAND, DNN-SAM).
contribution: A nine-page position paper sets out open problems and a research agenda for giving deep-network inference timing guarantees on embedded hardware; it reports no method or measurements.
flag: timing is the contribution: yes in topic, and safety-relevant applications are named (autonomous driving), but this is a research-agenda/position piece (Real-Time Systems 61:259-267) with no method, no evaluation and no numbers - fails the evaluation floor; could equally be coded E3. Useful only as a pointer list: the cited RTSS/RTAS papers (Kang et al. 2021, 2022a, 2022b, 2024b; Xiang and Kim 2019; Bateni and Liu 2018) are candidate records to check against the corpus.

title: Application of multimodal learning in robotic perception: an intelligent perception framework integrating vision, sound, and touch
evidence: "Operationally, this means ECTT sustains higher event pressure before breaching while still meeting the P99 < 25 ms deadline" (Sec 3.4 Runtime and compliance)
method: Event-clocked tactile transformer: computation advances only on tactile micro-events, one bounded-horizon update per event under a fixed FLOP budget, with a rate-vs-deadline feasibility test and calibrated confidence.
evaluation: Four contact-rich robot tasks, logs; baselines B1 vision-only and B2 frame-synchronous multimodal; deadline P99<25 ms on unnamed Jetson-class GPU; P95/P99 17/24 ms vs 19/31 and 28/47; violations/h 0.2 vs 0.6/1.9.
contribution: Event-clocked multimodal transformer that updates only on tactile micro-events, reporting P99 24 ms against a 25 ms deadline and fewer deadline violations than frame-clocked baselines.
flag: timing is the contribution: yes; application safety-relevant (contact-rich industrial robotics, human-aware navigation). Check: strong signs of machine-generated or unedited text - Related Work addresses the author in second person ("In your work, you adapt", "Your approach, however") and Secs 2.6-2.7 contain unrelated paragraphs (depression recognition, wheeled-robot creeping gait). Hardware is only "Jetson-class", no model named, so edge deployment cell not credited. Datasets, robot, sensor models, sample sizes and number of events are not described; single author; "deterministic" latency is measured, not proved (formal schedulability listed as future work). Abstract numbers (<25 ms P99) match Table 5. Results may not be reproducible or real.

title: Impact of cyberattacks on safety and stability of connected and automated vehicle platoons under lane changes.
evidence: "Simulation experiments using VISSIM reveals that traffic stream and CAV string is unstable under all three types of cyberattacks." (Abstract)
method: Emulates message falsification, denial-of-service and spoofing attacks on infrastructure-based CACC and lane-control advisories for CAV platoons; analyses string stability, driving volatility and surrogate conflicts.
evaluation: VISSIM microsimulation with SSAM conflicts; attack vs no-attack; volatility up 43-51%, over 3000 extra conflicts, rear-end 17 to 1325 and lane-change 15 to 3102; no hardware, no latency figures.
contribution: Simulation study showing that falsification, denial-of-service and spoofing attacks destabilise connected automated vehicle platoons and sharply raise rear-end and lane-change conflicts.
flag: timing is the contribution: no; application safety-relevant (CAV platoon collisions). No learned model and no inference timing: rule-based CACC and lane-control logic in VISSIM; communication delay is explicitly not modelled. Cybersecurity impact assessment, not a mechanism. Maintainer may only want to check whether it fits criterion (c) as an empirical multi-agent hazard study, but it proposes no detector or safeguard.

title: Proactive safety at CVIS-enabled intersections: a framework based on high-fidelity trajectory reconstruction and dynamic risk assessment
evidence: "intensive machine learning or deep learning models are deliberately avoided." (Sec 3.1)
method: Two-stage roadside pipeline: physics-informed outlier removal plus adaptive wavelet denoising for trajectory reconstruction, then vehicle-outline-based conflict detection (VOCA) for intersection risk warnings.
evaluation: Real intersection data on NVIDIA Jetson Xavier NX RSU prototype; baseline Wei et al. 2019 outline method misses most conflicts; 2.23-17.998 ms per frame against a stated sub-100 ms requirement; no tail figures.
contribution: Physics-based trajectory reconstruction and vehicle-outline conflict detection running on a Jetson Xavier NX roadside unit in under 18 ms per frame for intersection warnings.
flag: timing is the contribution: partly (mean per-frame latency reported against a sub-100 ms requirement, no tail, jitter or deadline-miss analysis); application safety-relevant (intersection collision warning). Excluded under condition (2): no learned model at all, the paper states ML/DL is deliberately avoided. Check: abstract says "under 100 ms per frame per vehicle" while body reports 2.23-17.998 ms per frame and <0.1 ms per data point - consistent but loosely worded. It issues warnings only, no override. Maintainer could consider criterion (c) (multi-agent conflict detection vs baseline) but no ground-truth collision rate is reported.

title: Prevail: A 6G spatio-temporal graph learning framework for traffic vulnerability prediction
evidence: "PREVAIL maintains accuracy above 83.5% even under a strict 40 ms latency, while baselines degrade more sharply." (Sec 5.2 Results and discussion)
method: Resource-aware spatio-temporal GNN for area-level traffic vulnerability prediction: latency/bandwidth-penalised training, anytime early-exit heads run to the largest depth meeting tau_max, hierarchical scheduling, corruption-aware training.
evaluation: SUMO plus METR-LA, PEMS-BAY, NYC Taxi, CTA; baselines DCRNN, Graph WaveNet, STGCN; budgets 40 and 100 ms: 83.5%/84.7% vs 76.1/74.6/72.8% at 100 ms; Jetson Nano <2.0 s, Raspberry Pi 5.2 s, Xavier AGX 0.4-1.0 s.
contribution: Budget-aware spatio-temporal graph network with anytime early exits that keeps traffic-vulnerability prediction accuracy near 84% under 40-100 ms latency budgets where baseline graph models degrade.
flag: timing is the contribution: partly (one of several claims alongside accuracy and robustness); application not directly safety-relevant (traffic vulnerability forecasting for management, no safety decision). Check: internal inconsistency - accuracy-vs-latency results quote 40 ms and 100 ms budgets and 55-95 ms end-to-end latency, yet measured edge latency is <2.0 s on Jetson Nano, 5.2 s on Raspberry Pi and 0.4-1.0 s on Xavier AGX at 50 timesteps; hardware for the 40/100 ms figures is not stated, and the stated target elsewhere is <1 s. Latency figures are read from plots (Figs 6, 10, 14, 15), no tail or miss-rate table. Text contains a leftover response-to-reviewers sentence ("Each reviewer concern ... is thus tied to an explicit variable"). "Accuracy" metric is loosely defined. Edge deployment cell credited on Jetson Nano/Raspberry Pi/Xavier AGX but doubt it. Could also touch criterion (b) (prediction over graphs); not credited. Likely to be overturned to E1 if a safety decision is required.

title: Edge-based multimodal sensor data fusion with Vision-Language-Action (VLA) model for real-time autonomous vehicle accident avoidance
evidence: Sec 3.1: a downstream accident detection module "triggers the REACT pipeline only if a hazard is detected"; Sec 3.7: residuals are added to the nominal trajectory, enabling "proactive modifications without discarding the original plan", then "provided to the vehicle control module for execution".
method: REACT: fine-tuned SmolVLM2-500M fuses camera frames, RSU hazard alerts, navigation and ego status; on a hazard trigger it predicts per-waypoint residuals that modify the AD stack's nominal trajectory before control.
evaluation: DeepAccident (CARLA, 691 scenarios; 942 val samples). Average CRR 77.0%, mIOU 59.1%, VPQ 48.2% vs AccidentGPT 57.3/45.2; module and input ablations report collision rate; 0.57 s on Jetson AGX.
contribution: A hazard-triggered edge VLM that corrects a vehicle's nominal trajectory with predicted residuals using roadside alerts, cutting predicted collisions by 77% on DeepAccident at 0.57 s per inference on a Jetson AGX.
flag: Pillar 1, borderline. Title on arXiv says "Vision Language Models (VLMs)" where the record says VLA; same work (REACT), accepted as a match. The mechanism is a hazard-triggered residual correction of the nominal plan, not a veto, halt or fallback layer: check whether a learned trajectory refiner counts as (a) or is a planner (then E1). Single ego vehicle; RSU/V2X input only, so (c) is not met. CRR is computed open-loop from predicted positions (5 m threshold) on a dataset, with no closed-loop driving, and no baseline CRR is tabulated; Tables 5-6 give ablation collision rates (15.0-45.5%) but not the full-model collision rate, so the ablation comparison cannot be read directly. Hardware inconsistent: abstract says Jetson AGX Orin, body says AGX Xavier. Abstract efficiency gains (93.67%, 95.25%) could not be verified from the body. 0.57 s latency is far from sub-15 ms. No human takeover.

title: Toward Linux-based safety-critical systems—Execution time variability analysis of Linux system calls
evidence: "the SyS_ioctl of UC1 is used to communicate with the GPU and execute the inference, so variability is far higher." (Sec 6 Analysis of the results)
method: Extends statistical path coverage of Linux system calls with execution-time analysis: per-unique-trace timing distributions and EVT-based probabilistic WCET estimates; proposes a future runtime monitor on trace identity.
evaluation: YOLOv3 emergency-brake app on NVIDIA Jetson Nano with CARLA, 2.9M SyS_ioctl calls, 80,118 unique traces; pWCET of commonest trace 590-721 us; compared with whole-syscall distribution; no deadline stated.
contribution: Shows on a Jetson Nano emergency-brake workload that each Linux system-call execution path has its own narrower timing distribution, enabling per-trace probabilistic worst-case estimates.
flag: timing is the contribution: yes (execution-time variability and pWCET); application safety-relevant (autonomous emergency braking). Borderline on condition (2): the timing analysed is of Linux kernel system calls, not of the network itself; the learned model (YOLOv3) enters only because the analysed SyS_ioctl call carries its GPU inference. Check: authors state the execution-time data FAIL the i.i.d. tests required for EVT, so the pWCET values (Table 4) are admittedly unsound; no deadline or budget is stated and no end-to-end inference latency is given; the comparison against whole-syscall analysis is shown in density figures without a numeric baseline bound, so the evaluation floor is met only weakly (possible E2). The runtime monitor that would trigger a safe state is future work, hence interceptor no. Kernel 4.9 without PREEMPT_RT. Maintainer may well overturn to E1/E2.

title: ASMAG-TRC: A safety-arbitrated runtime architecture for adaptive inference control on resource-constrained edge AI cameras
evidence: "The safety arbitration layer monitors for these unsafe patterns and applies protective overrides." (Sec. 3.5 Pure-function safety arbitration)
method: Frame-level inference gating for a fixed edge camera: motion cues choose detect/reuse/estimate/fallback; a stateless rule arbiter (three invariants) overrides the choice to force detection during active events; circuit breaker bounds energy.
evaluation: 131 videos, four datasets; Jetson Orin Nano. Event recall 0.980 vs 0.899 DQN gate; unprotected event FN 76 vs 617; 304 overrides in 118,226 frames; gate overhead 1.62 ms; energy -47.5%.
contribution: A training-free controller that decides per frame whether an edge camera runs its detector, with a deterministic arbiter that overrides skip decisions while an event is active so that energy savings do not cost event recall.
flag: neither - the arbiter does override a nominal decision at runtime, but the decision is whether to run a detector on a frame, not an action of an acting system, and the paper itself says "the protected property is event continuity, not end-to-end system safety" (Sec. 3.5). Single camera, no multi-agent hazard, no deferral or human. If the maintainer accepts missed-event frames as a safety outcome it would pass route (a) on evidence (baselines and ablation exist), so check that reading. Doubts: in Table 14 the proposed method has MORE unprotected event FNs (76) than the periodic (39) and FrameHopper-style (49) baselines; the 8.1x claim is against the DQN gate only. No direct arbiter-off ablation of unprotected FNs is reported (Sec. 6 argues it in prose). Single-author paper. Skimmed Sec. 2 and per-dataset tables; read Sec. 3, 5.9, 6, 7.

title: Formal verification of integrity attacks on connected medical devices in battlefield hospitals
evidence: "The gateway is modeled as a trusted enforcement point that receives" messages, "performs integrity checks, and forwards, blocks, quarantines, or isolates messages or sources." (Gateway-centered integrity checking and response policies)
method: Stochastic game model of field-hospital medical devices under integrity attacks; a gateway policy (alarm, patient-ID lock, quarantine, selective isolation) is synthesised by dynamic programming and PRISM-games to minimise bounded unsafe reachability under a resource budget.
evaluation: Synthetic digital twin, 12 patients, 5000 trajectories: unsafe reachability 0.392 no defense, 0.207 best baseline, 0.119 proposed; false alarm 0.039; 176 blocked per 1000; burden 32.5; PRISM runtime 0.90-28.70 s.
contribution: A formally synthesised gateway policy that blocks, quarantines or isolates tampered medical-device messages cuts modelled unsafe reachability from 0.392 to 0.119 in a synthetic field hospital, at the cost of the highest workflow burden.
flag: Pillar 1 - borderline: the gateway intercepts device MESSAGES (a security integrity filter), not the actions of an autonomous agent; the maintainer should decide whether a message gate ahead of therapy decisions counts as runtime interception of an acting system, else exclude-E1. Multi-patient and multi-device (ID swapping across patients) with unsafe reachability vs five baselines and an ablation (Tables 12, 13, 16), so the evaluation floor is met. All evidence is synthetic and model-based; the authors say it does not establish clinical risk reduction or deployment readiness. Baselines are described by the authors as deliberately simple and non-optimised. The gate's own decision latency is not reported (runtimes are offline verification). Hazard thresholds are author-chosen proxies (e.g. no adequate escalation for 3 s); many parameters are deferred to a supplementary file I did not have. Minor inconsistency: no-defense CI is 0.378-0.406 in text but 0.379-0.406 in Tables 12 and 13. Quarantine routes to manual review in the example trace but handoff is not studied. Abstract numbers were found in the body. Skimmed formal derivations and scalability figures.

title: Semantic complexity estimation and price-based multi-agent negotiation reduce tail latency and energy in edge-cloud generative inference
evidence: "query that misses the 2 s deadline or arrives at a full device queue is recorded as a miss and excluded from latency percentiles" (Simulator and hardware)
method: MAGS: on-device probe forecasts token count and entropy of an LLM query before decoding; devices bid for cloud capacity against a server congestion price (Stackelberg, PPO-trained), choosing split point and privacy level.
evaluation: Deadline 2 s. Simulation, 50 devices, 10 seeds, 8 baselines: p99 647 vs 781 ms (RPPO+), deadline misses 0.062. Testbeds: Jetson Orin Nano p99 661 vs 803 ms; 8-device Jetson AGX/Nano/Pi 5+Hailo-8 rig, burst p99 812 vs 1268 ms.
contribution: A price-based multi-device scheduler for split edge-cloud LLM inference that forecasts query cost before decoding and cuts 99th-percentile latency by 17 percent against a tuned PPO baseline under a 2 s deadline, confirmed on Jetson testbeds.
flag: timing is the contribution: yes - p99 latency and deadline attainment against a 2 s deadline are the headline outcomes, with ablations and forecast-error sensitivity; the application is NOT safety-relevant (general LLM question answering, GSM8K and HumanEval). Check: (1) the file is an Article in Press and the body repeatedly argues with reviewers ('the previous version stated', 'a reviewer asked', 'that claim ... is withdrawn'), so numbers may change in the final version; (2) the model is generative, so I did not credit non-generative inference; multi-agent here means competing devices, not a safety property, so multi-agent state not credited; (3) the 2 s deadline is loose and missed queries are excluded from the p99, so p99 is over admitted queries only - read it with the miss fraction (0.062 at 50 devices, 0.343 at 5000); (4) most results are discrete-event simulation; hardware rigs are 1 and 8 devices; (5) half the paper is differential privacy, off-topic for the review, and its guarantee is weak by the authors' own account (per-user epsilon 61.3). Privacy sections and the convergence analysis were skimmed only.

title: A latency-aware transformer for real-time prediction of driver braking intensity via neuromuscular dynamics under hardware constraints
evidence: "its latency increased to 0.0682 s on the Jetson Tegra X2 SoC, which does not meet the real-time requirement for 200 ms-ahead DBI prediction" (Sec. 8.4 Comparison with baseline methods)
method: LatFormer: transformer predicting driver braking pressure 200 ms ahead from two sEMG channels; evolutionary NAS with a learned latency predictor and a fitness term penalising predicted latency above a threshold Tmax.
evaluation: No numeric deadline stated; Tmax unreported, only the 200 ms prediction horizon. Driving-simulator sEMG, 22533 samples, 11 baselines; Jetson TX2 mean latency 14.4 ms (10 runs) vs Transformer 68.2 ms and 8-channel 57.6 ms; RMSE 0.4951 MPa.
contribution: A latency-aware neural architecture search yields a two-channel sEMG transformer that predicts driver braking intensity 200 ms ahead with 14.4 ms mean inference latency on a Jetson TX2.
flag: timing is the contribution: partly - latency enters the NAS fitness as a penalty above a threshold Tmax and the accuracy-latency trade-off is analysed, but the paper is mainly an application model reporting speed and accuracy; the application is safety-relevant (driver braking prediction for active safety). LIKELY TO BE ARGUED EITHER WAY: I excluded because the value of Tmax is never given, no deadline is stated beyond the 200 ms prediction horizon, and latency is a mean of 10 runs with no tail, worst-case or miss analysis. If the maintainer counts hardware-aware NAS with a latency threshold as budgeted inference, this becomes include with criterion d. Doubts: the text says a 68.2 ms Transformer 'does not meet the real-time requirement' although 68.2 ms is well inside 200 ms, so the actual requirement is unstated; NAS weights are beta 0.4, gamma 0.6 in Section 7 but beta = gamma = 0.5 in the discussion and conclusions; the accuracy-only search gives 456.8 ms latency yet no better RMSE (0.4995); subject-independent RMSE degrades to 0.6124; driving simulator only, no vehicle test; baseline configurations are in supplementary material not in the file.

title: Power- and Time-Aware Deep Learning Inference for Mobile Embedded Devices
evidence: "DeepRT is not to completely avoid deadline misses, but to support QoS management that minimizes the deadline misses" (Sec. II)
method: DeepRT: inference runtime with a MIMO PI feedback controller that every 500 ms adjusts CPU and GPU clock frequencies to hold periodic DNN inference tardiness (latency over deadline) and power at set targets.
evaluation: Soft deadlines 0.05 s (CaffeNet), 0.15-0.2 s (GoogLeNet) on Jetson TK1 with power meter; baselines Open, SISOmax, SISOopen. MIMO tardiness within 7 percent of target (SISOopen 42 percent off); under disturbance tardiness 1.18, settles in one period.
contribution: A feedback-controlled deep learning inference runtime that holds inference latency at a soft deadline and power at a target by jointly scaling CPU and GPU frequencies on a Jetson TK1, robust to workload disturbances.
flag: timing is the contribution: yes - holding DNN inference latency at a stated soft deadline (tardiness target) under disturbance is the paper's purpose, jointly with power; the application is not safety-relevant in the evaluation (image classification with CaffeNet and GoogLeNet), CPS safety is motivation only. Check: (1) the metric is AVERAGE tardiness per 500 ms window with 99 percent confidence intervals; the paper explicitly drops deadline-miss ratio as a metric, so there is no miss rate, tail or worst-case figure, and deadlines are soft; (2) most results are read off figures, few numbers in text, and Tables 3-6 did not survive text extraction, so periods and QoS goals per model could not be verified; (3) GoogLeNet target latency is given as 0.15 s in one experiment and 0.2 s in another; (4) the text says GoogLeNet has '152 layers', which is wrong (22) and suggests loose editing; (5) no accuracy trade-off, model compression is declared out of scope; (6) extends the authors' earlier DeepRT paper [10], check it is not also queued; old hardware (Jetson TK1, Caffe).

title: Using Imperfect Transmission in MEC Offloading to Improve Service Reliability of Time-Critical Computer Vision Applications
evidence: "The optimization goal is to maximize the service reliability, subject to the latency constraint." (Abstract)
method: Multi-user MEC offloading of object-detection tasks that tolerates up to 13% corrupted pixels; UE-ES association, resource blocks and CPU are allocated by semi-definite relaxation under a per-user latency threshold.
evaluation: Simulation only, 5000 Monte Carlo runs, 3 edge servers, 5 UEs; deadline 33, 40 or 66 ms; offloading failure (transmission failure or timeout) about 10x lower than zero-distortion; baselines exhaustive, distance-based; no hardware.
contribution: Shows by simulation that letting offloaded detection images arrive partly corrupted cuts the probability of missing a 33-66 ms deadline by about an order of magnitude versus error-free transmission.
flag: timing is the contribution: yes (timeout probability against a stated deadline is the objective); application generic time-critical vision (AR/VR, vehicles as motivation), not safety-specific. Check: purely numerical - no detector is run in the loop, SSD/YOLOv2 enter only as cycles/bit and a fitted accuracy curve; accuracy assumed unchanged up to 13% distortion, a figure borrowed from a face-recognition paper [11]; the order-of-magnitude gain is read off Figs 2-6 with no table; Table 2 parameters missing from the extracted text; no gain at 33 ms for large images.

title: An Extreme-Edge TCN-Based Low-Latency Collision-Avoidance Safety System for Industrial Machinery
evidence: "A detection triggers a stop of machine movement in real time." (Sec. I)
method: Nine ultrasound sensors on a woodworking machine feed a 560-parameter 8-bit temporal convolutional network on an STM32H7 microcontroller; a positive detection raises a GPIO that halts the machine.
evaluation: Real machine dataset, 5085 windows; derived budget Tmax 0.25 s; STM32H743ZI inference 5.0 ms, 8.2 mJ, acquisition 20.48 ms, both 2.3x below prior TCN [12]; noisy-data sensitivity 90.5%, specificity 95.2%, AUROC 0.972.
contribution: A microcontroller-hosted ultrasound obstacle detector that halts an industrial woodworking machine, with 5 ms inference shown to sit 50x inside a 0.25 s worst-case stopping budget.
flag: timing is the contribution: partly (low latency is one headline claim and is set against a derived 0.25 s budget, but the paper is mainly a dataset plus tiny-model application); safety-relevant: yes, machine halt for operator protection. Most likely to be overturned to E1 as an application paper reporting speed. Check: latency is a single mean, no worst-case or jitter; the budget ignores FPGA-to-MCU transfer and machine braking time; latency baseline is the authors' own earlier technical report [12] and accuracy is not comparable with it; no collision or missed-stop rate on the running machine, only offline window classification; Experiment 0 sensitivity 96.7% contradicts the text saying all medians exceed 97%; not certifiable under current standards by the authors' own statement. Criterion (a) arguable (halting monitor) but not claimed here.

title: Multi-Agent Meta Reinforcement Learning for Reliable and Low-Latency Distributed Inference in Resource-Constrained UAV Swarms
evidence: "we formulate the problem of CNN layer distribution and UAV trajectory planning (LDTP) as an optimization problem to improve latency, reliability, and resource usage" (Abstract)
method: CNN layers of LeNet and AlexNet are distributed across a UAV swarm and UAV positions planned to minimise total latency and transmit power, solved by iterative optimisation and by multi-agent meta-RL with A3C.
evaluation: Simulation on a desktop PC with Raspberry Pi capacity parameters; no deadline or budget; average total latency about 29% lower than MARL-AC/DQN/SAC and within about 9% of the optimisation solution; no tail figures.
contribution: Multi-agent meta-reinforcement learning that places CNN layers across a UAV swarm and plans trajectories to reduce average inference latency and transmit power in simulation.
flag: timing is the contribution: no (average total latency is minimised with no deadline, budget, bound or tail analysis); application is surveillance image classification, not a safety decision. Check: reliability here means a minimum data-rate constraint, not deadline reliability; the 29%, 23% and 9% figures appear only in the abstract and figures, no table of latencies in the text; Raspberry Pi devices are simulated capacity values, nothing runs on them; collision avoidance appears only as a reward term.

title: Managing Timing Uncertainties in Worst-Case Design of Machine Learning Applications
evidence: "Both platforms execute the critical task and send their result as fast as possible to a checker unit, which evaluates at the relative recoverable deadline DR if the results have been received and match each other." (Sec. V)
method: Timing Diversity: two redundant platforms run the same CNN and a checker takes the first matching result at a recoverable deadline, masking rare execution-time outliers; a second deadline triggers the safety layer.
evaluation: YOLOv5/v8 and MobileNets, 100,000-500,000 runs on NXP LX2160A, Intel i5-1240p, Jetson AGX Xavier; feasible deadline 230.06 ms Linux versus 371.01 ms VxWorks on NXP, 87.80 ms on Intel; nearly 6x on Jetson.
contribution: Measures worst-case CNN inference time on nominally identical embedded boards and shows redundant execution with a deadline checker masks timing outliers, allowing deadlines near average-case time on Linux and GPU hardware.
flag: timing is the contribution: yes (observed worst-case execution time and deadline setting for CNN inference); safety-relevant: yes, motivated by robot-human collaboration. Check: the deadlines are observed over finite runs, not proved bounds, and the authors concede simultaneous outliers on both platforms remain possible; no deadline-miss rate is reported in the text and Table 4 values were lost in extraction, so read the PDF table; the 6x claim rests on Fig. 13; the safety layer entered at the non-recoverable deadline is described but not evaluated, so runtime_interceptor yes is generous; the concept is reused from the authors' avionics work, novelty here is the GPU and physical-variation study.

title: A Vehicular-Edge Federated, Quantized YOLOv12 System for Real-Time 3D Hand-Gestures- Based AAV Control
evidence: "We target Te2e < 120 ms" (Sec. III) ... "demonstrates closed-loop viability within a sub-120 ms safety budget" (Abstract)
method: Federated-trained YOLOv12-Nano gesture detector, INT8-quantised to TensorRT, drives AAV commands through ROS 2, MAVLink and PX4; hysteresis filter and watchdog fall back to hover or land on missing gestures.
evaluation: Jetson Xavier NX plus AirSim/PX4 SITL; budget 120 ms camera-to-actuation; INT8 end-to-end 103.2 ms mean, p95 114.5 ms; detector 49.8 ms versus FP32 96.7 and FP16 62.1; mAP 0.947; task success 95-100%.
contribution: A quantised gesture detector on a Jetson Xavier NX controls a simulated drone with a per-stage latency breakdown showing 95th-percentile camera-to-actuation delay of 114.5 ms inside a 120 ms budget.
flag: timing is the contribution: partly (explicit 120 ms budget, per-stage means and p95, precision ablation, but the bulk is federated training and quantisation of an application detector); safety-relevant: weakly, drone teleoperation with hover/land fallback. Likely to be overturned to E1. Check: the 120 ms budget is self-chosen with no derivation; end-to-end latency for FP32 and FP16 is not given in the text so the budget comparison lacks a baseline at that level; only 5.5 ms of p95 headroom and the paper's own field budget (120-170 ms with wireless) exceeds 120 ms; flight is simulation only, yet the text asserts results persist in outdoor trials with no data; 58.2 FPS claimed with a 25 fps camera; watchdog and hover/land fallback are described, not evaluated; prose is formulaic and reads as possibly machine-assisted; tables did not extract, verify numbers in the PDF.

title: Confidence-Guided Multi-Exit Models for Energy-Optimized Object Detection in Road Environments
evidence: "Table 10 reports the mAP, expected latency, energy consumption, FLOPs, and exit coverage for each method." (Sec. IV, results)
method: Two early exits plus final head on MobileNet-V1/V2/V3 and EfficientDet-D0 detectors; a softmax-confidence threshold picks the exit per image to cut expected FLOPs and energy.
evaluation: BDD10K; baselines single-exit, BranchyNet, EENet, JEI-DNN gating. No stated deadline or budget. RTX-3070: exits 8/12/19 ms, energy -14.73%. Jetson AGX Orin: 72.5 ms, 2.18-2.26 J vs 2.67 J.
contribution: Confidence-gated multi-exit road-scene detectors that lower expected energy and mean latency per image on BDD10K, with no deadline, latency budget or tail analysis.
flag: timing is the contribution: no (energy and expected latency only; 'real-time constraints' asserted, never quantified); application safety-relevant (road perception). Check: Jetson AGX Orin figures are reported (72.5 ms) yet the threats-to-validity text says energy was measured on a desktop GPU and future work plans to validate on Jetson AGX Orin; Jetson energy is 2.26 J in abstract but 2.18 J in body; mAP given as 92.3, 90.9 and 0.332 in different places. Early exit trades accuracy against FLOPs, not against a stated latency budget.

title: A Deterministic Real-Time System for Monocular Depth Estimation on a Low-Cost Edge AI Platform: From Kernel to Inference
evidence: "The system achieved mean latency of 116,436 us (116.4 ms) with 99.9th percentile of 192,077 us (192.1 ms) and worst-case of 221,341 us (221.3 ms)." (Sec. V-C, end-to-end pipeline; 'us' is the micro sign in the original)
method: PREEMPT-RT kernel with an isolated core on Raspberry Pi 5 running ADALITE, a distilled INT8 TFLite monocular depth CNN, feeding a collision-warning GPIO alarm pipeline.
evaluation: Raspberry Pi 5 CPU. cyclictest 24 h: stock kernel spikes 3.4 ms vs RT 188 us; heavy load mean 1.34 us, p99.9 11 us, max 76 us. Pipeline over 1000 KITTI frames: mean 116.4 ms, p99.9 192.1 ms, max 221.3 ms; stated budget 100 ms.
contribution: Characterises scheduling jitter and end-to-end tail latency of a distilled monocular depth network on a PREEMPT-RT Raspberry Pi 5, showing microsecond scheduler determinism but a 192 ms p99.9 perception pipeline.
flag: timing is the contribution: yes (kernel jitter plus p99.9 and worst-case pipeline latency); application safety-relevant (collision warning). Check: introduction claims depth 'within 100 ms', a '16 ms execution budget' and '99.8% success in simulated AEB' with a citation, but none of these is evidenced in the body and the measured mean (116.4 ms) already exceeds 100 ms - no deadline-miss rate is reported. The only timing baseline is stock vs RT kernel on cyclictest (scheduler latency, not inference); inference latency itself has no RT-vs-stock comparison. 'WCET' is used for observed maxima (188, 109, 76, 20 us in different places), not analysed bounds. Claims of ASIL-B support are unsubstantiated. The alarm is a buzzer/LED warning, not an override.

title: CertiHybrid-B: A Lyapunov-Budget-Aware Quantized Neural Predictive Controller for Certification-Oriented RTOS–FPGA Co-Architectures
evidence: "the CPU-only architecture misses 46.1% of deadlines, the HetRTOS-style architecture misses 31.9%, and CertiHybrid misses 0.0%" (Sec. IV-B)
method: RTOS-FPGA co-architecture: quantised neural controller on streaming FPGA datapath with hardware Lyapunov monitor, budget-aware mode selector (neural, filtered, LQR fallback) and safety filter clipping the neural action.
evaluation: Simulation only: cart-pole 200 Hz (5 ms deadline), quadrotor 500 Hz (2 ms), lognormal jitter, up to 100 seeds. Miss rate 0% vs NN-CPU 2.3%, LQR-CPU 32.0%; divergence 8/100 to 0/100; RMSE 0.278 to 0.057 rad. Datapath 280-380 ns is an analytical estimate.
contribution: Moves a quantised neural controller, Lyapunov monitor and safety filter onto deterministic FPGA fabric, reporting zero deadline misses and no divergence in simulated cart-pole and quadrotor loops under scheduler jitter.
flag: timing is the contribution: yes (zero-deadline-miss controller path plus Lyapunov budget); application safety-relevant (hard real-time control, but toy plants). Check: NO hardware result - the paper itself says the FPGA figures are an analytical cost model cross-checked by an ARM software proxy on a Kria KV260, with no post-route synthesis ('no synthesis toolchain was available'), so 280-380 ns and <12% utilisation are projections and 'edge deployment' is not claimed here. The 0% miss rate is close to true by construction: the simulator gives the FPGA path a deterministic latency while CPU baseline WCET and jitter are simulator parameters, not measured RTOS traces. In the hard-regime table the CPU baselines' miss entries are N/A. Multi-input safety filter is admitted to be heuristic. Source code only 'on reasonable request'. Text reads as heavily hedged, possibly machine-assisted.

title: Hierarchical inference for efficient and trustworthy automated inspection of electricity grid components
evidence: "all scenarios are tested with three different acceptable latency thresholds per task before failure (100 ms, 60 ms, and 55 ms)" (Sec. IV, simulation setup)
method: Hierarchical inference for drone insulator inspection: calibrated quantised small model on-drone, confidence-threshold offloading of uncertain frames to a larger edge model; AUGRC-driven tuning and FMFP calibration.
evaluation: IDID dataset on Hailo-8L, Coral, Orca (Raspberry Pi 5), STM32MP257F, Jetson Orin Nano: 13-444 FPS. PureEdgeSim, 1-25 drones, budgets 100/60/55 ms (15 FPS, 66.7 ms frame): success ~100% at 100 ms, below 90% beyond 40% offload with 8-10 drones.
contribution: A drone-to-edge hierarchical inference framework that offloads low-confidence insulator images, with simulated task success measured against 55-100 ms per-task latency budgets across fleet size and offloading rate.
flag: timing is the contribution: partly (latency budget is one of five BLERP axes alongside calibration, energy, bandwidth and privacy; the paper is mostly a deployment and calibration study); application safety-relevant only loosely (grid maintenance inspection, no control action). LIKELY TO BE OVERTURNED to E1. Check: all deadline results come from the PureEdgeSim simulator, not hardware, and are shown as curves (Figs. 9-10) with no exact miss rates in the text; Table 5 shows 100% success throughout. Simulator uses 53.7 ms on-drone and 23.7 ms edge inference with 0.01 s fixed link latency, which does not obviously match the measured per-platform FPS tables; no jitter or tail statistics. Abstract says up to ten drones, body discusses 15-25. Baselines are the offloading-rate extremes (edge-only, on-drone-only) rather than a competing scheduler. Offload is deferral to a bigger model, not interception of an action. Author's accepted version, not final typeset; 190k chars, hyperparameter and calibration sections skimmed.

title: Latency Analysis of Cloud Infrastructure for Time-Critical IoT Use Cases
evidence: "The ping test is conducted to measure the round trip delay for the Azure and AWS clouds." (Sec. VI, Conclusion)
method: Ping round-trip-time measurements from one client in Muscat, Oman to Azure and AWS regions, compared with distance-based expected RTT; recommends fog/edge placement and cloud load balancing.
evaluation: Average ping RTT per region only (Azure Dubai 28 ms vs 6 ms expected; AWS Bahrain 71 ms; SE Asia 95 ms). No learned model, no deadline-miss or tail figures, no baseline; proposed load balancing unevaluated.
contribution: Reports average ping round-trip times from Muscat to Azure and AWS regions and recommends fog or edge placement for time-critical IoT, without any inference workload.
flag: timing is the contribution: partly (network RTT only, averages, no tail or jitter analysis); no learned-model inference is run at all - ML inference is only mentioned as motivation; application not safety-specific. Also fails the evaluation floor: the 'proposed approach' (cloud load balancing, recommended 5/33/100 ms tiers) is asserted without any experiment, and the recommended latency tiers are unsourced. Six-page conference paper; GCP excluded from measurements despite the title's 'big three'.

title: Uncertainty-Aware Adaptive Velocity Scaling for Precise Robotic Manipulation
venue: 2026 6th International Conference on Artificial Intelligence and Industrial Technology Applications (AIITA)
evidence: "This latency creates a blind window where the robot executes open-loop actions based on expired observations." (Sec. I)
method: U-VS: training-free execution layer that scales motor velocity down (floor 0.2) when consecutive ACT action chunks disagree, compensating for slow edge inference; plus INT8 quantisation and unified tensor input.
evaluation: Real SO-101 and Koch arms, 3 tasks; no stated deadline (25 Hz data rate only). BM1684X TPU inference 0.068 s SQ vs 0.048 s SQ+UTR, PC 0.053 s. Success 48-68% fixed-velocity vs 69-94% U-VS.
contribution: A plug-in velocity-scaling layer slows a robot arm when successive action-chunk predictions diverge, recovering near-PC task success for a transformer policy running on a low-power edge accelerator.
flag: timing is the contribution: partly (compensating for inference latency is the subject, but the measured outcome is task success, not a timing metric); application mildly safety-relevant (manipulator, no humans). Borderline on the timing floor: the only timing numbers are the Table 2 latency ablation and no deadline, budget, tail or jitter figure is given although the abstract claims jitter is eliminated. Text says SQ-only latency 0.614 s and SQ+UTR 0.103 s (about 6x) but Table 2 shows 0.068 s and 0.048 s. Trial counts, U-VS hyperparameter values and the slowdown in task time are not reported; the claimed approx 40% gain is roughly 20-30 points in Table 3. runtime_interceptor set to yes because the layer attenuates the commanded velocity at execution time, but it never vetoes or halts; maintainer may prefer no. Four-page conference paper.

title: Using Sentinels and Digital Twins to Secure Agentic AI in IoT Systems
venue: 2025 IEEE Annual Congress on Artificial Intelligence of Things (AIoT)
evidence: "The Digital Twin provides a stable schema and validates intents before any device actuation." (Sec. III SHEM - Smart Home Energy Management)
method: LLM smart-home energy agent wrapped by a WebAssembly sentinel requiring goal, plan and per-step justification, and a digital twin that rejects invariant-violating commands and serialises concurrent plans with time-scoped locks, capacity reservations and compensation.
evaluation: Simulated smart home; only measurement is digital-twin HTTP GET/POST cost with 50 concurrent clients and 2000 requests (Fig. 3, values not in text). No safety metric, no baseline.
contribution: An architecture that mediates an LLM home-energy agent's device commands through a signed WebAssembly sentinel and a locking, invariant-checking digital twin, demonstrated by scenario description and a request-latency measurement only.
flag: Pillar 1 - on topic (runtime gate that rejects or pre-empts LLM-agent commands, conflicting concurrent plans) but unevaluated as a safety mechanism: Sec. IV is one paragraph reporting only request cost of the twin, and says the sentinel and gateway were evaluated in earlier papers [36,37]. The four failure modes are narrated, not measured; the abstract and conclusion claim the approach "effectively mitigates" them and keeps sub-second latency, and neither is backed by a number in the text (Fig. 3 values are not in the extracted text - check the PDF figure). The "world model" is a state store with locks, not a learned predictor. Reference list contains IEEE template leftovers. 5 pages plus references; read in full.

title: A Policy-Aware Edge LLM-RAG Framework for Internet of Battlefield Things Mission Orchestration
venue: International Conference on Artificial Intelligence Systems (AIS)
evidence: "This additional validation layer ensures that generated actions satisfy operational policies before execution." (Sec. IV-G)
method: Edge-hosted LLM with policy retrieval (fuzzy plus Jaccard, top-3) emits JSON plans for simulated drones and UGVs; a JudgeLLM (same LLM, validation prompt) checks plans before and after dispatch.
evaluation: RoboDK simulation, 10 fixed commands, 4 quantised LLMs on a CPU-only Ryzen 7 7800X3D workstation; no baseline or ablation; no deadline; mean end-to-end latency 4.17 s (Gemma-2B) to 6.79 s (Qwen-2.5-7B).
contribution: A policy-retrieval LLM orchestrator with an LLM judge for simulated battlefield IoT assets, reporting 100% task success for Gemma-2B at 4.17 s mean latency on a CPU workstation, without baselines.
flag: timing is the contribution: no; application safety-relevant: yes (military mission orchestration, simulated). 'Low-latency' is claimed with no threshold, deadline, tail or jitter analysis; only mean latency in seconds, so it fails the Pillar 4 scope. Check: the JudgeLLM is a pre-execution gate that might read as criterion (a), but the paper never says what happens on a Failure verdict, the judge is the same LLM and also defines the success metric (circular), and there is no baseline or ablation and no violation or detection rate, so it would be E2 on that route too. Abstract claims 'significantly improves reliability' and 'effectively detects policy-violating commands' have no supporting comparison in the body. Hardware is a desktop workstation, not an edge device. Same paper as queued record arxiv:2604.09493 (duplicate; this is the published version) - merge.

title: Hybrid ST-GCN/HMM Tremor Detector for a Wearable MR-Fluid Exoskeleton
venue: 2025 IEEE 21st International Conference on Body Sensor Networks, IEEE BSN 2025
evidence: "(3) All latency and power numbers are analytic projections; oscilloscope-grade measurements on the final PCB remain future work." (Sec. IV, Limitations)
method: Three-block ST-GCN over a 6-axis IMU graph, fused with a small Bayesian network and smoothed by a two-state HMM, to give calibrated tremor posteriors that trigger an MR-fluid damper.
evaluation: Russell 34-subject ADL dataset, offline. Budget: under 80 ms sensor-to-actuator. Jetson Nano INT8, projected not measured: Hybrid 15.2 ms vs LSTM 21.6 ms, ST-GCN 16.6 ms. AUC 0.70 vs 0.55-0.68.
contribution: A graph-convolution plus hidden-Markov tremor detector for a wearable exoskeleton, with projected inference time inside an 80 ms closed-loop budget on an embedded board.
flag: timing is the contribution: partly (latency budget is a stated design goal, accuracy and calibration are the main results); application safety-relevant (wearable actuator on patients). Fails the timing floor as written: every latency and energy figure is an analytic projection from MAC counts, nothing was run on the Jetson Nano, and no closed loop or bench test exists. Maintainer could overturn if projected latency against the 80 ms budget with baselines is accepted. Inconsistencies: Sec. II-F says under 1 ms on Jetson Nano CPU while Table III gives 15.2 ms; text says hybrid 'raises F1 from .37 to .36'; hybrid F1 .36 and recall .32 are below plain ST-GCN (.47,.65); NLL values for baselines are not tabulated; energy stated both as sub-uJ and sub-10 mJ; 4-bit export vs INT8. Single-author paper.

title: Assessing Network Communication Metrics in Cloud-Based BCI Performance for Remote Wheelchair Training of Novice Users
venue: 2024 IEEE Colombian Conference on Communications and Computing (COLCOM)
evidence: "The experiment investigating the effect of latency on system performance varied latency from 500 to 3000 ms." (Sec. III-A)
method: Measurement study of a cloud-hosted SSVEP brain-computer interface (compressive sensing plus CCA classifier over ROS middleware) driving a virtual wheelchair, relating latency, jitter and message loss to accuracy and information transfer rate.
evaluation: 30 healthy subjects, wheelchair simulator; cloud VM Intel i5-2500. No deadline stated (600 s task cap only). Latency 500-3000 ms: accuracy 86.0 to 60.0%, ITR 30.4 to 13.7 bits/min; jitter 1-50 ms no effect. No baseline.
contribution: Correlational study showing that message loss and, more weakly, latency reduce the accuracy of a cloud-based brain-computer interface for virtual wheelchair training, while jitter up to 50 ms has little effect.
flag: timing is the contribution: yes (effect of latency, jitter and loss on a control decision); application safety-relevant only notionally (virtual wheelchair, training). Excluded because condition 2 fails: the classifier is CCA with compressive sensing, not a trained model, and it runs in a cloud VM, not at the edge; maintainer may overturn if CCA decoding is accepted. Also weak: no deadline or budget, no baseline, how latency, jitter and loss were imposed or measured is not described. Suspicious numbers: the latency and MLR experiments report identical ranges for accuracy (86.0 to 60.0%), CPU (13.0 to 15.5%) and RAM (68.2 to 71.5%), yet correlations differ sharply (-0.34 vs -0.99); CPU under jitter (6.2-7.8%) is below the other baselines; latency-CPU correlation is negative though text says CPU rose. Figure callouts are mislabelled and the page header is the unedited LaTeX template.

title: Adapt3D: Lightweight and Adaptive 3D Detection Framework for Mobile GPUs
venue: International Conference on Communication Systems & Networks (COMSNETS)
evidence: "Our scheduler aims to select the optimal execution branch that meets the latency SLO and maximizes accuracy, achieved through offline profiling and online prediction." (Sec. IV-B)
method: Adapt3D: multi-branch LiDAR 3D detector zoo (40+ models over five tuning knobs) with a look-up-table scheduler that picks at runtime the most accurate branch predicted to meet the current latency SLO.
evaluation: Waymo, nuScenes, KITTI on Jetson Orin and Xavier vs seven detectors. SLOs 50-350 ms Waymo, 100-250 ms nuScenes, 35-75 ms KITTI; changing SLO traces 35-65 ms (Orin), 50-125 ms (Xavier). PointPillars about 45 ms, SECOND about 70 ms fixed.
contribution: An adaptive LiDAR 3D detection system for embedded GPUs that switches among 40+ pre-loaded model branches to meet a changing latency SLO while maximising accuracy on Jetson Orin and Xavier.
flag: timing is the contribution: yes (accuracy traded against a stated, changing latency SLO); application safety-relevant (autonomous driving perception). Check: this is a 4-page poster-track paper and all results are in figures; no SLO-violation rate, tail or p99 latency is given, only that SLOs are met 'most of the time' on Xavier. The scheduler predicts latency from average execution times, so there is no worst-case or contention handling. Accuracy gains are quoted inconsistently (1-5%, 1-2.5%, 3-8%, 4-11% on Waymo; 2-7% vs 3-7% vs 5-7% on KITTI). Abstract says KITTI SLOs 35-75 ms, Fig. 8 caption says 50-150 ms. The 63.7% mAP/L2 at over 10 frames per second claim appears only in the contributions list. No vehicle or closed-loop test; offline datasets replayed on the boards.

title: Deterministic Embedded Machine Learning for Adaptive Fighter Aircraft HUD Stabilization
venue: IEEE International Conference on Communication Systems and Network Technologies (CSNT)
evidence: "execution time was measured over 10,000 consecutive on-target inferences using the STM32 hardware cycle counter" (Sec. VII-F Worst-Case Execution Time Analysis)
method: Gyroscope-only motion-state classifier (16-neuron MLP on 1536-sample windows) on a Cortex-M MCU selects predefined HUD rendering profiles; fixed-size windows and hysteresis keep inference time bounded.
evaluation: Budget: 20 ms display cycle (50 Hz). STM32F429 at 180 MHz. Max observed latency over 10,000 runs: MLP 3.3 ms, SVM 3.1, SEFR 2.0, RF 4.3, XGBoost 8.5; MLP balanced accuracy 97.50% (120 validation samples).
contribution: Benchmarks five lightweight classifiers on an STM32F429 for HUD motion-state detection, reporting measured worst-case inference time of 2.0-8.5 ms against a 20 ms display cycle.
flag: timing is the contribution: partly; safety-relevant: yes in framing (fighter HUD), but the ML only changes display gains and is isolated from flight control. Check: 'WCET' is the maximum observed over 10,000 runs, not a static or proved bound; Sec. VII-F says the MLP 'exhibits the lowest WCET' but Table I shows SEFR 2.0 ms and SVM 3.1 ms below MLP 3.3 ms; all five models pass the 20 ms budget with large margin so timing does not discriminate, selection is by accuracy; no HUD jitter or stabilisation result is measured despite abstract claims of improved visual robustness (only screenshots); uncertainty fallback is described but not evaluated; several references look mis-cited (ref 21 XGBoost cited for DO-178C, ref 15 an aerial-image TinyML paper cited for real-time theory), equation numbers blank; dataset is 600 bench sequences, not flight data. Could reasonably be E1 as an application paper reporting speed.

title: MAPLE-Edge: A Runtime Latency Predictor for Edge Devices
venue: IEEE/CVF Conference on Computer Vision and Pattern Recognition Workshops (CVPRW)
evidence: Sec 2.1.2: 'MAPLE-Edge normalizes all performance counters collected by Perf by the measured latency of the respective operator.'
method: Learned regressor that predicts a network's mean inference latency on an unseen edge device from its architecture encoding and six normalised CPU performance counters, adapted with 10 measurements.
evaluation: NAS-Bench-201 on Jetson Nano, TX1, TX2, Pi 4B, vs LUT, HELP, MAPLE. No deadline. Within-10% accuracy e.g. TX1 TRT 96.68% vs HELP 79.88%; up to +49.6 points over MAPLE.
contribution: Predicts mean inference latency of candidate networks on unseen edge devices from hardware performance counters, reaching about 91-97% of predictions within 10% on Jetson TensorRT runtimes with 10 adaptation samples.
flag: timing is the contribution: yes in the sense that predicting inference latency is the whole paper; application not safety-relevant (NAS tooling). BORDERLINE, maintainer to rule: condition 1 names 'predicting' inference timing, but what is predicted is mean latency for architecture search, with no deadline, budget, bound, tail or jitter anywhere in method or evaluation. The only quantitative result is prediction accuracy (share within +/-10%), which is none of the four result types the evaluation floor lists, hence E2; E1 is equally defensible. If mean-latency predictors are in scope, flip to include with criteria d and add edge deployment (latencies measured on real Jetson and Pi boards). No gain over the lookup-table baseline on Raspberry Pi TFLite (54.00% vs 55.18%). Same call made for PerfSAGE.

title: Training Strategies for Vision Transformers for Object Detection
venue: 2023 IEEE/CVF Conference on Computer Vision and Pattern Recognition Workshops (CVPRW)
evidence: "We showed that our strategies are able to improve inference-time by 63% at the cost of performance drop of mere 3%" (Abstract)
method: Down-scaling study of a multi-view DETR-style 3D detector: input resolution, cropping, decoder layers, embedding size, query count, NMS, TensorRT and float16.
evaluation: No deadline or budget stated (only "at-least 10hz"). NVIDIA T4 GPU. Latency 447 ms full model down to 62 ms TensorRT float16; AP per ablation row against unmodified detector.
contribution: Ablation of training and model-scaling choices for a multi-view transformer 3D object detector, reporting average latency on a T4 GPU against detection accuracy.
flag: timing is the contribution: no - speed and accuracy of a compressed detector are reported, with no deadline, budget, bound or tail analysis; application (autonomous driving perception) is safety-relevant. T4 is a datacentre GPU, not edge hardware. Check: text says 598x394 costs 1.4%/0.5% AP but Table 2 shows 0.4/0.9; baseline AP differs between Tables 2-3 and 5-7; the abstract's 63%/3% figure is not tied to one table row.

title: Collaborative Processing for Multi-Tenant Inference on Memory-Constrained Edge TPUs
venue: 2026 22nd International Conference on Distributed Computing in Smart Systems and the Internet of Things (DCOSS-IoT)
evidence: "SwapLess reduces end-to-end latency by up to 63.8% and 77.4% compared to the baselines" (Sec. V.C)
method: SwapLess splits each DNN once between Edge TPU prefix and CPU suffix; greedy hill-climbing over an M/G/1 and M/D/k queueing latency model re-allocates online to reduce memory-swap overhead.
evaluation: Coral USB Edge TPU on Raspberry Pi 5, 9 CNNs; vs Edge TPU Compiler, threshold partitioning, alpha=0 ablation; no deadline or SLO; mean latency cut up to 77.4%; model MAPE 1.9-6.8%; <3 ms decisions.
contribution: SwapLess partitions multi-tenant CNN inference between a Coral Edge TPU and Raspberry Pi 5 CPU cores using a queueing latency model, cutting mean end-to-end latency by up to 77.4% against the Edge TPU compiler.
flag: timing is the contribution: partly; application safety-relevant: no (safety-critical scenarios only as motivation). Title matches the record (arXiv id is correct). The objective (Eq. 5) is rate-weighted expected latency: no deadline, budget, SLO, p95/p99, jitter or worst-case bound, so it falls under 'minimises average latency'. The one thing that could argue for inclusion is the validated analytic latency predictor on real hardware (MAPE 1.9% single-tenant, 6.8% multi-tenant; 92.3% of predictions within 5%) - maintainer to decide whether timing prediction of means suffices. Abstract attributes 63.8% and 77.4% to the Edge TPU compiler; body says 'the baselines' at rho=0.5 without naming which.

title: Towards A Protocol-Agnostic Universal Middleware For IoT With Edge Intelligence
venue: 2026 22nd International Conference on Distributed Computing in Smart Systems and the Internet of Things (DCOSS-IoT)
evidence: "Phase 1 (Safety Shield) enforces absolute battery and signal thresholds." (Sec. III-C Client-Side Intelligent Protocol Selection)
method: IoT middleware with single-port O(1) detection of MQTT, CoAP and HTTP; on ESP32 clients a LinUCB bandit picks the transport, preceded by a threshold rule forcing a safe protocol on low battery or signal.
evaluation: ESP32 hardware-in-the-loop plus i7 server; 40-60 us core overhead, 12,000 msg/s, P99 latency 185.4 ms vs about 509 ms Mosquitto, jitter 2.5x lower, 99-100% delivery. Shield not evaluated separately.
contribution: A protocol-agnostic IoT middleware whose edge clients choose between MQTT, CoAP and HTTP with a contextual bandit behind a battery and signal threshold rule, reducing latency jitter against static protocol configurations.
flag: neither - the "safety shield" is a two-condition threshold check (battery, RSSI) at the top of the protocol selector (Algorithm 2, Phase 1); it is a minor component of a networking middleware paper, and safety here means reliable message delivery, not hazard prevention. No result isolates the shield: no violation or intervention rate, no shield-off ablation; thresholds and the safe protocol are not specified. No multi-agent hazard, no deferral or handoff. The abstract's sub-50 us decision latency is not supported by a measurement in the evaluation section (only 40-60 us core overhead is reported). Short paper (4 pages), read in full.

title: Safety-Prioritised Multimodal Navigation for Edge Smart Glasses with Constrained on-Device Language Models
evidence: "LLM outputs are treated as candidate actions and are validated against safety constraints before being issued to the user" (Sec III-F, Hierarchical Decision-Making Framework)
method: Five-state FSM on Jetson Orin Nano ranks audio hazard, object under 1 m, QR and LLM guidance; hazard states suppress or reject candidate actions from a quantised Qwen 0.5B model.
evaluation: Component tests: YOLOv5 vs SSD, audio CNNs, 20 human-rated prompts (0.5B 0/20 wrong, 1.8B 13/20), LLM latency 2.17 s; one 9 min 45 s supervised corridor trial.
contribution: Smart-glasses navigation aid in which a rule-based hazard-first state machine overrides a small on-device language model, shown working in one supervised indoor trial without a measured safety rate.
