flag: Pillar 1 by mechanism (FSM veto over LLM actions), but the mechanism has no quantitative safety result and no baseline or ablation: the paper says 'a full ablation study was not conducted' and the only system evidence is one single-participant trial 'without collision'. The 0/20 vs 13/20 error rates compare two LLM sizes, not the FSM on vs off. Also single-agent, single-user guardrail, so E4 is a defensible alternative. The safety envelope is specified (Sec IV-A, eq. 1a-1b) but never evaluated: the paper promises 'compliance with the runtime safety envelope' and unimodal-vs-fused ablations in Sec III and the abstract, and neither appears in Results; the conclusion admits 'limited assessment of dialogue correctness and safety-task performance' and lists safety-violation rates as future work. All numbers are system metrics (inference 3-4 s INT8, RAM, CPU). The latency-quantile gate is a neat idea for RQ2 but with 3 s inference it is far from a reflex. Section numbering jumps from II to IV in places and the fusion adapter described is not evaluated either. Passenger dialogue rather than control: it 'defers ultimate control authority' to the vehicle stack, so not a Pillar 3 deferral paper.

title: Mutual Information and Latency-Aware Adaptive Control for Resource-Efficient Graph Neural Networks
venue: International Conference on Machine Learning and Computing
evidence: "We evaluate test set accuracy, precision (true positives over predicted positives), energy consumption (mJ per inference), and latency (ms per inference)." (Sec 4.1, Metrics)
method: MLC-GNN: an MLP controller adjusts GNN depth, bit precision and channel width per inference from a mutual-information estimate, with a PID guard holding energy near a target.
evaluation: Four node-classification graphs, five baselines, ablation; Raspberry Pi 5 and Jetson Nano. No latency deadline or budget stated; mean latency only, e.g. Cora 4.2 ms vs GCN 5.1; ogbn-arxiv 11.9 vs 16.8.
contribution: Adaptive GNN that varies depth, precision and width at inference time under an energy target, reporting lower energy and slightly lower mean latency than static and quantised baselines on small edge boards.
flag: timing is the contribution: no - energy is the controlled quantity (PID guard on mJ, energy budget Ehmax never given a value) and latency is only a reported mean with no deadline, budget, bound or tail; application not safety-relevant (citation and co-purchase graph benchmarks). Check: abstract and conclusion claim inference delay cut 'by up to 50%' and Sec 4.2 says 'over 50%', but Table 1 shows at most about 30% (ogbn-arxiv 16.8 to 11.9 ms) and 18% on Cora, and only 0-0.1 ms better than DeltaGNN; Table 1 does not say which of the two boards the figures come from; energy sampled at 1-second intervals yet reported per inference in mJ; CUDA 11.8 stated for a setup that includes Raspberry Pi 5; several references look unreliable (author lists for TinyGNN, DeltaGNN, Degree-quantized GNN, SkipNet do not match the known papers), which suggests machine-assisted drafting. Title says latency-aware but latency never enters the controller inputs.

title: Hierarchical Scheduling of Hybrid DNN Tasks in Embedded Real-Time Systems
venue: International Conference on Parallel and Distributed Systems
evidence: "The experimental results show that LHTS can achieve more sufficient use of heterogeneous CPU and GPU resources in embedded real-time systems, reduce the worst-case execution time and enhance the schedulability performance of hybrid DNN tasks." (Abstract)
method: LHTS: integer-programming, layer-level scheduler that maps each layer of periodic real-time and best-effort DNN tasks to CPU or GPU and sets non-overlapping start times so deadlines are met at minimum utilisation.

contribution: Layer-by-layer CPU/GPU scheduling of mixed real-time and best-effort DNN tasks formulated as an integer programme, reporting a higher schedulability ratio than EDF and a fixed-priority layer scheduler in simulation.
flag: timing is the contribution: yes (deadline-constrained scheduling of DNN inference layers); application not safety-relevant in itself (autonomous driving only named as motivation). Check, this is the weakest include: a 2-page poster-length paper; no neural network is ever run - the 'DNN tasks' are randomly generated periodic task sets, so condition (2) holds only by task model; all results are in figures, the only number in the text is the 70-90% schedulability ratio, with no baseline values stated; 5 runs per point; units of periods not given; the constraint list has a stray '(9f)' label and the algorithm itself is not described beyond the optimisation problem. If the floor requires numeric baseline values in the text, this becomes exclude-E2.

title: CLF-SFC: Freshness-Aware Service Function Chain Orchestration Across End-Edge-Cloud
venue: International Conference on Parallel and Distributed Systems
evidence: "We define a Control-Loop Freshness (CLF) objective that combines 95th/99th-percentile (P95/P99) end-to-end latency with an Age of Information (AoI) proxy." (Abstract)
method: CLF-SFC: jointly picks YOLOv5 variant and end/edge/cloud placement for a perception-fusion-policy chain; union bound splits a tail-risk budget across stages and Cantelli's inequality turns profiled mean/variance into per-stage percentile budgets.
evaluation: SLO tau=50 ms. Profiles from i7-12700, Xeon 8255C, RTX 3090; network synthesised. vs SLP, NRH, edge-only, cloud-only: P95 48.2 vs 51.4/58.7 ms at 150 Mbps; P99 54.5 vs 57.7/65.0 ms at 100 Mbps.

flag: timing is the contribution: yes (P95/P99 and SLO-violation control with a proved Pr(L>tau)<=eps bound for a chain containing YOLOv5 inference); safety-relevant only as motivation (embodied AI, navigation), no safety task evaluated. Check: results are NOT measured end to end - per-stage times are sampled from offline profiles and links use an analytic 8p/B+RTT model with 0-3 ms injected jitter, so I did not tick edge deployment (the 'end' and 'edge' tiers are a desktop i7 and a Xeon server; the edge tier reuses the CPU profile); the P95 figures quoted at 150 Mbps (48.2/51.4/58.7 ms) are repeated verbatim as the P99 figures at 150 Mbps, a copy error in one of the two; SLO-violation results are given only as a figure with no numbers; Fig 5 label reads 'P95 > SLA'; AoI gains (8% vs NRH, 6% vs SLP) are stated without a table and the text says AoI is 'recorded but not plotted'; the Cantelli bound assumes profiled mean/variance stay valid; fusion and policy stages are lightweight or rule-based, only perception is a learned model.

title: Stream-to-Act: ROS 2 Native Token Streaming for Continuous Motion Execution of Vision-Language-Action Models
venue: Proceedings - IEEE International Conference on Robotics and Automation/Proceedings
evidence: "We therefore define the minimal safe start time S0 that guarantees contiguous execution (no stalls)" (Sec IV-F, Stream-to-Act Formulation)
method: ROS 2-native llama.cpp pipeline that streams VLM plan tokens straight to an executor; execution starts at a computed minimal start time S0 and skills stretch within Tmin/Tmax so token gaps never stall motion.
evaluation: MiniCPM-2.6 on RTX 4080, Jetson AGX Orin, Orin Nano (34.2/4.8/0.58 tokens/s). No fixed deadline; stall-free bound proved. E2E 15.5+-1.0 ms vs 101.8+-8.6 ms HTTP/JSON on AGX Orin; Carla braking demo vs naive and wait-then-act.
contribution: Token-streaming execution for vision-language planners on ROS 2 that derives the earliest start time guaranteeing gap-free motion and removes HTTP/JSON serialisation delay, measured on Jetson boards.
flag: timing is the contribution: yes (when to start acting on a token stream so execution never stalls, plus end-to-end latency of the serving path); safety-relevant: yes in framing (Euro NCAP rear-braking scenario in Carla). Check: no deadline or latency budget is stated, so I did not tick latency/jitter aware - inclusion rests on the proved stall-free start time S0 and the 15.5 vs 101.8 ms comparison; the conclusion cites 'stall ratio and stop-and-go count' but neither is reported anywhere, stalls are shown only as timeline plots; the collision outcomes (naive hits trailing car, wait-then-act hits lead car) are a single qualitative demo with no trials or rates; the stall-free claim is a proof sketch assuming regular token arrivals and equal nominal skill durations, and the paper itself lists a formal characterisation as future work; the 15.5 ms figure excludes model inference (it covers capture and serialisation only) and the HTTP baseline is fed a pre-encoded JPEG, so the comparison is not like for like; on Orin Nano S0 reaches 76.6 s, i.e. the method works by waiting; not a runtime safety interceptor - it delays the start of a plan, it cannot veto one; title says vision-language-action but the model is a VLM emitting skill calls.

title: Process-State-Aware Remote MEC GPU Sharing for Vision-Guided Collaborative Robotic Welding

title: Scaling Concurrent LLM Services via Self-Adaptive Load Balancing in Edge Environments
venue: 2026 IEEE International Conference on Web Services (ICWS)
evidence: "achieving a P99 tail latency reduction exceeding 50% at N = 3" (Sec. IV, comparative evaluation, Hotspot scenario)

BORDERLINE: throughput is the headline metric (Table I is throughput only); tail latency is a control signal and a secondary result with no deadline or budget, and P99 values are given only as '>50% reduction' and '12-28 s' read off box plots (Fig. 6), no latency table. Acknowledgment says Claude was used for language polishing. If the maintainer requires a deadline or budget, this is E1.

title: EdgeReasoning: Characterizing Reasoning LLM Deployment on Edge GPUs
venue: Proceedings - 2025 IEEE International Symposium on Workload Characterization, IISWC 2025
evidence: "Evaluation of test-time scaling methods to maximize accuracy under dynamic latency constraints." (Sec. I, contributions)
method: EdgeReasoning: characterisation study of reasoning LLMs (DSR1-Qwen-1.5B/Llama-8B/Qwen-14B, L1, non-reasoning peers) on an edge GPU; fits analytical prefill+decode latency and energy models; maps token-budget, model-size and parallel-scaling choices to an accuracy-latency Pareto frontier.
evaluation: Budgets: latency regimes (<1 s real-time, sub-5 s, 15-30 s, >30 s; example 20 s), no single deadline or miss rate. Hardware: NVIDIA Jetson AGX Orin 64GB. MMLU-Redux (3000 questions). Time-between-tokens 0.024/0.10/0.186 s for 1.5B/8B/14B; latency model MAPE <2% on 50 held-out questions; 14B at 256-token cap 21 s vs 8B unconstrained 87 s at similar accuracy; non-reasoning Llama3.1-8B 6.60 s vs 87.2 s for 5.7% less accuracy.
contribution: Characterises reasoning-LLM inference on a Jetson AGX Orin, with a validated token-to-latency model and a Pareto map showing which model size and token budget maximise accuracy within a given latency budget.
flag: timing is the contribution: yes; application safety-relevant: no (robotics is motivation only; evaluated on MMLU-Redux question answering). Latencies are seconds to minutes, three orders of magnitude from the review's sub-15 ms target; useful as evidence that LLM reasoning cannot sit in a fast safety loop and for the predictable-latency model. No deadline-miss rate or tail/percentile analysis: all figures are average latency per question, and 'deterministic latency control' is claimed via hard token caps rather than measured jitter. Authors are NVIDIA staff evaluating NVIDIA hardware. I read the main body and conclusions; quantisation (Sec. V-F), parallel-scaling energy details and the appendix tables (X-XXI) were only skimmed.

title: FlexInfer: A Multi-Agent Reinforcement Learning Approach for Device–Edge–Cloud Collaborative Inference
evidence: "Constraint C2 requires that each task meet its delay requirement." (Sec. III, problem formulation)
method: FlexInfer: MAPPO-derived multi-agent RL where each device picks execution node (device/edge/cloud), model partition point and compression level; reward is delay normalised by task deadline plus compatibility, cost and accuracy terms.
evaluation: Simulation only (Python, Ray RLlib, NS-3; Wake Vision workload); no real hardware. Deadlines: 10-30 ms device, 50-200 ms edge, 500 ms-2 s cloud tasks. Vs Edge-First, DQN-Offloading, IA2C: lowest deadline violation rate across load, about 17% below IA2C at arrival rate 1.5; lower end-to-end delay CDF (moderate tasks). No tabulated latency figures.
contribution: A cooperative multi-agent RL scheduler that jointly chooses offload target, model split and compression for deadline-tagged inference tasks, cutting simulated deadline violations by about 17% relative to independent A2C.
flag: timing is the contribution: yes (deadline-constrained scheduling, deadline violation rate is a primary metric); application safety-relevant: no (generic AI inference tasks). Check: entirely simulated with abstract compute models (GFLOPS, cycles/bit) and an assumed accuracy-decay formula A0*exp(-gamma*r); no neural network is actually partitioned or timed, so 'learned-model inference' holds only at the modelling level. Results are given as curves (Figs. 2-5) with a single quoted number (17%, unclear whether relative or percentage points); no seeds, variance or absolute DVR values in the text. Multi-agent here means RL agents for offloading, not multi-agent state for safety. Short INFOCOM-volume paper (appears to be a workshop/poster-length paper; venue track not stated in the text).

title: Toward Real-Time On-Device WLAN Handover Control via Prompt Refinement
evidence: "This violates the real-time constraint, as the next decision epoch arrives before the previous inference concludes" (Sec. IV-B.2, Inference Latency and Feasibility)
method: Local quantised Llama-3.1-8B acts as slow supervisory controller tuning the WLAN handover RSSI threshold every 30 s from a 10 s context; three prompt strategies compared, including one refined by a Gemini teacher.
evaluation: Budget: 30 s control period. Hardware: workstation, Intel i9-9920X + NVIDIA RTX 2080 Ti (edge surrogate, not an edge device). Replay of a ~1000 s 1 Hz Wi-Fi trace. Inference time: attention-biased prompt 48.40 s (+85.3%, exceeds budget), teacher-guided 18.58 s (-28.8% vs baseline prompt, implying ~26 s); teacher-guided ~10 fewer handovers, -2.7 dB mean RSSI; biased +4.0 dB.
contribution: Shows that prompt structure decides whether an on-device LLM handover supervisor fits its 30 s control period: a teacher-refined prompt cuts inference time to 18.6 s while a verbose one overruns at 48.4 s.
flag: timing is the contribution: partly (latency against the control period is the headline feasibility result, but the lever is prompt wording); application safety-relevant: no (Wi-Fi QoS). Workshop paper (INFOCOM GenAINet 2026), thin evaluation: one trace, single latency number per prompt, no variance or percentiles, no non-LLM handover baseline for latency. Inconsistencies to check: abstract and intro say 8-bit quantised, Sec. III-B says 2-bit (q2_K GGUF); the teacher-guided prompt is called Pguide in text but Pcons in Table II; the baseline prompt's latency cell did not survive extraction (about 26 s implied) which would also fit the 30 s period, so the claim that the guided prompt is the only one that fits 'comfortably' is soft. The 30 s 'real-time' budget is self-chosen to accommodate the model. Hardware is a desktop GPU, so no edge-deployment cell. Figures were garbled in the extracted text.

title: Poster Abstract: DeepRT: A Predictable Deep Learning Inference Framework for IoT Devices

contribution: A poster proposing DeepRT, a deadline-aware deep learning runtime that tracks per-layer milestones and uses feedback-controlled frequency scaling to hold inference response time at a target on an embedded board.

title: FPGA Acceleration of DL-Based Real-Time DC Series Arc Fault Detection
venue: IEEE International Symposium on Parallel & Distributed Processing, Workshops and Phd Forum
evidence: "The execution time limit is set to 10 milliseconds." (Sec. III-A)

evaluation: 30,000 recorded current windows (160 samples at 16 kHz). Budget 10 ms. Avnet Ultra96-V2: 60 us float 4 PEs (192 us 1 PE; 42 us half), 3.04 W, 99.07%. Jetson Xavier NX: 143-381 us, 98.96%.
contribution: An FPGA accelerator for neural-network DC series arc fault detection that runs in 60 microseconds on an Ultra96-V2 board, against 143 microseconds on a Jetson Xavier NX, well inside a 10 ms limit.
flag: timing is the contribution: partly; application IS safety-relevant (arc fault / fire protection, detection should trigger shutdown). Reads as an application paper that deploys a small classifier on edge hardware and reports average runtime: budget of 10 ms is stated but beaten by about 100x with no deadline-aware mechanism, no tail, worst-case or jitter figures, pre-recorded data only (no ADC in loop; about 100 us memory read excluded). If the maintainer counts 'average latency against a stated budget on real hardware vs a GPU baseline' as enough, this flips to include (d). Inconsistency: GPU peak power 2936 mW in text vs 2963 mW in Table I vs 2.96 W in abstract.

title: ArtFL: Exploiting Data Resolution in Federated Learning for Dynamic Runtime Inference via Multi-Scale Training
venue: International Symposium on Information Processing in Sensor Networks
evidence: "The key idea of ArtFL is to utilize the data resolution, i.e., frame resolution of videos, as a knob to accommodate dynamic inference latency requirements." (Abstract)
method: Federated multi-scale training so one model accepts several input resolutions; at inference a linear program picks per-frame resolution under time budget T using adjacent-frame similarity; latency-based data dropping shortens FL rounds.

contribution: A federated learning system that trains one multi-resolution model and then selects per-frame input resolution at runtime to meet inference deadlines of 10-30 ms on Jetson devices with little accuracy loss.
flag: timing is the contribution: partly; application safety-relevant by framing (traffic-sign recognition on a 1/10-scale car, patient activity monitoring). Roughly half the paper is federated TRAINING efficiency (multi-scale training, data dropping, waiting time), which the rulings exclude; the inference half trades accuracy against stated deadlines, which qualifies. Headline 36.36% and 47.81% gains are from the abstract; I did not trace them to a specific table. Read: abstract, Sec. 1-3, 4.2-4.3 in part, 6.2, 7.2; skimmed the rest. flag: timing is the contribution: no; application is safety-relevant (pedestrian collision warning). No learned model anywhere - all four predictors are closed-form geometry, so Pillar 4 condition 2 fails. Timing is reported only as speed, with no deadline or budget and no baseline; execution times were measured offline on a desktop CPU, not on the edge unit; authors admit many false positives and no ground truth for accuracy. The alert only warns a person, nothing is overridden.

title: Reinforcement-Learning-Empowered MLaaS Scheduling for Serving Intelligent Internet of Things
evidence: "We evaluate our approach under the scenario of meeting strict SLO target, i.e., 95th percentile latency SLO of 235 ms for Inception and 1060 ms for DeepSpeech." (Sec. VI-F)
method: Region-based reinforcement learning (RRL Plus) tunes request-level and operation-level parallelism or GPU batching in TensorFlow Serving to minimise latency or meet a latency SLO under changing load.
evaluation: Ten dual-socket Xeon servers with GTX 1080 Ti; Inception, ResNet, DeepSpeech; baselines CAPES, DeepRM. SLO p95 235 and 1060 ms (loose 400-2500 ms). Latency down to 88.9%, SLO violations down to 91.6%.
contribution: A region-based reinforcement-learning scheduler for cloud model serving that tunes parallelism to meet 95th-percentile latency objectives, cutting objective violations by up to 91.6% against two deep reinforcement-learning tuners.
flag: timing is the contribution: yes (SLO-aware serving, p95 latency and SLO-violation reduction against baselines); application not safety-relevant (image classification and speech serving). Recommended exclude only because the inference runs on a cloud server cluster, not at the edge, on a device or split - condition 2 as worded fails. If the maintainer counts cloud MLaaS serving IoT clients as in scope this becomes an include with criteria d. Check: violation percentages are relative reductions read from figures, absolute violation rates are not given in text; the full Xeon model number was not read; journal extension of a conference paper [1].

title: To Improve Service Reliability for AI-Powered Time-Critical Services Using Imperfect Transmission in MEC: An Experimental Study
evidence: "it is more important to minimize the timeout probability by shortening transmission latency than perfect error-free transmission" (Abstract)
method: Models service reliability of offloaded DNN image classification as transmission reliability, timeout probability and inference accuracy; offloads over UDP tolerating image distortion, plus early termination of image reception (ETR).
evaluation: Intel NUC to Jetson TX2 over WiFi; AlexNet, VGG16, ResNet-50; thresholds 30-100 ms (33/66/99). UDP about 90% normalised reliability vs TCP under 20% at 30 ms; VGG16 105.81 ms on TX2; ETR 80% to 90%.
contribution: Experimental study showing that for deadline-bound offloaded image classification, lossy UDP transfer beats TCP because lower timeout probability outweighs the small accuracy loss from distorted images, with an early-termination scheme adding up to 10%.
flag: timing is the contribution: yes (timeout probability against a latency threshold, latency CDFs over real WiFi, accuracy traded against the deadline); application is only motivated as safety-relevant (autonomous driving, remote surgery) - the experiments are ImageNet-style classification. Check: thresholds apply to transmission latency (inference time is treated separately), parts of the reliability results (packet-loss and BER sweeps, ETR) are numerical simulation built on the measured distributions, not end-to-end measurements; the abstract's up to 70% gain is read from figures. Baseline is TCP offloading. No interception of any action.

title: Dynamic Compression Ratio Selection for Edge Inference Systems With Hard Deadlines
evidence: "The key idea is to balance the tradeoff between communication cost and inference accuracy" (Abstract); objective is the number of tasks completed correctly before their hard deadline (Sec. II).
method: Edge server picks a per-task image compression ratio from queue state via an MDP (offline DP as upper bound), with entropy-triggered retransmission at lower compression and packet-loss-aware retransmission.
evaluation: Simulation only, deadline 12 slots; MNIST MLP and CIFAR-10 MobileNet-v2 at edge server; vs fixed resolution, offline DP. 97.5% tasks completed on MNIST at rate 0.5 (+4.5%); online within 0.2% of offline. No hardware.
contribution: Chooses the data compression ratio per offloaded inference task with an MDP so that the most tasks finish correctly before a hard deadline, nearly matching an offline optimum in simulation.
flag: timing is the contribution: yes (hard per-task deadline is the constraint and deadline-and-correct completion ratio is the metric); application not safety-relevant (image classification; safety only as motivation). Check: purely simulated - time is in abstract slots (the companion magazine article says 1 slot = 10 ms, this paper as read does not give a wall-clock value), only communication delay is modelled, server inference time is ignored, no hardware. No proved bound; the offline DP is an empirical upper bound. Several results are given only as approximate gains (about 1%, 2%, 4%, 5%) and the fixed-resolution comparison has no exact figure in the text. Accuracy lookup for CIFAR-10 is said to come from the training set in one place and test set in another. Uncertainty-based augmentation is worse than plain online when the deadline is small. Abstract has no numbers. Overlaps with the inference case study in arxiv 2009.11065 (same group).

title: A Framework for Runtime Safety of Industrial Control Systems Through Runtime Verification
evidence: "To address violations detected by the verifier, an OC module is responsible for selecting the appropriate correction strategy and sending the corresponding instructions to the ICS via OPC UA" (Sec IV-A Framework Overview)
method: PSRVer: non-intrusive stream runtime verification for PLC systems. TeSSLa timed specifications become monitors that read several controllers over OPC UA and send online correction commands on violation.
evaluation: Four injected-fault scenarios on a three-PLC material-processing line (CODESYS soft-PLCs, Factory I/O simulator). Detection traces shown; feature-table comparison with prior frameworks. No rates or timing statistics.
contribution: Platform-independent runtime verification framework for industrial control that monitors timed safety properties across several cooperating PLCs over OPC UA and issues online corrections, demonstrated on four injected-fault case studies.
flag: Pillar 1 and the closest fit in this batch: a genuine runtime monitor with correction across three controllers (Scenario 4 is a cross-PLC load invariant). It fails the evaluation floor as written: evidence is four hand-injected scenarios with single traces, and the only comparison is Table II, a yes/no feature checklist against prior tools, not a measured baseline. No detection rate, false-alarm rate, overhead or latency distribution. If the maintainer accepts case-study verification papers as formal-methods evidence this is the one to reconsider. Note the monitor is reactive, not pre-emptive: it corrects after the violation is observed (Scenario 1: violation at 51.624, M2 stopped at 52.330, about 0.7 s later), with a 1 s verification cycle and 20 ms OPC UA collection, and the authors concede network delay 'could lead to invalid verification results'. Only Scenarios 1 and 4 show a correction; 2 and 3 show detection only. Multi-controller cooperation is a feature claim, not the primary measured outcome, so (c) not credited.

title: StateShield: Real-Time Defense Against Adversarial Attacks on Edge-Deployed DRL Agents
evidence: "providing worst case response time (WCRT) bounds that account for detector, mitigator, and policy network costs on both clean and attack paths" (Sec. I, contributions)
method: Detects adversarial observation attacks on a DRL agent by checking a small predictable state subset (SSR), replaces attacked states with a GRU reconstruction, and pipelines detector, reconstructor and policy in parallel or speculatively with WCRT analysis.
evaluation: Jetson AGX Xavier; robot navigation, cluster scheduling, Atari Pong; baselines Foresight, GRU-VAE. 96.2% detection, overhead cut up to 96%; stress test under rate-monotonic load: Foresight mean about 28 ms, tail past 38 ms, StateShield about one-third.
contribution: A lightweight runtime defense for edge reinforcement-learning agents that detects and repairs adversarial observations within a per-step deadline, with worst-case response-time bounds and measured response-time distributions on a Jetson AGX Xavier.
flag: timing is the contribution: yes (WCRT bound for the defended inference pipeline plus response-time distributions against two defenses); application is safety-relevant in framing (robot obstacle avoidance) but tasks are Gazebo simulation, a scheduler and Pong. Check: the numeric per-step deadline and periods sit in Table V, which did not survive text extraction, and I found no deadline-miss rate in the prose - compliance is argued from boxplots (Fig. 16), so confirm the latency cell against the PDF. Interceptor acts on the observation (substitutes a reconstructed state), not on the action: (a) is borderline. Cross-domain cell rests on robot navigation plus cluster scheduling, both simulated. Table values for FPR and clean performance not read (tables lost in extraction).

title: Multimodal Sensing, Aerial Communication, and Edge Inference in Open RAN-Empowered LEO Satellite-Assisted Low-Altitude Networks
evidence: "The tolerated latency d = 80 ms" (Sec. V-A Simulation Setup); uRLLC-slice E2E service delay must stay below d (Sec. II, eq. 3)
method: Dual-timescale O-RAN slicing for UAV+LEO split DNN inference: attention-enhanced MAPPO picks sensing time and AlexNet split layer; expert modules do subcarrier matching and hybrid FCFS-EDF satellite scheduling that discards infeasible tasks.
evaluation: Simulation only: 5 UAVs, one LEO satellite, AlexNet split, 12/20 GFLOPS; uRLLC deadline 80 ms; baselines no-expert ablation, MAPPO, MADDPG; utility and average uRLLC latency in figures only, about 4.5% ablation drop.
contribution: Slice-aware multi-agent RL jointly sets sensing duration and DNN split point for UAV-to-LEO edge inference under an 80 ms uRLLC delay constraint, with EDF scheduling at the satellite; simulated only.
flag: timing is the contribution: partly; application (UAV disaster sensing) not safety-relevant in the evaluation. Headline metric is a composite system utility, not deadline-miss rate; the delay constraint enters as a +1/-1 reward term. Average uRLLC latency vs bandwidth (Fig. 7) is plotted but no numeric latency or miss-rate values are given in the text - check whether Fig. 7 clears the evaluation floor, else E2; could equally be judged E1 as a resource-allocation paper. All simulation, FLOPs-based delay model, no hardware, no tail analysis.

title: A Real-Time Cardiac Decision Support System for Internet of Medical Things Using Edge AI and DDS
evidence: "the worst-case one-way wireless latency was 22.0540 ms, which remains below the 300 ms threshold typically recommended for real-time medical telemetry" (Sec. VI-B Communication Performance)
method: ECG arrhythmia decision support: demographic-specific MobileNetV3 classifiers at an inference node, alerts published over RTI Connext DDS (Reliable vs Best Effort QoS) to a Raspberry Pi 5 caregiver node.
evaluation: Budget 300 ms end-to-end, 30 ms jitter. GPU workstation publisher, Raspberry Pi 5 subscriber; wired vs Wi-Fi, 10,000 pings: worst-case one-way 22.05 ms, jitter 19.78 ms, inference 12.77 ms, composed end-to-end 99.97 ms; accuracy 98.39%/99.43%.
contribution: A DDS-based edge ECG alerting pipeline whose wireless latency and jitter are measured against a 300 ms medical telemetry budget: worst-case one-way link latency 22 ms and a composed end-to-end figure of 99.97 ms.
flag: timing is the contribution: partly (roughly half the paper is classifier accuracy); safety-relevant application (clinical cardiac alerts to caregivers). Check: the 99.97 ms 'worst-case' is NOT a measured end-to-end figure - it is a sum of 2x worst-case link latency plus separately measured software stage delays (unclear if those are means). Inference runs on a GPU gaming workstation, not edge hardware; the Raspberry Pi 5 only receives alerts, so 'edge deployment' not claimed. Comparison is wired vs wireless and Reliable vs Best Effort, no competing system measured (MQTT/cloud comparison is from literature). Lab Wi-Fi hotspot only. Author's accepted version with template header 'VOL. 14, NO. 8, AUGUST 2021'. Text extraction of figures garbled; read all sections except parts of the energy analysis.

title: RMS: A Delay Sensitive Road Monitoring System Using Edge Intelligence
evidence: "It uses a deep learning model for the decision-making about road-hindering alerts" (Abstract); "We have not done any other testing." (Sec. IV)
method: Road monitoring system: vehicles offload accelerometer/gyroscope data to an edge RSU, a small neural network flags accidents, KNN clustering groups vehicles for alert distribution, cloud for severe events.
evaluation: Analytic delay and energy model with assumed link rates, no hardware, no deadline: delay 12-44% lower than SVRS and 15-53% lower than DTP across 500-3000 Mb/s loads; local processing sometimes faster.
contribution: An edge-offloading road-incident alert architecture whose average delay and energy are computed from an analytic transmission model and compared with three offloading schemes.
flag: timing is the contribution: no - only average delay from a closed-form transmission/processing model, with no deadline, budget, bound or tail analysis; safety-relevant application (road accident alerts). Delay figures come from assumed parameters (group formation delay alone 4.23-9.02 s), not measurement or inference timing. Neural network trained with MATLAB fitnet on own accelerometer data, validated only by RMSE; authors state no other testing. Local processing (LIP) beats RMS at most loads.

title: PAES: Priority-Aware Adaptive Scheduling for Multi-Model Edge AI Systems
evidence: "achieves the lowest deadline miss rate at high load (17.1%)" (Abstract); deadlines are soft, 200-600 ms per model (Table II)
method: PAES: runtime min-heap scheduler for non-preemptive multi-model DNN inference on one executor, scoring each task by priority plus inverse expected latency plus inverse expected energy; no offline profiling.
evaluation: Soft deadlines 200-600 ms per model; 5 DNNs, 6 devices incl. Raspberry Pi 5 and Jetson Orin Nano; vs FIFO, RR, static priority, EDF, PQ+Deadline, QoS: miss rate 17.1% at high load, queue wait -32.6% vs FIFO, overhead <1.8 us.
contribution: A composite priority-latency-energy score for scheduling concurrent DNN inference on a single edge executor, cutting queue wait by about a third against FIFO and giving the lowest deadline-miss rate at high load on Jetson Orin Nano.
flag: timing is the contribution: yes (deadline-miss rate and queue wait of scheduled DNN inference, EDF baseline); application not safety-relevant (generic delivery-robot workload, soft deadlines only, no worst-case guarantee). Doubts: PAES is WORST on miss rate at low load (25.3%) and trails QoS under burst (24.4% vs 11.9%); PAES and QoS queue wait overlap. Reported mean queue waits (45,400 ms synthetic, 6,728 ms pipeline) dwarf the 200-600 ms deadlines yet miss rate is 17% and 0% respectively - looks internally inconsistent (queue wait may be summed, not per-task); average latency is 237.2 ms in Table III but 162.4 ms in Table V for the same balanced config. 22% of tasks used Gaussian-simulated latency, not real inference. On Raspberry Pi 5 all schedulers tie at 0% miss. Independent researchers, 4-page letter, generative AI used for language; energy is a TDP proxy. arXiv ids appear only in the reference list.

title: A Safety-Performance Metric Enabling Computational Awareness in Autonomous Robots
evidence: "we select 1.36 seconds based on the relatively less capable Xavier hardware" (Sec. IV-B, safety timing threshold for the YOLO-DynaSLAM task)
method: Safety-performance (SP) metric over a stochastic heterogeneous DAG task model: probabilistic response-time thresholds on safety-critical nodes and paths are penalised when violated, performance rewarded only once timing is safe.
evaluation: Jetson AGX Xavier, 5-task DAG (YOLOv4-DynaSLAM, GPU RRT, MPC, fastdepth, TSP), thresholds 1.36 s SLAM and about 1 s RRT; 13 FIFO/CFS schedules; SP vs worst-case and average makespan; SLAM response under 1 s to over 6 s.
contribution: A safety-first timing metric for robot computation graphs that treats response times as distributions and distinguishes safe from unsafe Linux schedules that worst-case and average makespan cannot tell apart, measured on Jetson AGX Xavier.
flag: timing is the contribution: yes (probabilistic response-time thresholds as nominal safety); safety-relevant by framing (robot nominal safety) but no robot or collision outcome is measured. Most likely point of dispute is condition 2: only two of five DAG tasks are neural (YOLOv4 inside DynaSLAM, fastdepth); RRT, MPC and TSP are classical, and the SLAM timing variation is traced to CPU depth-mask recursion, not DNN inference - maintainer may rule E1 (timing work not about learned-model inference). It proposes a metric, not a scheduler; the SP-optimising scheduler is future work. Results are bar charts (Figs. 5-6) with few numbers in text (Pearson r=0.608 between SLAM response time and mask size); no deadline-miss rate reported, so the evaluation floor rests on the SP vs makespan comparison. Thresholds were chosen by the authors from other papers' benchmarks. Reference list not read.

title: Edge Learning with Timeliness Constraints: Challenges and Solutions
evidence: "introduce the concept of timely edge learning" (Abstract); the two case studies summarise the authors' earlier papers.
method: Magazine overview of delay-constrained edge training and edge inference: delay breakdowns, challenges, and candidate solutions (data and model compression, device scheduling, resource management), with two recap case studies.
evaluation: Case studies from prior work: federated MNIST under 50 s training budget; edge inference with 12-slot (120 ms) deadline, completion over 90% vs under 70% uncompressed at rate 0.5. Simulated, no hardware.
contribution: A magazine overview that frames edge training and edge inference under timeliness constraints and surveys compression, scheduling and resource-management techniques, illustrated by two case studies from the authors' earlier work.
flag: timing is the contribution: yes in topic, but this is a magazine overview/survey (15 references, no new method or new experiment) so E3; application not safety-relevant beyond an autonomous-driving motivation. Half of it is training timing, which is out of scope anyway. The inference case study is the already-queued doi:10.1109/jiot.2020.2997128 (arxiv 2005.12235) - useful as a pointer only; it is the source for 1 slot = 10 ms. Accuracy values of the training case study are in a figure only.

title: Context-Aware Layer Scheduling for Seamless Neural Network Inference in Cloud-Edge Systems
venue: International Symposium on Embedded Multicore/Many-core Systems-on-Chip
evidence: "While reducing the average runtime, the worst case inference execution time is raised by one scheduling decision and the first branch executed on the slowest device" (Sec. IV-D Worst Case Execution Time)
method: Layer-wise edge-cloud DNN scheduler that re-plans at branching points from measured per-layer time and energy, and on link failure re-executes the last branch on the edge; gives a WCET expression.
evaluation: Simulated: no deadline stated (tmax symbolic). Cloud NVIDIA A6000, edge = Simba-like/Eyeriss-like accelerators emulated by CNNParted scaling. FCN-ResNet50 142.51 ms edge-only vs 5.62/8.84/12.23 ms with 0/1/2 link failures; GoogLeNet 9.62 vs 6.88/7.63/8.69 ms; scheduler overhead 0.3-1.0 ms.
contribution: Dynamic layer scheduling between edge and cloud that recovers from link failures mid-inference at a worst-case cost of one branching interval, cutting simulated FCN-ResNet50 latency from 142 ms to 12 ms.
flag: timing is the contribution: partly (latency and energy reduction with a bounded-WCET recovery claim); application not safety-relevant beyond naming automotive/agriculture workloads. Check: no numeric deadline or budget anywhere, tmax is only a symbol; the WCET formula is stated, not proved and not measured (worst measured case is 2 injected failures); edge device is simulated by scaling server timings, no real edge hardware; baselines are only edge-only and cloud-only execution, and the static scheduler is described but not reported in Table II; link failures are injected deterministically (0, 1 or 2), no tail or miss-rate analysis; ts is called scheduler time in Table II but transmission time in the text. Abstract figures (142.25 to 12.23 ms, 105.02 to 5.46 mJ) match Table II. Borderline against E1 (latency minimisation) or E2 (floor).

title: Vehicular Edge Computing for Multi-Vehicle Perception
venue: 2021 Fourth International Conference on Connected and Autonomous Driving (MetroCAD)
evidence: "However, as we only focus on profiling the native pipeline of F-Cooper, the relative time it takes to receive and also inference the example timing is not tested." (Sec. IV-B Run Time Average)
method: Proposes, as a general formulation only, an edge-side scheduling pipeline for cooperative perception of connected vehicles; the actual work is a GPU profile of the existing F-Cooper pipeline.
evaluation: Profiling of F-Cooper on one GeForce GTX 1060: 32% GPU utilisation, about 1.9 GB memory, 0.048 s voxel forward and 0.191 s post-process per example. No deadline value, no baseline, no scheduler result.
contribution: A profiling study of the F-Cooper cooperative-perception pipeline on a desktop GPU, with an unevaluated proposal for deadline-tracking edge scheduling of vehicle requests.
flag: timing is the contribution: no (deadline-capable scheduling is claimed but only a runtime profile is reported); application is safety-relevant (cooperative perception for autonomous vehicles). Check: the abstract claims real-world experiments on different device architectures and scenarios and a real-time deadline capable pipeline, but the body reports one GPU, one frame, no deadline figure and no comparison; the scheduling optimisation is a generic expression never instantiated or run; the GTX 1060 is not edge hardware; the paper itself says its proposed algorithm is future work. E1 would also be defensible (speed merely reported).

title: Probabilistic Latency Modeling for Heterogeneous Inference Tasks in Resource-Constrained Networks
evidence: "This paper presents a Bayesian Neural Network (BNN) based framework for predicting per-frame latency across heterogeneous devices and varying network states." (Abstract)
method: Two-stage probabilistic latency predictor: a BNN ensemble with MC dropout predicts frame duration from task and system configuration, then Gaussian process regression predicts end-to-end inference task latency with prediction intervals.
evaluation: 995 samples, 80/20 split; no deadline or budget stated; devices are unnamed CPU tiers (2-6 cores), bandwidth 0.5-70 Mbps, latencies ms to 2.5 s. GPR R2 0.9985, RMSE 0.0088 s, PICP 0.969; BNN R2 0.9963, PICP 0.944; baselines SVR, Ridge, MLP, RF, LightGBM R2 <= 0.19.
contribution: A Bayesian neural network plus Gaussian-process pipeline that predicts per-frame edge inference and transfer latency with calibrated uncertainty intervals across bandwidth, compute and compression settings.
flag: timing is the contribution: yes (predicting inference latency with uncertainty is the whole paper); application safety-relevance only asserted (mission-critical, military setting), none demonstrated. Check: evaluation floor is doubtful - the metric is prediction error and interval coverage, not a deadline-miss rate, tail latency or latency against a budget, so E2 is arguable; no named hardware and nothing run on an edge device; the inference workload and model being timed are never identified; baselines are implausibly weak (R2 0.05-0.19 vs 0.9985) and the Ridge and LightGBM rows of Table III are identical, suggesting baselines lacked the stage-1 feature or a copy error; intervals rely on post-hoc scaling factors (3.625 for a 95% interval, 2.575 called 99% yet reported coverage is 96.9%); Sec. IV-B says predictions are plotted against transfer duration, a possible leak of the target; text has signs of machine-generated drafting (duplicate references 1 and 2, interpretation columns in tables). Abstract numbers match Tables I-II.

title: Edge-Cloud Collaborative Streaming Video Analytics With Multi-Agent Deep Reinforcement Learning
evidence: "For each Ek, we aim to maximize the average inference accuracy during the system running time T, while ensuring the average processing latency is close to a preset latency threshold" (Optimization Objective)
method: OsmoticGate2: per-edge MAPPO agents (centralised training, decentralised execution) choose resolution, bitrate, YOLOv8 variant and cloud offload ratio to maximise accuracy while holding processing latency at a target.
evaluation: Real testbed: 4 Jetson Xavier NX plus RTX3090 server, UA-DETRAC traffic video, Oboe bandwidth traces. Latency target 1 s, penalty threshold 1.5 s. Ours about 1.0 s at 0.79 accuracy; OsmoticGate 0.88 s/0.76; FastVA 4.67 s/0.815; also DeepDecision and heuristics.
contribution: Multi-agent reinforcement learning controllers on Jetson edge nodes adapt video resolution, bitrate, detector size and cloud offloading to hold a 1 s latency target while maximising detection accuracy.
flag: timing is the contribution: partly (accuracy is maximised subject to a stated latency target, an explicit accuracy-latency trade); application is traffic video analytics, not safety-relevant as evaluated. Check: the target is a soft 1 s on AVERAGE latency enforced by a reward penalty - no deadline-miss rate, tail or jitter figures, and the method is rewarded for staying near the target, not under it; the strongest baseline OsmoticGate is actually faster (0.88 s) at slightly lower accuracy, so the win is on the reward, not on timing; numbers are read off Fig. 3-4 and quoted in prose only, no table, single run, no variance; baseline OsmoticGate is the authors' own prior system; this is an IEEE Network magazine article with few details. Multi-agent here means distributed controllers, not multi-agent safety state.

title: Adaptive Acceleration of Inference Services at the Network Edge
venue: IEEE International Conference on Mobile Cloud Computing, Services, and Engineering
evidence: "The goals of the system are to maximize the accuracy of inference results and the number of requests the edge cluster can serve while meeting latency requirements." (Abstract)
method: Controller with online and periodic offline bin-packing heuristics that jointly routes video-frame inference sessions to edge workers and adapts DNN model choice, input size and dynamic batching per client latency SLO.
evaluation: Testbed: 3 Jetson Nano plus 1 Xavier NX, Triton, per-frame deadlines 0.5/0.7/0.9 s. Frames meeting SLO over loads W1-W4: prototype 100/97.4/97.1/93.5% vs high-accuracy baseline 100/59.9/51.0/50.0%, low-accuracy baseline 100%. Simulation, 32 workers: reward +44.8% vs LA, +16% vs round-robin.
contribution: Deadline-aware joint request routing and model-quality adaptation for an edge inference cluster, meeting per-frame latency SLOs for 93.5-100% of frames on Jetson hardware while raising served accuracy.
flag: timing is the contribution: yes (accuracy traded against per-session latency SLOs, deadline-met rate is the headline metric); application is generic video analytics, not safety-relevant. Check: no raw latency values are reported, only the percentage of requests meeting the SLO; at maximum load (W4) the prototype is worse than the low-accuracy baseline on both SLO rate (93.5 vs 100%) and reward (23.6 vs 27.9), and the paper admits the heuristic failed to place a session; accuracy is assumed from published ImageNet/COCO scores, not measured (and reported 0.810 vs 0.816 in Table II); abstract 9.7% higher accuracy is 9.7 points absolute (0.810 vs 0.713) and 43.5% more frames is the W4 gap to the high-accuracy baseline only; workloads are synthetic clients from a desktop PC; the second evaluation is simulation; soft real-time, no worst-case bound.

title: Scalable Physics-Embedded Neural Networks for Real-Time Robotic Control in Embedded Systems
venue: Midwest Symposium on Circuits and Systems
evidence: Sec V-A: "For the practical deployment of PENN in embedded systems aimed at real-time control, below 5ms latency is required due to the motor PWM control update rates."
method: Lagrangian physics-embedded NN for robot-arm torque estimation with a scaling factor and two-step training; RL (LSTM) architecture search penalises candidates whose estimated MCU latency exceeds the budget.
evaluation: Budget 5 ms (PWM rate). MATLAB-simulated 3-DoF arms; STM32F4 latency by analytic formula: baseline NAS 8.58 ms vs constrained 4.98 ms, error 2.37% to 0.56%; 3X faster than random search.
contribution: Shows a latency-penalised RL architecture search that fits a physics-embedded torque model under a 5 ms control-loop budget on an STM32F4-class microcontroller, using estimated rather than measured latency.
flag: timing is the contribution: partly (one of three contributions; the rest is model accuracy); application is robot-arm control, safety-relevant only loosely. CHECK: all latency figures are ESTIMATED from an operation-count formula (eq. 16, Fig. 6b 'latency estimation'), nothing is measured on hardware, so edge deployment is not claimed; budget is enforced at design time in the NAS reward, no deadline-miss, tail or jitter analysis; robots are MATLAB simulations; 4-page MWSCAS paper. If measured timing is required, this becomes exclude-E2.

title: HERTI: A Reinforcement Learning-Augmented System for Efficient Real-Time Inference on Heterogeneous Embedded Systems
venue: International Conference on Parallel Architectures and Compilation Techniques
evidence: Sec III-C: "MSEP generates an efficient model slicing and execution plan ... to efficiently execute the target inference workload with a strong deadline guarantee."
method: DQN planner slices a DNN across big/little CPU clusters, GPU and NPU with per-slice DVFS, using profiled latency/energy estimators; states whose estimated latency exceeds the deadline get a fixed penalty.
evaluation: Per-model deadlines 75-250 ms (medium 90-210 ms); HiKey 970 (Kirin 970), TFLite, 7 CNNs. HERTI meets all deadlines; 8 TFLite variants, MOSAIC-E and exhaustive miss (1.2-25x deadline). Energy -28.4% vs AutoScale.
contribution: A reinforcement-learning planner that partitions DNN inference across heterogeneous mobile processors and frequency levels to minimise energy subject to a per-model inference deadline, measured on a HiKey 970 board.
flag: timing is the contribution: yes (deadline-constrained inference scheduling); application not safety-relevant in the evaluation (ImageNet classifiers; autonomous driving only as motivation). CHECK: the 'strong deadline guarantee' is empirical only - plans are chosen offline from linear latency estimators (3.0% mean error) and results are averages of 100 runs, with no worst-case, tail or miss-rate distribution and no proof; deadlines are synthetic (eq. 12, scaled between best-case and energy-optimal latency), not application-derived; latency is shown only normalised to deadline in Fig. 5 (bar values read from garbled figure text). Planning is offline, not a runtime interceptor.

title: MERCI: Adaptive Multi-Expert Inference for Dynamic and Large-Vocabulary Vision Perception
venue: Annual IEEE International Conference on Pervasive Computing and Communications
evidence: Sec VII-A: "Streaming accuracy is an online accuracy measured after its latency, better reflecting the XR user experience by penalizing delayed outputs."
method: On-device runtime that greedily composes class-specific detector experts from a model zoo to cover the active class set, and asynchronously merges experts on a server into compact models.
evaluation: No stated deadline (20 FPS stream). Jetson AGX Xavier and Orin NX, TensorRT; EgoObjects, Wanderlust, DexYCB. Streaming accuracy up to +26.96% vs direct integration; class-specific 9.01 ms vs 160.83 ms full model; mean latency only.
contribution: Composes and merges class-specific detector experts on Jetson devices so that large-vocabulary video perception keeps low average latency, improving latency-penalised streaming accuracy over single-expert adaptation baselines.
flag: timing is the contribution: partly; application (XR perception) not safety-relevant. Excluded because no deadline, budget, bound or tail is stated or analysed - only average latency and streaming accuracy at 20 FPS; 'Soft Real-Time Performance' is a design goal without a number. CHECK: streaming accuracy does couple accuracy to latency against the frame clock, and Fig. 6 gives an accuracy-latency trade-off, so a maintainer who reads the 50 ms frame period as an implicit budget could overturn to include. The up-to-18x speedup and 26.96% are best-case figures; class-set acquisition is assumed, not implemented.

title: GazeLight: Understanding the Feasibility of Gaze-based Adaptive Streaming for AR-Mediated Human-Robot Systems
venue: 2025 IEEE International Conference on Pervasive Computing and Communications Workshops and other Affiliated Events (PerCom Workshops)
evidence: Sec IV: "gaze-based adaptation incurs only 36.72% of the total latency of the full sized image (121.37 ms vs. 330.49 ms). We note that this is only slightly over the target latency of 100 ms"
method: Gaze-fixation-driven region-of-interest cropping and rate adaptation of robot-to-AR-headset video (DBSCAN fixations, ORB homography), optionally with edge line drawings and FCN-ResNet18 object highlighting.
evaluation: Target 100 ms glass-to-glass. Unitree Go2 with Jetson Nano, HoloLens 2, private WiFi; GestRight and HoloAssist gaze data. End-to-end 121.37 ms vs 330.49 ms full image (target missed); ROI step 11.137 ms.
contribution: Feasibility study showing that predictable gaze fixations let a teleoperated robot stream only a cropped region to an AR headset, cutting end-to-end streaming latency from 330 ms to 121 ms.
flag: timing is the contribution: partly (video streaming latency against a 100 ms target); application is human-robot teleoperation, loosely safety-relevant. Excluded on condition 2: the timed path is image streaming to a human, not learned-model inference - the gaze mechanism is DBSCAN plus homography, and the one learned model (segmentation for object highlighting) is an optional pre-processing step whose timing is not isolated. CHECK: preliminary workshop paper; 100 ms target is not met; means only, no tail or jitter; no user study; abstract says 121.36 ms, body 121.37 ms; reported KS-test wording (D=0.000164, p>>0.05 'rejects') is inconsistent.

title: AI ARMORS: An Experimental C-V2X Framework for Road Safety over 5G SA with Computer Vision
venue: IEEE International Symposium on Personal, Indoor and Mobile Radio Communications
evidence: Sec IV: "the most stable of all is the 5G SA with an average delay of 47.85ms."
method: Smartphone accelerometer/gyroscope thresholds raise a crash alert over MQTT to geofenced devices; nearby cameras stream RTMP video to a back-end YOLO11n model that confirms the crash before notifying responders.
evaluation: KPI target 20 ms end-to-end. Alert-message latency, static sender: WiFi 40.2 ms, public 5G NSA 62.5 ms, private 5G SA 47.85 ms (averages). YOLO11n 3.1 ms/frame on RTX 4070 Ti Super vs 31.3 ms CPU.
contribution: An experimental smartphone-based C-V2X crash-alert framework that confirms sensor-triggered alerts with a back-end YOLO model and reports alert-message latency over WiFi, public 5G and private 5G SA.
flag: timing is the contribution: partly (network latency of the alert path is the main measured result); application is safety-relevant (road crash alerting). Excluded as an application/framework paper: the measured latency is of MQTT alert messages, not of the inference path, and inference speed is merely reported on a desktop GPU server (not edge hardware); only averages, with WiFi spikes noted qualitatively, no tail or deadline-miss analysis. CHECK: all three networks miss the paper's own 20 ms KPI yet the conclusion calls results 'close to the target KPIs'; detection accuracy is a vague 'over 80%' with no baseline; a maintainer who counts wireless-delay measurement of a time-critical alert as in scope could overturn.

title: Compressing VAE-Based Out-of-Distribution Detectors for Embedded Deployment
venue: 2024 IEEE 30th International Conference on Embedded and Real-Time Computing Systems and Applications (RTCSA)
evidence: "we propose the design methodology shown in Fig. 1 to compress an existing VAE-based OOD detector" (Sec. I); goal is to minimise "execution time and memory usage while maintaining accuracy above a given threshold" (Sec. IV)
method: Quantisation (fp16 GPU, qint8 CPU), pruning-aware knowledge distillation and final pruning applied to beta-VAE and optical-flow VAE out-of-distribution detectors for an embedded vehicle.
evaluation: No stated deadline or budget. Jetson Nano (Duckiebot). Mean execution time 56-90 ms across quantisation modes; time down 20-38% with AUROC within 1-5% of uncompressed baseline. No tail or WCET.
contribution: Compresses VAE-based out-of-distribution detectors by quantisation, distillation and pruning, cutting execution time by 20-38% on a Jetson Nano while keeping AUROC within 1-5% of the uncompressed model.
flag: timing is the contribution: no (compression reported as mean speed, memory and AUROC; accuracy threshold is the constraint, not a deadline); application safety-relevant: yes (OOD detector for an autonomous vehicle, intended to trigger a safe state or human handback, but that path is not implemented or evaluated). Check: RTCSA venue and abstract wording may suggest real-time deadlines; I found no numeric deadline, WCET or tail figure. The 38% and 20%/28% headline numbers come from figures I could not see value by value; baseline AUROC 0.852 is in the text.

title: Demo: Deadline-Aware Real-Time Planning on F1TENTH
venue: IEEE International Conference on Embedded and Real-Time Computing Systems and Applications (RTCSA)
evidence: "MPC and MPPI fail to complete a lap as single MPC step takes 81 ms and an MPPI step 500 ms, far exceeding the 40 ms control deadline, so both miss the deadline and crash." (Sec. III Experimental Results)
method: Deadline-Aware MCTS: a small network reads the remaining time budget and search progress and shifts action sampling between aggressive, cautious and learned GP-prior modes; SVGP dynamics model; particle-filter localisation.
evaluation: Physical F1TENTH car, Jetson Orin Nano, 40 ms control deadline (25 Hz). Fastest lap 26.45 s vs pure pursuit 36.25, Stanley 30.06; MPC (81 ms/step) and MPPI (500 ms/step) crash. No DA-MCTS step latency given.
contribution: Two-page demo of a deadline-aware Monte Carlo tree search planner running on a Jetson Orin Nano F1TENTH car, where baselines exceeding the 40 ms control deadline crash and DA-MCTS completes the fastest real-car lap.
flag: timing is the contribution: partly; application safety-relevant (autonomous racing, crash avoidance). Two-page demo abstract: the only measured outcome for DA-MCTS is lap time; no planning latency, deadline-miss rate or jitter is reported for the proposed method, only step times of the MPC and MPPI baselines against the 40 ms deadline and a 15 ms WCET for the localiser. If the maintainer counts baseline step times vs the stated deadline as meeting the floor this becomes an include. The deadline adaptation acts on search sampling, not on learned-model inference as such (learned parts are GP models and a small mode-selection network). Full method is ref [1] (DA-MCTS, same RTCSA 2026 proceedings) - check whether that paper is queued and prefer it. Run-time assurance is stated as future work, so not an interceptor.

title: DNN Hardware Accelerator Selection for Feasible Deployment of MARL-Based MAC Protocols in Industrial IoT Networks
venue: International Forum on Research and Technologies for Society and Industry Leveraging a better tomorrow
evidence: "Instead of minimizing the inference latency, the criterion selects the subset of accelerator instances that guarantee an inference latency less than ttarget." (Sec. V-C)
method: Design-space exploration of Simba DNN accelerator instances for a MAPPO-learned MAC policy MLP; keep instances whose inference latency is under the slot guard time, then pick by energy, area and protocol KPIs.
evaluation: Simulation only (LAMBDA simulator, Simba at 300 MHz). Budget ttarget 5 us; selected instances 2.55-2.77 us, 0.606-0.657 uJ, 0.501 mm2 for memory M=1..4. No baseline hardware; ablation over M; 2 IoT devices, 1000 runs.
contribution: Selects a DNN hardware accelerator configuration so that a multi-agent-RL MAC policy can be inferred within a 5 microsecond slot guard time on IoT devices, reporting simulated latency of 2.55-2.77 microseconds.
flag: timing is the contribution: partly; application not safety-relevant (industrial IoT medium access). Inference latency against a stated 5 us budget is the feasibility criterion, but it is one of three deployment KPIs alongside energy and chip area, and all latency figures come from the LAMBDA accelerator simulator - no fabricated chip or real edge hardware, so no edge-deployment cell. No CPU/GPU or other baseline latency is reported; the only comparison is across accelerator instances and memory length M, so the floor is met weakly (ablation only). No tail or jitter analysis. Tiny setting (2 devices, 2 PDUs, 2x64 MLP). Likely overturn candidate to exclude-E1 or E2.

title: ApNet: Approximation-Aware Real-Time Neural Network
evidence: "we propose ApNet, a timing-predictable runtime system that is able to guarantee deadlines of DNN workloads via efficient approximation" (Abstract)
method: Per-layer sub-deadline assignment using approximation potential; swaps layers for approximated variants (LowRank, XNOR-Net, BNN etc.) to meet deadlines; runtime monitor exploits GPU sharing between concurrent DNNs to reduce approximation.
evaluation: NVIDIA Jetson TX2; deadlines 12 ms and 24 ms. CaffeNet/AlexNet WCET about 28.8/28.9 ms adjusted to 10.75/10.57 ms. 4 concurrent DNNs, 1000 iterations vs Baseline, Best Effort (SqueezeNet), ApNet-SP: turnaround CDF, accuracy score.
contribution: ApNet meets hard deadlines for DNN inference on a Jetson TX2 by assigning per-layer sub-deadlines and approximation degrees, trading bounded accuracy loss against a 12 ms or 24 ms deadline in single- and multi-DNN workloads.
flag: timing is the contribution: yes; application safety-relevant (motivated by autonomous driving perception, evaluated on image classifiers only). Check: abstract says accuracy improved by up to 8% while the introduction says by an average of 1% vs best effort and Sec. V-B says the maximum improvement over ApNet-SP is 80% - these figures do not obviously reconcile. Accuracy is a per-layer score heuristic, not measured end-task accuracy. The deadline guarantee is on measurement-based WCET (Table V, units appear to be microseconds) and the multi-task deadline result is a CDF figure; I did not find a tabulated deadline-miss rate. The schedulability property allows skipping a layer entirely (100% approximation), which the authors themselves call unusable. Mechanism adapts the model, it does not veto an action.

title: PredJoule: A Timing-Predictable Energy Optimization Framework for Deep Neural Networks
evidence: "Experiments show that PredJoule rarely violates job deadlines, and can improve energy by 65% on average compared to five existing approaches and 68% compared to an energy-oriented approach." (Abstract)
method: Layer-aware CPU/GPU DVFS controller for DNN inference: tracks an execution deficit at each layer boundary and picks per-layer frequency configurations to meet the job latency target while minimising energy.
evaluation: Jetson TX2; five DNNs, tight deadlines 20/20/50/50/100 ms, loose 25/25/100/100/150 ms; 1000 iterations vs Max-N, Max-Q, Race2Idle, Poet, Poet-GPU. PredJoule deadline misses 0/0/10/3/0% (VGGNet others 99-100%); energy -65% avg.
contribution: PredJoule tunes CPU and GPU frequency per DNN layer on a Jetson TX2 so inference meets stated 20-150 ms deadlines while cutting energy by about 65% against five DVFS baselines.
flag: timing is the contribution: yes (deadline-constrained DNN inference with deadline-miss ratio as a headline metric, jointly with energy); application safety-relevant by motivation (autonomous driving), evaluated on image classifiers. Check: the conclusion claims "no deadline miss" but Table III shows 10% misses for GoogleNet and 3% for VGGNet, zero only after the first 50 iterations; Race2Idle beats it on GoogleNet. Timing predictability is empirical and feedback-based, with no proved bound or WCET analysis. Accuracy is untouched (DVFS only), so no accuracy-latency trade. The maintainer may view this as mainly an energy paper; I count the deadline as the binding constraint.

title: Pipelined Data-Parallel CPU/GPU Scheduling for Multi-DNN Real-Time Inference
evidence: "This paper presents DART, a DNN scheduling framework that offers deterministic response time to real-time tasks and increased throughput to best-effort tasks." (Abstract)
method: DART: pipeline of heterogeneous CPU/GPU nodes with data-parallel workers, real-time and best-effort classes, CUDA stream priorities, measurement-based layer WCET profiling, response-time schedulability analysis, admission control and node configuration search.
evaluation: Intel Xeon E2620 v4 + GTX 1080 and Jetson TX2; RT deadlines 150/200 ms (300-500 ms in random tasksets). vs BaseCPU, BaseGPU: max response time -98.5% (TX2, batch 32), -89.9% unbatched; schedulable taskset ratio; BE throughput +17.9%.
contribution: DART schedules multiple DNN inference tasks across CPU and GPU pipeline stages with an analysable worst-case response time, cutting maximum observed response time by up to 98.5% on a Jetson TX2 against Caffe-style baselines.
flag: timing is the contribution: yes (worst-case response-time bound and tail latency of multi-DNN inference); application safety-relevant by motivation (self-driving camera pipeline), workloads are AlexNet, PilotNet, LeNet, VGG classifiers. Check: the 98.5% figure is the maximum observed response time at batch size 32 against a batching GPU baseline, the most favourable case; unbatched it is 89.9%. WCET is measurement-based (maximum of profiled runs), so the deterministic bound is not a static guarantee. Baselines are the authors own priority-queue re-implementations of single-node Caffe. Response-time CDFs are in figures; I did not find a tabulated deadline-miss rate. Schedulability experiments use analysis on random tasksets, not execution. Pipeline is a scheduler, not an interceptor.

title: RED: A Systematic Real-Time Scheduling Approach for Robotic Environmental Dynamics
evidence: RED is designed to "satisfy realtime constraints (i.e., end-to-end deadline of an operation)" (Sec. I)
method: EDF scheduling of multi-DNN robotic DAGs with proportional intermediate deadlines recomputed at each scheduling point, MIMONet encoder sharing via DAG refinement, and on-demand synchronisation.
evaluation: ENet, UNet, AutoPilot, YOLO, MIMONet on Jetson Nano/TX2/Xavier/Orin; tight/loose deadlines e.g. Orin 2400/3600 ms; miss rate -40.5% and latency -24.7% vs EDF; ROS 2 case: miss rate -67.3%; overhead 1.2-27.3 ms.
contribution: A real-time scheduler for multi-task DNN workloads on robots that assigns and recomputes intermediate deadlines to cut end-to-end deadline misses on Jetson devices when the environment changes the task set.
flag: timing is the contribution: yes - deadline-miss rate of DNN inference tasks is the primary measured outcome; application (robot/driving perception and control) is safety-relevant but no safety outcome is measured. Check: miss-rate figures are relative reductions averaged over platforms, absolute rates are in Fig. 8 which I could not read; benchmark deadlines are seconds-scale (2.4-11.3 s for a task set), far from sub-15 ms; no DNN accuracy reported; no schedulability proof, results are empirical; tasks are reported as dropped but I found no explicit dropping policy, so runtime_interceptor is no.

title: Response-Time Analysis of a Soft Real-time NVIDIA Holoscan Application
evidence: "Our response-time analysis again provides a close upper bound for most graphs, with no observed WCRTs exceeding our upper bounds." (Sec. VII-C)
method: Static worst-case end-to-end response-time analysis for NVIDIA Holoscan operator DAGs (edge ML sensor pipelines), modelling blocking from upstream and downstream queue conditions; lemmas for linear chains and arbitrary DAGs.
evaluation: No deadline stated. 8 HoloHub DAG structures with busy-wait placeholder operators (100 ms+) on Jetson AGX Orin, 30 min runs, plus simulation; bound never exceeded; analysis 0.4 ms; 3 ms per-operator overhead added.
contribution: A static analysis that upper-bounds worst-case end-to-end response time of NVIDIA Holoscan edge pipelines under queue backpressure, validated against simulation and Jetson AGX Orin measurements.
flag: timing is the contribution: yes; application safety-relevant (medical devices) but only as motivation. CHECK condition 2: no learned model is ever executed - the DAG shapes come from HoloHub AI apps but every operator is a busy-wait placeholder with random 100 ms to n*100 ms execution time, so this is generic dataflow WCRT analysis and could fairly be E1. Abstract claims bounds 'as close as 0.3%' of measurements; I cannot find 0.3% in the body (conclusion says 'within 99% accuracy'). Hardware bound is made safe by an empirical 3 ms per-operator overhead, not by proof. Assumes fixed per-operator execution time, queue capacity 1, one core per operator. Superseded by sibling record doi:10.1109/rtss66672.2025.00018.

title: DuoJoule: Accurate On-Device Deep Reinforcement Learning for Energy and Timeliness
evidence: "DuoJoule auto-balances latency, energy, and algorithm performance under-budgeted DRL training across different platforms." (Sec. V-B)
method: Runtime controller for on-device deep RL training: a metric tracker scores projected total latency and energy against user budgets and tunes batch size, training frequency and GPU DVFS, with early exit.
evaluation: Budgets relative (soft 75%, hard 50% of peak), no absolute deadline. Jetson AGX Xavier and Orin Nano; CartPole and Breakout; vs Default, MAX-A, MIN-E, R3; DuoJoule 0 latency-budget overruns vs 6, 1, 2 of 6; overhead under 10.69 ms.
contribution: A framework that keeps on-device deep reinforcement learning training within latency and energy budgets by co-tuning batch size, training frequency and DVFS on Jetson boards.
flag: timing is the contribution: partly (co-equal with energy); application not safety-relevant (Atari, CartPole, DonkeyCar simulator). Excluded as on-device TRAINING: the latency budget is on the end-to-end duration of a training session (seconds), not on inference. Check if the maintainer reads the train-inference cycle as in scope. Hardware naming is inconsistent: intro says Jetson AGX Orin, testbed section says Jetson AGX Xavier; case study ran on a desktop GPU. Only one of at least 3 runs is shown. Most numbers live in Fig. 8 which did not extract; text gives only relative percentages.

title: Faster, Exact, More General Response-Time Analysis for NVIDIA Holoscan Applications
evidence: "We present a scalable method to compute exact worst-case end-to-end latency in applications built on the NVIDIA Holoscan SDK, a framework increasingly adopted for soft real-time ML workloads in medical devices, surgical instruments, and robotics." (Abstract)
method: Reduces Holoscan DAG scheduling semantics to homogeneous synchronous dataflow graphs, then a dynamic trace-graph algorithm (TG-DFS plus maximisation) derives exact worst-case response time for variable execution times and arbitrary queue sizes, with proofs.
evaluation: No deadline stated. 8 HoloHub ML apps with operator times profiled on IGX Orin; analysis run on Xeon server. Exact (0% pessimism) vs prior RTA 0.69-18.23%; Multi AI Ultrasound 0.015 s vs UPPAAL over an hour.
contribution: An exact, proved worst-case end-to-end latency analysis for NVIDIA Holoscan ML pipelines that handles variable execution times and buffer sizes and runs in milliseconds where model checking takes over an hour.
flag: timing is the contribution: yes; application safety-relevant (surgical and medical ML pipelines) as motivation only. CHECK condition 2: the analysis is model-agnostic dataflow WCRT; the learned models enter only as profiled min and max operator execution times from real HoloHub apps on IGX Orin, and no measured end-to-end latency on the device is compared with the bound (the evaluation is analysis runtime and pessimism). One app (G) crashed and uses borrowed execution times. Table I gives 136 ms runtime and 20.5% prior pessimism for the Multi AI app while the text gives 0.015 s and Table II gives 17.97% for app H - possibly different configurations. Extends sibling record doi:10.1109/rtss62706.2024.00015; decide the pair together.

title: Automated risk detection for medical device networks with hard real time requirements
venue: IEEE/SICE International Symposium on System Integration
evidence: "In this paper, we propose a method to automatically check whether certain real time requirements of medical device networks will be met at runtime." (Abstract)
method: Design-time static timing analysis: builds a datastream DAG from ISO/IEEE 11073 device description files and a TDMA (Ethernet Powerlink) configuration, computes maximum data age per input and checks three cycle-time and age constraints.
evaluation: Powerlink testbed: X20-CP1585 master, 8 BeagleBone Black slaves, cycle 15 ms, 75 ms hop; predicted vs measured data age deviates at most 0.6 ms over 11 scenarios; analysis under 100 ms below 50 devices. No baseline.
contribution: A static check that a TDMA medical device network meets per-input cycle-time and data-age limits, with predictions within 0.6 ms of testbed measurements.
flag: timing is the contribution: yes; application safety-relevant (surgical instrument control). Excluded because there is no learned model anywhere: devices are rule-based medical modules and the work is network timing verification at integration time, not a runtime mechanism. No baseline or competing method is compared. Minor error in text: 'granularity (CC = 15ms)' should be the cycle time CT. Slaves only forwarded data with PT = 0, so device processing time was never exercised.

title: Device-Centric Benchmarking of Compressed Graph Neural Networks for IoT Anomaly Detection
venue: International Conference on Smart Computing, IoT and Machine Learning (SIML)
evidence: "The quantitative latency and memory data currently reported in Section VI were collected on an RTX 5060 Ti GPU." (Sec. V-A)
method: Benchmarking protocol for compressed GNN intrusion detectors: GraphSAGE teacher distilled to an SGC-like LightGNN student, with planned structured pruning, degree-aware INT8 QAT and ONNX/TensorRT export to ARM and Jetson gateways.
evaluation: No deadline; targets p95 speedup 3x, memory 4x, F1 drop 2 points - none met. RTX 5060 Ti workstation only: p95 2.491 to 1.467 ms (CICIoT2023), 2.992 to 1.965 ms (Edge-IIoTset); macro-F1 falls 8.4 and 7.6 points.
contribution: A proposed device-centric benchmark protocol for compressed graph neural network intrusion detection, with only a workstation-GPU pilot of a distilled student reported.
flag: timing is the contribution: no (compression reported as speed and accuracy; p95 is a reported metric, not a budget or deadline); application not safety-relevant (IoT intrusion detection). Despite the title nothing is measured on an edge device: ARM, Jetson, INT8, pruning, QAT and energy results are all declared future work, and the paper's own acceptance targets are missed. Text reads like an unfinished reviewer-response revision ('The revision separates...', 'converts the reviewer request into an explicit experiment matrix'); no artifact released. CICIoT2023 teacher macro-F1 is only 0.578. E2 would also be defensible.

title: Zero-Trust Secure Network Slicing for Autonomous Vehicle Platooning
venue: 2026 IEEE International Conference on Smart Computing Workshops and Other Affiliated events (SmartComp Companion)
evidence: "When trust falls below the threshold, ZTDS denies control-plane admission and activates fallback control." (Fig. 4 caption, Sec VI Results)
method: Per-message trust score gates V2V data into each follower's controller; below threshold the vehicle falls back to local-sensor control with longer headway, while control-slice bandwidth rises with aggregate risk.
evaluation: Own simulation, 9-vehicle platoon, false-data plus delay attacks, two fixed-slicing baselines: spacing error 0.141 vs 0.600 m, p95 latency 69.6 vs 129.5 ms, min TTC 5.90 vs 5.29 s.
contribution: Zero-trust platooning framework that admits or denies each inter-vehicle message at runtime, falls back to local sensing when trust drops, and adapts headway and network-slice reservation to cyber risk and delay.
flag: Pillar 1, criteria (a) and (c): a runtime admission gate with safe fallback over a multi-vehicle platoon, measured on safety outcomes (string gain, min TTC, attack acceptance) against two baselines. Include is on the letter of the criteria; the evidence is weak and the maintainer should weigh it. (1) The 'transparent simulation' is by the paper's own words 'a Python script that generates the figures from explicit data-generation routines' and 'intentionally parameterised rather than hidden behind a complex simulator'; attack-period latency and drop are modelled as worse 'especially under fixed slicing', so the latency gain may be assumed rather than produced. (2) Confidence intervals look synthetic: p95 latency is +-0.09 ms for all three methods and the three means are spaced almost exactly 10 and 60 ms apart. (3) The gate itself adds nothing over the TAF baseline on attack acceptance (both 0.000); the safety gain attributable to the gate is PFS to TAF (string gain 3.115 to 0.540, TTC 4.28 to 5.29), and the proposed method's extra is the slicing. (4) No collisions or violation rate reported; min TTC stays above 4 s even for the worst baseline. (5) Workshop companion paper, 5 pages, supplementary bundle not seen; prose reads possibly machine-assisted. Abstract percentages do reproduce from Table II. Latency about 70 ms p95, well above the review's 15 ms target; MEC deployment is assumed, not tested.

title: Securing Agentic AI in IoT Systems
venue: International Conferences on Smart Internet of Things
evidence: "The Digital Twin stores these invariants as part of the model and rejects commands that would violate them." (Sec IV Agentic AI in a Smart Home)
method: Dual-proxy, seven-plane LLM gateway in Rust with WebAssembly filters; a Goal-Plan-Step sentinel checks an agent's published plan and justifications, and a Digital Twin validates and rejects device commands.
evaluation: Throughput only: WASM overhead (480 vs 118 ns) and closed-loop load test of a prompt-validation microservice, 1000 requests at 1-500 clients on a GCP e2-medium. No safety metric, no baseline.
contribution: Gateway architecture for LLM agents controlling IoT devices that forces plan publication with step-level justification and routes commands through a Digital Twin, evaluated only for proxy latency under load.
flag: Pillar 1 by design only. The sentinel and Digital Twin are described through a hypothetical smart-home agent (SHEM) and three imagined failure modes; neither is evaluated, and it is not clear from the text that the twin or the smart-home scenario was implemented at all. The whole evaluation is latency of a prompt-validation microservice, so no safety result, no blocked-action count, no baseline. Inconsistencies: abstract says median latency 'below 0.8 seconds' for 1-10 clients, body says below 0.06 and 0.08 for 1-10 clients and up to 0.8 at 100; units are missing in the body and figure numbers in the text are off by one; reference list contains IEEE template leftovers ('K. Elissa, Title of paper if known', 'M. Young, The Technical Writer's Handbook'). Overlaps the authors' own EUSPN 2025 paper 'Governance-as-Code' (ref 10), which is said to hold the fuller evaluation; check whether that one is in the queue.
