title: Closed-Loop Neural Prostheses with On-Chip Intelligence: A Review and A Low-Latency Machine Learning Model for Brain State Detection
venue: IEEE Transactions on Biomedical Circuits and Systems
evidence: Sec V-A: 'shallow trees perform fast inference to reduce system latency'.
method: Review of closed-loop neural prostheses plus a depth-variant gradient-boosted tree ensemble with cost-aware training that lowers detection latency and power for on-chip seizure detection.
evaluation: iEEG, 11 patients, vs uniform depth-4 ensemble. No numeric deadline. Estimated latency 2.12 s to 0.86 s (0.52 s cost-aware), 91.1% sensitivity. 65 nm ASIC layout, simulated power, no silicon.
contribution: Reviews on-chip machine learning for closed-loop neural prostheses and proposes a depth-variant tree ensemble that cuts estimated seizure-detection latency about 2.5x at under 3% sensitivity loss.
flag: timing is the contribution: partly; application is safety-relevant (seizure and tremor detection for neurostimulation). Excluded because latency is minimised with no stated deadline or budget ('strict latency requirements' is said, no number), and the latency figures are estimates from average root-to-leaf path length in bit-accurate software models, not measured detection delay or measured hardware time. Roughly half or more of the paper is a review, so E3 is also arguable. Chip is layout plus PrimeTime simulation, not fabricated; this work is marked non-closed-loop in Table I. If the maintainer accepts anytime-style output (latest tree output reused) without a budget, it could be a weak include. I read the first 100k of about 135k characters; the tail (later ResOT results, conclusion) was covered only in the summary returned.

title: LightNAS: On Lightweight and Scalable Neural Architecture Search for Embedded Platforms
venue: IEEE Transactions on Computer-Aided Design of Integrated Circuits and Systems
evidence: "LightNets strictly satisfy the given latency constraints, while at the same time coming at an extremely low search cost of 10 GPU hours" (Sec. IV-B)
method: Differentiable hardware-aware NAS that learns the tradeoff multiplier so one search hits a target latency LAT(alpha)=T, using an MLP latency predictor; evolutionary channel search with a batchwise training proxy.
evaluation: ImageNet, budgets 20-30 ms at batch 8 on Nvidia Jetson AGX Xavier; predictor RMSE 0.04 ms vs 0.41 ms LUT; LightNet-24ms +0.9% and ++ +1.6% top-1 over FBNet-Xavier; Raspberry Pi 4 via HW-NAS-Bench.
contribution: One-shot differentiable architecture search that returns a network meeting a stated on-device latency budget (20-30 ms on Jetson AGX Xavier) without hyperparameter retuning, with higher ImageNet accuracy than FBNet at equal latency.
flag: timing is the contribution: partly (the claim is hitting a stated latency budget exactly in one search, and accuracy is compared at that budget; but it is a design-time NAS method, latency is mean batch-8 latency with no tail, jitter or worst-case analysis, and half the paper is search cost and channel search); safety-relevant: no (autonomous vehicles only as motivation; ImageNet and COCO). Borderline - the maintainer may rule this E1 as model design reported as speed and accuracy. Check: Table II per-model latency and accuracy figures are an image and are absent from the extracted text, so how closely measured latency meets each budget could not be verified numerically; Raspberry Pi figures come from a benchmark lookup, not own measurement.

title: OptMRT: Near-Optimal Partitioning for Mixed Real-Time Tasks on Heterogeneous Architectures
venue: IEEE Transactions on Computer-Aided Design of Integrated Circuits and Systems
evidence: "OptMRT maintains 100% HRT schedulability up to a utilization of 0.9" (Sec. VII-C)
method: Bi-partitions GPU streaming multiprocessors into a hard-real-time partition and a shared partition, with dual-mode mapping, WCRT-guided SM allocation and end-to-end response-time analysis for mixed hard and soft real-time CPU-GPU tasks.
evaluation: Synthetic task sets plus CUDA SDK, Rodinia and self-built NN tasks on Xeon 8369B + NVIDIA A100; vs STGM, SHAPE, MPCP, GEDF, Linux-RT: full HRT schedulability to 0.9 vs 0.4 utilization; middleware overhead tens of microseconds.
contribution: GPU partitioning and response-time analysis for mixed hard and soft real-time tasks on CPU-GPU platforms, sustaining full hard-deadline schedulability up to 0.9 utilization, 2.25x beyond prior schedulers.
flag: timing is the contribution: yes (deadline guarantees, WCRT analysis, schedulability vs baselines); safety-relevant: only as motivation (autonomous driving perception named as an HRT example). Excluded on Pillar 4 condition 2: tasks are generic CPU-GPU segments, the only learned-model content is unnamed 'self-built neural network models' mixed into the benchmark set, no inference-specific result is reported, and the platform is a Xeon + A100 server, not edge hardware. The maintainer could overturn if generic GPU real-time scheduling motivated by AI workloads is accepted as inference timing. Tables III-V and all schedulability curves are images, not in the text; lemma proofs and the supplementary material were not checked.

title: Distributed and Collaborative High-Speed Inference Deep Learning for Mobile Edge with Topological Dependencies
evidence: "an early-branching mechanism based on the latency requirements called GNN-edge" (Sec. 1, contributions)
method: Graph neural network over neighbouring Wi-Fi access points, partitioned with early-exit branches so light layers run on the AP; trained by collaborative and compressed (momentum-corrected) SGD among APs; compared with cloud GNN.
evaluation: Simulated 802.11ax dense WLAN, 16 APs, vs GNN-cloud: no scheme meets a 100 ms requirement, edge variants meet 200 ms and above, cloud only 500 ms and above (Fig. 14); no hardware, figures only.
contribution: Early-exit graph neural network run on Wi-Fi access points and trained collaboratively, meeting 200 ms configuration-latency requirements in simulation where cloud-hosted GNN inference needs 500 ms or more.
flag: timing is the contribution: partly (early-exit GNN inference traded against stated latency requirements of 100, 200 and 500 ms is one result; most of the paper is collaborative on-device training, communication overhead and WLAN throughput, which the scope ruling excludes); safety-relevant: no (Wi-Fi spatial-reuse configuration). Likely to be overturned to E1 or E2: the only budget result is Fig. 14, all results are plots with no numeric values in the text, no tail or jitter analysis, simulation only with no device named, and the early-exit mechanism is thinly specified. Wording is loose (dissatisfied requirements shown as 'negative accuracy').

title: Smart-City Spatiotemporal Data-Driven Trajectory Prediction for Autonomous Vehicles via Attention Mechanisms and Self-Supervised Learning
evidence: "with the vast majority of inference steps well below the real-time threshold of 100 ms" (Sec. IV-F Closed-Loop Validation)
method: Attention-based multimodal trajectory predictor with path-search candidate anchors, feature selection and self-supervised auxiliary tasks (path classification, interaction strength); feeds a risk-aware sampling planner (IPP).
evaluation: nuScenes vs MTP, Trajectron++, AgentFormer, LaPred, PGP, DICE etc: minADE/minFDE/MR; 14.9 ms per frame for 8 agents on RTX 4090, 1.39-8.69x faster; ViL closed loop on RTX 4080 vs IDM; no deadline except nominal 100 ms.
contribution: A path-anchored attention trajectory predictor for driving that beats DICE on nuScenes displacement error and runs in 14.9 ms per frame for eight agents on a desktop GPU.
flag: timing is the contribution: no; application safety-relevant (autonomous driving). Speed is merely reported (average runtime on desktop RTX 4090/4080, no edge hardware, no tail or miss analysis; the 100 ms threshold appears once, read off a figure). Excluded on Pillar 4 scope only: as a multi-agent predictor with baselines it may meet criterion (b) under another pillar - check whether it is queued there. Table values (III-VII) are images and absent from the text, so the 32.6%/40.8% and 14.9 ms figures could be confirmed only in prose.

title: Knowledge-Based Ultra-Low-Latency Semantic Communications for Robotic Edge Intelligence
evidence: "a new air-interface framework targeting the said systems, called knowledge-based robotic semantic communications (SemCom)" (Abstract)
method: Robot uploads Int8 feature vectors to an edge knowledge-graph server using uncoded high-bit-error transmission; classifier margin absorbs channel errors; retransmission or multi-view pooling restores accuracy.
evaluation: No numeric deadline. Simulation only (Rician channel, 1 MHz). Linear classifier and VGG-11 on ModelNet40. Latency one to two orders of magnitude below coded URLLC baseline at equal accuracy (about 0.97); DNN tolerates BEP about 1e-3.
contribution: Shows that a classifier's margin lets robot-to-edge feature uploads skip channel coding, cutting transmission latency by one to two orders of magnitude versus URLLC, with accuracy scaling derived analytically.
flag: timing is the contribution: partly (latency reduction of the air interface carrying edge inference is the aim and accuracy is traded against it analytically, but there is no stated deadline or budget, no tail or outage analysis; it minimises latency relative to URLLC); application safety-relevant: no (object search by a robot). Check: maintainer may judge the accuracy-vs-latency scaling law (accuracy 1 - O(sqrt(Pb))) as enough for condition 1; if so it has a baseline and quantitative relative latency, all simulated. Protocol mentions a termination time limit without a value. Latency is transmission time only (symbols over bandwidth), no measured inference time.

title: Revisiting Outage for Edge Inference Systems
evidence: "we propose a theoretical framework that introduces and mathematically characterizes the inference outage" (Abstract); end-to-end latency constraint T_max = 10 ms covering on-device computation and feature transmission (experiment settings)
method: Defines inference outage as probability that end-to-end accuracy falls below a threshold; derives it for linear and CNN classifiers; optimises number of observations and transmitted features under a latency deadline.
evaluation: Deadline 10 ms end to end. Simulation only (Jetson TX2 speed assumed, VGG16, ModelNet; Rayleigh channel). At 0.05 inference outage, tolerates channel outage 0.3 (linear), 0.2 (CNN) vs 0.06, 0.08 for baselines; matches brute force.
contribution: Introduces inference outage - the probability that split edge inference misses an accuracy target within a 10 ms deadline - and uses it to balance sensing computation against feature transmission over unreliable channels.
flag: timing is the contribution: yes (accuracy reliability under a stated 10 ms end-to-end deadline, with the computation-vs-communication split optimised inside it and a sweep over the latency constraint); application safety-relevant: no (generic multi-view object classification). Check: entirely analytical and simulated; latency is modelled as FLOPs over device speed plus 0.3 ms per feature slot, nothing is measured on hardware, so edge-deployment cell not claimed. The timing result is an outage probability under the budget rather than a measured latency. Gains are read from tolerance thresholds in the text; figure values (Figs. 8-11) not seen. Baselines are the authors' own heuristics (MaxFeat, MaxObs, ATB variants) plus brute force.

title: Attention in Motion: Secure Platooning via Transformer-Based Misbehavior Detection
venue: IEEE Transactions on Intelligent Transportation Systems
evidence: Sec. V-C: "TFLite exhibits the fastest quantized inference (0.13ms individual, 0.26ms global)"; Sec. III-A: "Successful misbehavior detection can trigger the credential revocation mechanisms"
method: AIMformer: transformer-encoder misbehaviour detector over 1 s windows of platoon CAM beacons, with per-vehicle temporal offsets and a precision-focused BCE loss; RSU-hosted global or on-vehicle variants.
evaluation: SUMO CACC simulation, 4 controllers, 9 falsification attacks; baselines LSTM/BiLSTM/CNN/GRU/MLP/Transformer. F1 0.93-0.98, AUC 0.91-0.99. Jetson Orin Nano Super: mean 0.13-0.26 ms TFLite int8, ~0.4-0.8 ms TensorRT; no tail or miss rate.
contribution: A transformer misbehaviour detector for vehicle platoons that flags falsified beacons with F1 of 0.93 or more in simulation and runs in under 1 ms on a Jetson Orin Nano.
flag: timing is the contribution: no (detector paper that reports average speed); application is safety-relevant (platoon security). The <100 ms figure is cited in the intro as a general requirement and matches the 10 Hz CAM interval, but latency is reported only as 1000-run averages, with no p99, worst case, jitter or deadline-miss rate, and no timing baseline beyond runtime/format comparison (TFLite vs ONNX vs TensorRT). Detection only outputs labels; credential revocation is mentioned, not implemented, so not criterion (a). Check whether the maintainer wants it considered under (c) instead: attacked-platoon detection among several vehicles with F1/AUC against baselines, but the measured outcome is detection accuracy, not collision or hazard rate. Read from the arXiv preprint 2512.15503, not the IEEE T-ITS version; title matches. Abstract '>=0.93' does not name the metric; body shows F1 0.93 as the lowest V x T global value.

title: MobiSplit: Mobility-Aware Inference Partitioning and Offloading for Efficient Edge Intelligence
evidence: "Constraint C1 guarantees that offloading delay does not exceed the mobile terminal's connection time." (Sec. III-E Problem Formulation)
method: MobiSplit: mobility-aware block-level DNN partitioning between device and edge server, with a distributed truthful auction for offloading and resource allocation, minimising weighted latency plus energy subject to a connection-time limit.
evaluation: Simulation only (SUMO traces, 30-100 devices, 5-25 servers; AlexNet, ResNet-18, VGG-16, GoogLeNet). Deadline: connection time; tolerable latency 1-5 s. Success rate 0.94-0.96 vs 0.82-0.88 at 90 km/h; 5-10 ms vs 25 ms MCAIO. No hardware.
contribution: A mobility-aware auction that splits DNN inference between moving devices and edge servers so offloading finishes within the connection window, raising simulated service success from about 0.85 to 0.95 at 90 km/h.
flag: timing is the contribution: partly; application not safety-relevant (generic CIFAR-10 classification, driving named only as motivation). BORDERLINE, likely overturn: the objective is weighted average latency plus energy; the only deadline is the connection-time constraint C1 and the timing result against it is the service success rate - if that does not count as a deadline, this is E1. All results simulated, no hardware. Doubt: Fig. 4 reports accuracy falling from about 80% to 41-60% after offloading, which lossless partitioning should not cause and which contradicts the claim of maintained accuracy; latency in Figs. 9-10 is 150-190 ms vs 5-10 ms in Fig. 5 (different metric, unexplained). Same group as doi:10.1109/tmc.2026.3675369.

title: Time-Sensitive Multi-DNN Inference on CPU-GPU Edge Platforms
evidence: "we set a 400 ms deadline for each task to ensure timely object detection" (Sec. VII-B End-to-End System Evaluation)
method: BlastNet: duo-blocks (paired CPU and GPU variants of each DNN block, found by NAS) scheduled EDF at block level across CPU and GPU to minimise deadline misses under an accuracy bound, with memory-aware duo-block selection.
evaluation: F1/10 car on Jetson TX2, four ResNet18 tasks, 400 ms deadline: miss rate <5% (max 4.25%) vs 18.96-19.97% Layer_Sched. Xavier/TX2/desktop: 10.63% vs 45.70%, accuracy loss <=1.63%; ViT-Tiny 0.75% vs 46-61%.
contribution: Block-level CPU-GPU co-scheduling of concurrent DNNs on Jetson-class boards that cuts deadline-miss rate by up to 35 points over layer-level scheduling at under 2% accuracy loss.
flag: timing is the contribution: yes; application safety-relevant (traffic-sign perception on an F1/10 autonomous car, 400 ms deadline argued as a safety bound). Check: many multi-task results come from a trace-driven simulator fed with times profiled on Xavier, TX2 and desktop, not from live runs - only the F1/10 TX2 experiment is clearly end to end. Metric is deadline-miss rate with soft deadlines; no worst-case bound or tail percentiles. Abstract 35.07% is an absolute difference (10.63% vs 45.70%) and is found in the body. Extended journal version of an earlier BlastNet conference paper - check for a duplicate record.

title: Task-Oriented Integrated Sensing and Semantic Communications for Multi-Device Video Analytics
evidence: "The latency requirement T max is set as 150 ms" (Sec. V-A Evaluation Setup)
method: SenSem: CSI-based localisation crops the region of interest, a lightweight on-device MobileNet scores blocks, and joint block selection plus power control maximises pose-estimation accuracy within a transmission latency budget; CSI-assisted ViTPose at the edge.
evaluation: Budget 150 ms (71 ms device compute + 79 ms uplink). Raspberry Pi 5: evaluator 71 ms cropped vs 507 ms full; existing encoders all exceed 150 ms. Multi-device mAP vs H.264, YOLO, average, ablations; uplink simulated from WARP CSI.
contribution: A sensing-assisted semantic-communication pipeline that keeps multi-camera pose analytics inside a 150 ms budget by cropping with channel-state information and sending only the most informative 5.5% of image blocks.
flag: timing is the contribution: partly; application weakly safety-relevant (surveillance pose estimation, public safety as motivation only). Accuracy is maximised under a stated 150 ms budget, which fits the accuracy-vs-budget clause, but the paper is mainly a wireless resource-allocation and semantic-communication paper; latency is a constraint, never a measured end-to-end distribution. Only the device-side evaluator is timed on real hardware (Raspberry Pi 5); the multi-device uplink is simulated with collected CSI, and server inference time is not counted in the budget. mAP figures for baselines are in plots, not text. No miss rate or tail latency. Maintainer may overturn to E1.

title: Adaptive Inference Acceleration With Fine-Grained Model Partitioning for Mobile Edge Intelligence
evidence: "The objective is to minimize the total task completion time across all MDs over a given time horizon." (problem formulation section)
method: Layer-level DNN partitioning and offloading across devices, edge servers and cloud; Lyapunov optimisation turns long-term average completion time under queue-stability constraints into per-slot problems solved by QMIX multi-agent RL.
evaluation: Simulation only (5 devices, 3-7 servers, ResNet18, GoogLeNet, VGG16, AlexNet; 32 slots of 0.07 s) vs Greedy, Genetic, MAD2RL: completion time 68-72% lower at 3 servers. No deadline, budget, tail or hardware.
contribution: A Lyapunov-plus-QMIX scheme for fine-grained DNN partitioning across mobile devices and edge servers that lowers simulated average task completion time while keeping task queues stable.
flag: timing is the contribution: no (average completion time minimised, queue stability as the only constraint; no deadline, budget, bound or tail analysis); application not safety-relevant. Simulation only with synthetic CPU capacities; absolute latency values appear only in figures. Companion to MobiSplit (doi:10.1109/tmc.2025.3620438) by the same group, which adds a connection-time constraint; decide the two consistently.

title: Deadline-Guarded Edge Inference With FPGA Preemption
evidence: "Upon prediction of a miss, the system activates the FPGA as a deadline guardian to run a smaller DNN for the same task to meet the deadline." (Abstract)
method: GPU runs the primary DNN; lightweight predictors on progress waypoints plus hardware status forecast a deadline miss and pre-empt to a smaller guardian DNN on an FPGA; simulation picks multitask preemption plans.
evaluation: Jetson AGX Orin plus Xilinx ZCU102; ResNet-50 deadlines 15-18 ms (mean 16 ms); vs WCET (ResNet-18) and early-exit: miss rate under 1%, effective accuracy 0.74-0.756 vs 0.70 and ~0.6; 9-20x miss reduction.
contribution: A GPU-FPGA system predicts DNN deadline misses mid-inference and pre-empts to a smaller guardian model, cutting miss rates 9-20 times on Jetson AGX Orin and ZCU102 hardware.
flag: timing is the contribution: yes; application safety-relevant only by motivation (autonomous driving perception benchmarks: ImageNet, COCO, KITTI), no driving task run. Interceptor set to no because it aborts and replaces an inference, not an action - check if you read that as override. Deadlines are self-chosen (Z-scores of mean latency, or set so 10-20% of runs miss), not application deadlines. Abstract says accuracy gain 'more than 10%', contribution list says 'up to 10%'. Table II/V/VI values are images, not in the text; multitask figures from prose: Acce 0.823 to over 0.95, miss 10-20% to below 3.5%, control overhead under 6%.

title: Adaptive Image Batching and Slicing in Edge Networks for Delay-Critical Small Object Detection
venue: IEEE Transactions on Parallel and Distributed Systems
evidence: "Any SOD task that fails to finish before its deadline is marked as a failed task, with its detection results set to empty." (Sec. V-C)
method: Deadline-prioritised batching of YOLOv11n detection tasks using an offline batch-size-to-delay map, peer-edge offloading via linear load prediction, and image slicing that spends deadline slack on accuracy.
evaluation: 3 Jetson Xavier NX servers, VisDrone-2019, Shanghai Telecom arrivals; per-task deadlines from {100,300,500,700,900} ms; six baselines plus three ablations; success rate +19%, mAP +0.5%, mean delay -12.8% on average.
contribution: Deadline-prioritised batching, edge collaboration and adaptive image slicing raise the share of small-object detection tasks finishing within deadline by 19% on a three-node Jetson Xavier NX testbed.
flag: timing is the contribution: yes (deadline-constrained scheduling of DNN inference with accuracy traded against per-task deadline slack); safety-relevant by motivation only (driving, aerial surveillance). Check: deadlines are randomly assigned from a fixed set, arrivals are a replayed telecom trace with an assumed SOD ratio; most baselines are cloud models handicapped by a sampled 200-300 ms link delay, so the 19% gain is largely vs cloud - the fair comparison is edge YOLOv11n and the ablations. Table II per-setting figures are images, not in the text; no tail or worst-case latency reported, only success rate and mean delay. Jitter test is one injected 100 ms delay (under 1% success-rate change).

title: Measurement-Informed Safe Reinforcement Learning for Quantum Battery Charging via Harmonic-Syndrome Diagnostics and BMS Constraints
evidence: "The shield projects the raw PPO action a_t into a one-step-safe set A_safe(x_t) defined by a learned voltage surrogate" (Sec. IV-C, Safety Filter and Mitigation Policy)
method: PPO charging controller for a simulated quantum battery: harmonic-spectrum features become a 3-level risk syndrome, reward carries BMS penalties, and a one-step voltage shield projects actions into a predicted-safe set.
evaluation: Digital-twin simulation only, N=1-16, 50 seeds. Baselines PPO, threshold-grid, Lagrangian-PPO, CPO. Metrics final ergotropy, high-risk ratio, voltage-violation rate (<0.1%); 0.4% violations under -10% predictor bias. Estimated 19-20 us tick budget.
contribution: A safe-RL charging controller for simulated quantum batteries that turns harmonic-spectrum diagnostics into a three-level risk code and adds a one-step voltage shield on top of reward penalties.
flag: Pillar 1, borderline, recommended out because the runtime shield is a minor part: it is called a 'light action shield', is absent from the listed contributions C1-C4 (syndrome, penalty-based RL, digital twin, statistics), and none of the four ablations removes it, so its own effect on violations is never isolated - only its robustness to predictor bias (Table 9). Safety comes mainly from reward penalties, which do not meet (a). If the maintainer judges 'Shielded-PPO (ours)' as the mechanism, it would pass (a) and the evaluation floor. CHECK: the abstract says the framework is demonstrated 'on a benchtop transmon setup with N = 1-2, reporting shield trigger/violation rates' and KL/EMD drift, but Sec. IX states 'no physical prototype is implemented in this work' and lists the benchtop as future Phase 1; I found no hardware results. The 20 us latency is an estimated budget (Table 6 is titled 'Estimated'), not a measurement. Tables 6, 7 and 9 did not survive text extraction, so the per-method numbers could not be read; values quoted are from the prose. Single-agent, physical-domain simulation, no human handoff.

title: Bending-Aware Vision Co-Pilot for Intelligent Robotic Assistance in Endovascular Intervention
evidence: "the current system should be interpreted as a practical assistive closed loop rather than a strict high-frequency hard-real-time controller" (Sec. IV)
method: DSA-image microwire segmentation, centerline and curvature give a bending-risk value; a sigmoid regulator applies bounded modulation to the teleoperating physician's advance and rotation commands on an endovascular robot.
evaluation: Six vascular phantom paths and nine in vivo animal trials, with vs without co-pilot: mean max risk 113.0 to 49.0 and 239.8 to 80.5; RTX3090; latency estimated 95-115 ms at 8 fps, no deadline.
contribution: A vision co-pilot for a teleoperated endovascular robot estimates microwire bending risk from angiography and modulates the operator's commands, roughly halving peak bending risk in phantom and animal trials.
flag: timing is the contribution: no - an application paper that reports its speed; application IS safety-relevant (vessel injury in surgery). Latency is partly ESTIMATED (20-40 ms segmentation forward pass is taken from earlier work, only 10 ms image and 60 ms command link delays are measured), no deadline or budget, no tail figures, and the compute is a desktop RTX3090, not edge hardware. Check outside Pillar 4: the regulator attenuates a human operator's commands at runtime (shared control), which is close to criterion (a)/(e); I set interceptor to no because the text says it 'does not replace the operator command' and only modulates it, with no halt or handoff - maintainer may read that differently. Only comparison is own system with vs without assistance; small n, single-agent.

title: Ultra-Low-Latency Edge Inference for Distributed Sensing
evidence: "We consider an E2E deadline so that the sensing and transmission must be completed within a duration of T seconds" (Sec. III)
method: Optimises short-packet length for uploading sensor features to an edge classifier under an end-to-end deadline, trading finite-blocklength reliability against the number of views or snapshots that fit.
evaluation: Simulation only; deadline T = 1 ms (sensing 0.1 ms/shot), 100 kHz; GMM linear classifier and split VGG16 MVCNN on ModelNet; vs brute force, URLLC, Shannon-rate; 1-8 dB SNR gain over URLLC (MVCNN), matches brute force.
contribution: An analysis and closed-form packet-length design for distributed sensing with split inference that maximises classification accuracy under a millisecond end-to-end deadline using finite-blocklength transmission.
flag: timing is the contribution: yes - accuracy is maximised under a hard stated E2E deadline (1 ms) for device-edge split inference; application is motivated by autonomous driving (30 ms cited) but none is evaluated. Check: simulation only with a channel model, no hardware and no measured latency - the deadline is a constraint in the formulation and the reported outcome is accuracy at equal deadline, so whether this meets the quantitative timing floor (latency against a stated budget) is the maintainer's call; accuracy curves and the deadline sweeps are only in figures I could not read, the text gives SNR gains only; deadline covers sensing plus transmission and appears to exclude compute time; fetched arXiv version may differ from the 2025 TWC version.

title: Ultra-Low-Latency Robust Edge Inference: An Integrated Computation and Communication Design
evidence: "formulate optimization problems to minimize total computation and communication latency while ensuring inference accuracy under limited wireless resources" (Sec. VII)
method: Derives accuracy bounds versus number of snapshots or views and feature-upload bit error rate, then jointly optimises sensor selection, transmit power and compute/communication time to minimise latency under an accuracy constraint.
evaluation: Simulation only: Gaussian-mixture features and VGG-11 on ModelNet40 over Rayleigh channel; vs error-free upload benchmark; accuracy target e.g. 0.9; no latency deadline or budget, no real hardware, latency values only in figures.
contribution: Tolerating bit errors in uploaded features, a joint computation-communication design minimises edge-inference latency subject to an accuracy constraint, shown in simulation to beat error-free upload.
flag: timing is the contribution: partly - latency is the objective, but it is MINIMISED under an accuracy constraint with no stated deadline, budget, timing bound or tail analysis, which the scope ruling puts in E1; safety-relevant by motivation only (autonomous driving). Most likely to be overturned: the multi-view case minimises the maximum (slowest-sensor) latency and the paper trades accuracy against latency explicitly, so a maintainer could read it as budgeted inference with the roles swapped; the bounds proved are on accuracy, not timing. All results simulated (Jetson only cited to justify an energy coefficient); no numeric latency appears in the text, only in figures. A sibling file 'Ultra-Low-Latency Edge Inference for Distributed Sensing with Short Packets' exists in the folder - possibly related work by the same group.

title: Cooperative Augmented Reality: Displaying Occluded Vehicles using V2X Communications
evidence: "These results demonstrate that the E2E latency for intelligently triggering the X-ray system off is done under the 300 ms threshold set by ETSI for road safety applications." (Sec. VI-C)
method: AR headset shows cyclists a virtual 'X-ray' car from V2X messages; YOLOv9t on a Jetson Orin Nano detects visible vehicles in the headset stream to switch the overlay off.
evaluation: Real-world demo, 100 frames. Budget: ETSI 300 ms. HoloLens 2 plus Jetson Orin Nano: stream 152.90+-14.75 ms, detection 100.42+-77.08 ms, E2E 266.46+-78.67 ms, 3.75 FPS. Only resolution/FPS and Wi-Fi-vs-USB comparisons; no baseline system.
contribution: Field demonstration of a V2X-plus-AR occluded-vehicle display for cyclists, with a per-stage latency breakdown showing a mean end-to-end delay of 266 ms against the ETSI 300 ms budget on a Jetson Orin Nano.
flag: timing is the contribution: partly; application safety-relevant (cyclist collision warning, advisory display only). Read as an application paper that deploys a detector and reports its speed against a threshold, hence E1, but the maintainer may overturn because latency is measured stage by stage against a stated 300 ms budget on real hardware. Check: 'within 300 ms' holds for the mean only - 266.46+-78.67 ms implies a sizeable share of frames exceed 300 ms and no percentile or miss rate is given; the 81.53 ms V2X path figure is quoted from the authors' prior work [10], not measured here; no baseline method, no user study, single site, n=100 frames; headset display latency not included.

title: Latency Guaranteed Edge Inference via Dynamic Compression Ratio Selection
venue: IEEE Wireless Communications and Networking Conference
evidence: "By dynamically selecting the optimal compression ratio with the awareness of the remaining latency budget, more tasks can be timely completed and get the correct inference results under the communication resource constraint." (Abstract)
method: Edge server picks a lossy compression ratio per offloaded inference task from queue deadline slack, via offline dynamic programming and an online MDP; uncertainty-triggered retransmission at lower compression.
evaluation: Simulation, MNIST MLP on edge server; deadline tau=12 slots (resolutions cost 1, 3, 10 slots; accuracy 0.89, 0.97, 0.98). Metric: share of tasks on time and correct, versus fixed resolution and no retransmission; >97.5% at arrival rate 0.5. No hardware, no ms.
contribution: Deadline-aware edge inference that chooses input compression per task from the remaining latency budget with an MDP, and uses output uncertainty to trigger retransmission, raising the share of tasks finished on time and correct.
flag: timing is the contribution: yes; application not safety-relevant (MNIST digits; autonomous driving only named as motivation). Check: entirely simulated in abstract time slots - no hardware, no milliseconds, static channel, Bernoulli arrivals, inference compute time not modelled (only transmission time); results are in Figs 6-9, text gives only >97.5% at rate 0.5, 'over 4.5%' gain from retransmission with known correctness and 2% with uncertainty; no deadline-miss rate reported separately from accuracy; toy model (one-hidden-layer MLP); 'guaranteed' means tasks that cannot meet the deadline are dropped. Eq. 5-6 use min where max is meant.

title: A Case Study for Vulnerable Road Users Protection: Systematic Approach for Managing and Scheduling C-ITS Workloads in Heterogeneous Clusters
venue: 2025 IEEE World Forum on Public Safety Technology (WF-PST)
evidence: "Across all evaluated scenarios, the system achieved 100% reliability in meeting the maximum 300-millisecond overall delay and the 10Hz frequency requirements for Collective Perception Messages (CPMs), as shown in Table III." (Sec. V-B)
method: Network-aware scheduler replacing the Kubernetes/KubeEdge scheduler: 0-1 ILP places VRU-detection inference workloads under delay constraints, weighting delay versus energy by alpha, using lookup-table delay/energy profiles and live network metrics.
evaluation: Real testbed, two camera intersections; Jetson Nano, Orin 30W/50W, A5500 workstation. Budgets: 300 ms overall, 100 ms processing (10 Hz), 100 ms network. Three scenarios, alpha sweep: max total delay 70-153 ms, max processing 10-94 ms. No baseline scheduler.
contribution: Deadline-constrained placement of roadside VRU-detection inference across heterogeneous Jetson and workstation nodes by an ILP scheduler using live network metrics, meeting ETSI 300 ms and 10 Hz limits on a campus testbed while trading delay against energy.
flag: timing is the contribution: yes; application safety-relevant (vulnerable road user protection). Check: the only comparison is the alpha sweep (alpha=1 delay-only versus alpha=0 energy-only) - no native Kubernetes scheduler or other baseline, so the baseline/ablation floor is met weakly; '100% reliability' rests on means collected 6-8 min after each decision plus max values, and max processing delay reaches 92-94 ms against the 100 ms limit, which the authors admit 'introduces unpredictability'; the DA Service is a precomputed lookup table, not a learned predictor; the cloud node is a local workstation with artificial delay; RSU-to-vehicle hop excluded; Scenario 3 is titled network latency but described as artificial processing delay; the labels cidelay and irdelay are swapped between Table I and Sec. IV-D and the constraint on cidelay is missing from Eq. 1; detection model not named.

title: Cloud-edge collaborative state monitoring and fault diagnosis for smart distribution system operation and maintenance
venue: International Conference on Intelligent Transportation Systems and Automation Control
evidence: "If the entropy exceeds the threshold tau, the edge node stores a tentative diagnosis but blocks automatic actuation and sends the compressed feature, waveform thumbnail, equipment identifier, and multimodal context to the cloud." (Sec. 2.4)
method: Quantised CNN-attention-Transformer on an edge board classifies power-quality disturbances from wavelet maps; an entropy and interlock gate allows bounded local commands or blocks actuation and defers to cloud digital-twin review.
evaluation: 120,000 simulated windows, 10 states; six classifier baselines; 99.23% accuracy, 18.6 ms on ARM-A72. Feeder emulation vs cloud-only: alarm-to-command 27.9 vs 186.7 ms, false-action rate 0.36% vs 1.26%, 7.4% events deferred.
contribution: An edge power-quality fault classifier for low-voltage distribution areas that issues bounded control commands locally only when confidence and interlock checks pass, and otherwise blocks actuation and defers the event to cloud review.
flag: neither as recommended, but borderline for Pillar 3 (and Pillar 1): the confidence and safety gate is a real runtime gate that blocks actuation and defers to a cloud safeguard, yet the paper's main contribution and most of its evaluation (Tables 2 and 3, all ablations) is the INT8 classifier; the gate is a fixed entropy threshold plus rule interlocks with no ablation of its own and no threshold or coverage-risk analysis. The only safety-relevant number for it is the false-action rate 0.36% vs 1.26% against a cloud-only pipeline, a comparison that changes diagnosis location and gating together, so the gate's effect is confounded; the text says both arms use 'the same event stream and controller logic', which makes the baseline's higher false-action rate unexplained. If the maintainer treats that as a sufficient baseline, the paper could enter under Pillar 3 route (iv), safety-critical runtime gate. Deferral is to a cloud digital twin, not a person; human-supervised fallback is future work. All results are emulation, the authors say so. SPIE proceedings paper from utility-company authors; the conclusion says the paper 'repositioned EIQ-CaT', suggesting a reworked classifier paper. No uncertainty or variance reported for the control-in-the-loop metrics.

title: In-network P4-based Low Latency Robot Arm Control
evidence: "the creation of correct TCP segment containing a reply message to the robot with a 'magic word' command to immediately stop the robot movement" (Sec. 2, System Overview)
method: A P4 switch between a simulated UR robot arm and its controller parses position messages, matches a threshold and injects a TCP stop command itself, keeping SEQ/ACK numbers in sync.
evaluation: Proof of concept with URSim and an emulated controller-link delay. No numbers, tables, baselines or hardware reported; results are stated qualitatively only.
contribution: A three-page poster showing that a programmable P4 switch near a robot arm can detect a position threshold in transit and inject the stop command itself, instead of waiting for a distant controller.

title: SAGE: A Split-Architecture Methodology for Efficient End-to-End Autonomous Vehicle Control
venue: ACM Transactions on Embedded Computing Systems

Check: network is swept as a parameter with zero packet loss and RTT from averaged pings - no live wireless, no jitter, no tail latency, no deadline-miss count; only a statement that 100 ms is met down to about 320 Kbps for low-res input. title: BlastNet: Exploiting Duo-Blocks for Cross-Processor Real-Time DNN Inference
venue: SenSys 2022 - Proceedings of the 20th ACM Conference on Embedded Networked Sensor Systems
evidence: "set the deadline for each task as 400ms, which is enough to detect an" (Sec 6.2 End-to-end System Evaluation)

title: Repercussions of Using DNN Compilers on Edge GPUs for Real Time and Safety Critical Systems: A Quantitative Audit
venue: ACM Journal on Emerging Technologies in Computing Systems
evidence: "This causes inference latencies to vary across engines for the same" (Sec 5, Observation 6)

AutoTVM figures 8-10x faster than TensorRT (0.49 vs 3.93ms ResNet-18) look implausible; check measurement method. Pre-processing (about 15ms) dominates response time. Secs 2, 4, 5.4-5.6 and related work skimmed.

title: Color-based Lightweight Utility-aware Load Shedding for Real-Time Video Analytics at the Edge

title: OffloaD: Detection Failure-based Scheduler for Offloading Object Detection
venue: ACM Transactions on Embedded Computing Systems
evidence: "We use the DFM to drive the scheduling decision as it maximizes the detection accuracy and prioritizes local processing" (Sec. 3.2 Scheduler)
method: Device-edge offloading scheduler for object detection: a learned failure predictor (SVM or MobileNet-v2), a device-vs-edge agreement score and a network-latency score decide which detector is master.
evaluation: No stated deadline or budget. Jetson NX device + Jetson AGX edge, YOLOv4/tiny-YOLOv4, ImageNet VID. Mean e2e latency 0.14 s vs 0.22 s edge-only; real-time mAP 0.58; 50-200 ms injected delay.

flag: timing is the contribution: partly; application not safety-relevant as evaluated (generic video detection; drones and robots only as motivation). Excluded because it reduces MEAN e2e latency with no deadline, budget, bound, tail or miss-rate figure; the latency-score constant tau (max acceptable network latency) is never given a value. Could be overturned under the 'how delay or jitter degrades a decision' clause: Sec. 4.4.2-4.4.3 and Fig. 9, 10, 12 study 50-200 ms delay, jitter, loss and bandwidth against a latency-aware accuracy (real-time mAP), e.g. 26.36% accuracy loss at 200 ms vs 33.73% for DeepDecision - but those are figure-only and the DeepDecision curve is copied from its paper. Checks: Table 9 says intro-DL 12.973 ms is 9.12% of a 177.98 ms pipeline (it is 7.3%); ref [19] is called 'Russakovsky et al.' in Sec. 4.5.1 but is Ran et al.; Table 8 compares against maxima reported by other papers on other hardware.

title: Agile3D: Adaptive Contention- and Content-Aware 3D Object Detection for Embedded GPUs
venue: ACM SIGMOBILE International Conference on Mobile Systems, Applications, and Services
evidence: "The controller's main objective is to dynamically select the optimal branch at each timestamp that satisfies the latency SLO and maximizes accuracy, given the current input point cloud and hardware contention." (Sec. 3.4)
method: Multi-branch LiDAR 3D detector (about 50 models, five knobs) with a learned contention- and content-aware controller (supervised then DPO fine-tuned) choosing a branch per frame under a latency SLO.

contribution: Agile3D keeps LiDAR 3D object detection inside 100-500 ms latency budgets on Jetson Orin and Xavier under GPU contention by switching among about 50 detector branches with a learned controller, holding latency violations below 10%.
flag: timing is the contribution: yes; application safety-relevant (autonomous-driving LiDAR perception) though no safety outcome is measured. Budgets are soft SLOs with up to 10% violations tolerated, not hard deadlines - Table 2 shows the full method at 5.27% and 5.64% violations (Light, Peak) while the simpler SL and Stat controllers violate less at slightly lower accuracy, so the gain is accuracy at an accepted miss rate. Conclusion claims '33-75 ms on KITTI (Orin)' but the body evaluates KITTI on Xavier only; abstract says 1-5% accuracy gain, conclusion says +3% and +7%. Controller overhead 8 ms (CARL), branch switch under 1 ms. No arXiv id in text.

title: Towards Accurate, Adaptive, and Real-time Machine Perception on Resource-constrained Platforms

LIKELY TO BE OVERTURNED: this is a 3-page single-author MobiSys '25 doctoral/extended abstract with no evaluation of its own - every number is restated from ARIA (MobiSys 2025) and Panopticus (MobiCom 2024), with no tables, no baseline names, no per-device latency and no miss-rate breakdown. The maintainer may prefer exclude-E2 here and queue the two primary papers instead; check whether they are already in the record set. No arXiv id in text.

title: Safety-Critical Offloading with Constrained Reinforcement Learning for Multi-access Edge Computing
evidence: "The safety layer regulates the output of the RL agent so that unsafe offloading decisions are calibrated before they are executed." (Sec. 5, Conclusion)
method: TD3 task-offloading agent for multi-access edge computing with an Informer state forecaster on the input and a pretrained linear safety layer that projects each action to the nearest deadline-feasible one.
evaluation: Simulation only. Baselines all-server, random, matching, PPO, TD3, LSTM-TD3; ablations with and without safety layer. Deadline miss rate at load 2.9: TD3 11.2%, safety layer only 7.4%, full 5.5%.
contribution: A constrained-RL scheme for offloading deadline-bound tasks to edge servers that corrects each proposed action through a learned safety layer before execution, cutting deadline misses relative to reward-shaped RL baselines.
flag: Pillar 1, criterion (a): the safety layer (after Dalal et al., extended to several simultaneous constraints) corrects the policy's action at decision time, and Tables 3 and 4 isolate it (TD3-SO vs TD3-O) on deadline miss rate. Maintainer should check three things. (1) 'Safety' here means a task meeting its computation deadline in a simulated offloading system; no physical hazard is modelled, autonomous driving is motivation only. If deadline misses are not accepted as a safety metric this becomes E1. (2) The abstract says the layer 'effectively eliminates deadline misses', but CRLO still misses up to 5.5% (Table 3) and 2.1% (Table 4); the ablation shows the Informer forecaster helps more than the safety layer (6.7% vs 7.4% at the highest load). (3) The layer is a learned linearised constraint model, so no guarantee; a separate rule shifts tasks to the cloud when a miss is predicted. Single mobile-device agent with other devices as background load, so not multi-agent. No hardware, no measured decision latency, no variance or seeds reported. 37-page article: read abstract, introduction, contributions, safety-layer section 3.2, setup 4.1 and results 4.3-4.5 and conclusion; skimmed the system model and complexity analysis.

title: Edge-Cloud Orchestration of Assertion-Based Monitors for Robotic Applications
venue: ACM Transactions on Embedded Computing Systems
evidence: "the capability of optimizing the end-to-end latency of verification at runtime by exploiting a distributed computing architecture (i.e., edge-cloud)" (Note to Practitioners)
method: Platform (Carmine) that synthesises ROS2 monitors from signal temporal logic assertions and migrates them across edge and cloud at runtime with a MILP on CPU and network statistics; drops events under overload.
evaluation: 125 ms (8 Hz) control period on an RB-Kairos robot, Jetson Xavier NX + i7 board + server. Makespan 115 ms without monitors, 140 ms with 201 monitors, 125 ms after migration. Only with/without-monitor comparison.

flag: timing is the contribution: partly (keeping monitor overhead from breaking a 125 ms control period), but there is no learned model anywhere in the mechanism - the monitors are STL automata and the allocator is a MILP - so condition (2) fails; application safety-relevant (industrial mobile manipulator). The robot does run a DNN image-recognition node but its timing is not studied. Maintainer may want to look at it under criterion (a) runtime monitoring instead: I marked runtime_interceptor no because the monitors only report violations; enforcing fail-safe behaviour is mentioned as a possibility, not implemented or tested. Evaluation is thin: one synthetic 3-node run (Fig. 6, MILP solve 27 ms per second) and one robot mission with a single makespan triple, no repetitions, no detection-delay or miss-rate metric, no competing orchestrator; authors admit the event-dropping overload mode can cause false negatives and that timing upper bounds are future work. Publication date in the text is March 2026.

title: PipeMLLM: Accelerating on-device Multimodal LLM Inference via Speculative Sensing and Encoding
evidence: "Under a 200 ms latency constraint, the optimizer selects more complex configurations for harder questions" (Sec 4.3.2)

Check: 7-page workshop paper; baseline comparison exists only as Figure 5 with no numbers in text; headline 213 ms exceeds the 200 ms constraint used in Sec 4.3.2 and no budget for the headline run is stated; no miss rate or tail latency; sensing delays emulated by sleep; motivation numbers (80 ms saving) come from a different lip-reading task; abstract says Jetson Xavier, body says Xavier NX.

title: End-to-End Model Generation with Large Language Models for Adaptive IoT Application Deployment
venue: Proceedings of the 2026 IEEE/ACM 48th International Conference on Software Engineering

title: Frame-based Synchronization for Multi-view Multi-sensor Fusion in Embedded Systems
venue: Research in Adaptive and Convergent Systems
evidence: "it successfully prevents the catastrophic deadline misses that cause the performance of DNN-SAM to degrade much more severely" (Sec 4)
method: FBAIS: frame-based dispatcher with worst-fit core assignment that skips and then prioritises infeasible fusion tasks, plus EDF-style effective deadlines and adaptive input-resolution scaling so YOLOv7 inference finishes before the synchronisation deadline.

Fails the evaluation floor as written: no deadline-miss rate, latency figure or proved bound is reported, only F1-score loss in which missed or skipped tasks are scored with stale results; the bounded-tardiness claim is asserted, not proved or measured. title: SEEB-GPU: Early-Exit Aware Scheduling and Batching for Edge GPU Inference
evidence: "An SLA violation occurs when the response time of a request exceeds its deadline. We set each deadline to 120% of its expected execution time, based on offline profiling." (Sec 4)
method: SEEB-GPU: per-task GPU TPC masks for spatial isolation plus an EDF-inspired scheduler that picks batch size and early-exit confidence threshold from an offline linear latency model so predicted latency meets the earliest deadline minus slack.
evaluation: RTX 3090 with Alibaba PAI, Poisson and Gamma traces; deadline 120% of profiled execution time; baselines Batch, BranchyNet, DeepRT, GSLICE; PAI latency 0.047 s vs 0.084-0.738 s; Poisson SLA violations 0% vs 45.6-60.2%; ablation; overhead about 1 ms.

flag: timing is the contribution: yes; application not safety-relevant in itself (multi-tenant image classification; driving named only as a workload label). Check: called edge GPU but evaluated on a desktop RTX 3090, no Jetson results, so edge deployment not credited; deadlines are soft and self-defined (120% of profiled time); BranchyNet also reaches 0% violations so the deadline-miss gain is over non-early-exit baselines only; accuracy drops to 83.5% vs 96.3% on PAI; no worst-case guarantee, latency model is a profiled linear fit. Did not read related work in detail.

title: MMEdge: Accelerating On-device Multimodal Inference via Pipelined Sensing and Encoding
evidence: "The optimizer selects the configuration with the highest predicted accuracy that meets the given latency constraint." (Sec. 4 System Overview).

title: nn-Live: Predicting Runtime Latency for Concurrent DNN Inference on Mobile Devices
venue: Proceedings of the 32nd Annual International Conference on Mobile Computing and Networking
evidence: "Given an 85 ms latency budget, the system triggers a prediction whenever the main task arrives or environment shifts occur, selecting the highest-capacity configuration that satisfies the constraint." (Sec. 7 Case Study)

Check: evaluation floor is met only loosely - headline metrics are prediction error (MAPE, RMSE, P99 of prediction error), not deadline-miss or tail latency of inference; the only budget result is the Sec. 7 case study (85 ms budget, ResNet34 variants at 72.6-77.7 ms, v0 would hit 94.9 ms) which is one trace with no baseline and no miss rate.
