title: Fat Block: Narrowing the Boundary of pWCET Analysis on GPU
venue: Proceedings of the 2026 3rd International Conference on Autonomous Driving and Intelligent Sensing Technology
evidence: "This paper presents a GPU-oriented pWCET analysis framework that narrows execution-time uncertainty by enforcing controlled execution semantics at the SM level." (Abstract)
method: Fat Block: resource-saturating thread blocks force one block per GPU streaming multiprocessor via persistent kernels; device-side timing samples under load injection are fitted with extreme value theory (POT/GPD) for pWCET.
evaluation: NVIDIA Jetson Thor; kernels SRAD, CONV2D, BFS, GEMM; baseline blocks. pWCET at 0.9999: conv2d 127.19 to 61.33 us, gemm 88.03 to 52.36 us; mean time up 20-56%. No deadline stated.
contribution: Fat Block constrains each GPU streaming multiprocessor to a single saturating thread block and applies extreme value theory, tightening probabilistic WCET bounds for GPU kernels on Jetson Thor.
flag: timing is the contribution: yes, but no learned model in it; motivation is safety-relevant (autonomous driving) but nothing safety-related is evaluated. Subjects are individual GPU kernels (SRAD, Apollo CONV2D and BFS, CUTLASS GEMM labelled 'ML Inference'), not inference of a trained network, so it fails condition 2. Maintainer may want to check whether CONV2D/GEMM kernels count as learned-model inference - I judged not. Also: no stated deadline; text says '105 samples' (probably 10^5 lost in extraction); method-comparison (Sec 6.2) is CONV2D only and read from a figure; small conference (ADIST 2026), EVT i.i.d. assumptions not validated.

title: Linux AGX: An Adaptive GPU eXtension to Linux Fair Scheduling for Physical AI and Robotic Systems
venue: ACM SIGOPS Symposium on Operating Systems Principles (SOSP)
evidence: "vanilla EEVDF raises p99 perception-to-control latency to 114.6 ms and deadline misses to 43.6%, while EEVDF+Tune reduces them only to 95.0 ms and 30.8%." (Sec. 6.4)
method: AGX: user-space profiler computes per-task importance from GPU share, CPU-GPU handoffs and dependency criticality; kernel applies it as an effective weight plus bounded boost for GPU-gating feeder tasks in Linux EEVDF/CFS.
evaluation: Jetson Orin AGX, Orin Nano, RTX 3060 desktop, TurtleBot; vs CFS, EEVDF, EEVDF+Tune, Heuristic, DREAM. Deadline 66.7 ms (15 Hz): p99 114.6 to 70.5 ms, misses 43.6% to 9.8%; makespan -6.0-20.0%.
contribution: AGX extends Linux fair scheduling with GPU- and dependency-aware task weights, proving a bounded GPU launch delay and cutting p99 perception-to-control latency and deadline misses for on-device ML robotic pipelines on Jetson.
flag: timing is the contribution: partly - headline metrics are makespan and GPU utilisation (throughput), but Sec. 6.4 and the TurtleBot study report p99 latency and deadline-miss rate against the 66.7 ms update period, and Sec. 5.2 proves a K-independent gate-delay bound (Theorem 5.5). Application is safety-relevant only loosely (mobile robot perception-to-control freshness); no safety outcome measured. Check: AGX is explicitly best-effort, not a hard real-time guarantee; the deadline is the pipeline period, not a certified deadline; ML models served through Triton/ONNX including LLM/VLM, so learned-model inference is the workload but the mechanism is a generic CPU scheduler. 24 pages with appendices; I read abstract, intro, Sec. 6 and conclusion closely and only skimmed Sec. 4-5 proofs and appendices. Physical-robot p99 figures (25-30 ms typical vs 60-86 ms) are read from a moving-average plot.

title: AlignDual: Real-Time Multimodal 3D Detection on Resource-Constraint Edge Device via Inter-Stream Cooperation
venue: Proceedings of the ACM on Interactive Mobile Wearable and Ubiquitous Technologies
evidence: "the real-time Compliance Rate (CR-100), the percentage of frames processed within a 100ms latency budget." (Sec. 7.2)
method: AlignDual: edge 2D detections guide point-cloud compression; cloud fuses camera and LiDAR using motion-prediction synchronisation instead of waiting; fuzzy-PID closed loop adapts compression and sync mode to a latency target.
evaluation: Jetson Xavier NX edge + L40 cloud, KITTI at 10 fps, 20-80 Mbps and real 4G/5G; vs DECS, REFL, Venus, AWStream. Budget 100 ms: CR-100 up to +22.3%, mAP +18.2%; 4G/5G 71.1 mAP, 73.2% CR-100; edge about 38.5 ms.
contribution: AlignDual co-designs cross-modal compression and prediction-based synchronisation for edge-cloud multimodal 3D detection, raising accuracy and the share of frames meeting a 100 ms budget on a Jetson Xavier NX testbed.
flag: timing is the contribution: partly - half the paper is accuracy-preserving compression, the other half is meeting a 100 ms end-to-end budget under network jitter (compliance rate, prediction-based sync that trades mAP for deadline compliance, fuzzy-PID latency control); application is safety-relevant (autonomous driving/roadside perception, KITTI replay, no closed-loop safety outcome). Check: compliance is far from guaranteed (73.2% CR-100 on real 4G/5G; feedback controller 95th percentile 125.5 ms against a 90 ms setpoint); prediction ablation gains 41.3% CR-100 at the cost of 14.9% mAP at 20 Mbps; most per-bandwidth numbers are in figures, not tables; baselines are the authors' own multimodal adaptations of prior systems; heavy inference runs in the cloud (L40), the edge only runs YOLOv8 and compression. 37 pages: I read abstract, intro, Sec. 2, 6.1, 7 and ablations; Sec. 4-5 details and appendices skimmed only.

title: MCSched: Memory-Controller-Aware Scheduling for Embodied LLM Workloads on NVIDIA Jetson
venue: ACM SIGOPS Asia-Pacific Workshop on Systems (APSys)
evidence: "MCSched throttles LLM inference only when memory pressure coincides with signs that the protected robotics task is approaching, or has already entered, deadline risk." (Sec. 3.2)
method: MCSched: runtime scheduler on Jetson combines memory-controller pressure (ACTMON) with ROS 2 callback slack and miss telemetry, and suspends background LLM inference (SIGSTOP/SIGCONT) around foreground task releases at deadline risk.
evaluation: Jetson Orin Nano Super, ROS-LLM, 3 LLMs via llama.cpp; vs uncontrolled co-run. Camera miss rate 74.30-85.56% to 1.66-2.76% (p95 62-97 to 28-30 ms); PCL 85.71-96.61% to 22.50-35.00%; LLM throughput loss 1.20-1.97%.
contribution: MCSched gates on-device LLM inference when memory-controller pressure threatens co-running robotics tasks, cutting camera-task deadline misses from about 80% to under 3% on a Jetson Orin Nano at under 2% LLM throughput cost.
flag: timing is the contribution: yes (deadline-miss rate and p95 of real-time tasks); application safety-relevant in motivation only (robot sensing/control), nothing safety-related measured. LIKELY TO BE OVERTURNED on condition 2: the deadlines belong to emulated non-learned ROS sensor tasks (camera preprocessing, point-cloud gather); the learned model (LLM) is the background interferer being throttled, with no deadline of its own - it is deadline-aware scheduling of LLM inference only in that sense. Other checks: 7-page workshop paper (APSys 26) labelled preliminary; absolute deadline values are never stated (set from task period); abstract's 'up to 83.35% and 74.11%' are percentage-point drops (85.56 to 2.21; 96.61 to 22.50); PCL still misses 22-35%; single platform, synthetic tasks, only baseline is no control. It pauses the LLM process, not an action, so runtime_interceptor is no.

title: Towards Untethered Industrial Physical AI: Profiling Cloud–Edge VLA over O-RAN
evidence: "Under O-RAN, the average end-to-end latency increases to 1379.40 ms, 38.11% above the wired reference." (Sec. 4.2)
method: Measurement study: pi0 VLA policy served from a central GPU server, robot-side edge PC does sensing, action buffering and control; five-stage observation-to-command latency profiled over wired Ethernet vs srsRAN O-RAN 5G.
evaluation: No stated deadline or budget. Real IMETA Y1 arm, edge PC, 2x A100 server; 9 task-object combos. Mean e2e 998.74 ms wired vs 1379.40 ms O-RAN; P95 1022-1122 vs 1323-1526 ms; uplink 18.58 vs 398.90 ms; inference about 866-872 ms.
contribution: Profiles stage-wise and P95 observation-to-command latency of a cloud-edge VLA manipulation loop over a real O-RAN 5G testbed, showing uplink request delivery and inference dominate the added delay.
flag: timing is the contribution: yes (pure latency profiling of the wireless path carrying VLA inference, with P95); application industrial manipulation, safety-relevant only loosely. Check: 6-page workshop paper (WIPAI 26); NO stated deadline or budget - a buffer-derived deadline is only proposed as future work, so latency/jitter-aware cell not claimed; inference runs on a 2x A100 central server, the edge PC is unnamed, so edge-deployment cell not claimed; only 5 successful executions per combination retained for latency (failed trials dropped), so P95 rests on few cycles; in-system inference about 870 ms vs about 170 ms in a separate single-GPU profile; no mitigation mechanism, baseline is wired Ethernet only; task success comparable so no measured degradation of the decision. Include is marginal - rests on the tail/path-analysis clause alone.

title: Beyond LLM Serving: Characterizing Vision-Language-Action Workloads for Embodied AI System Design
evidence: "The control period, roughly 33 ms for contact-rich manipulation, therefore acts as a recurring deadline" (Sec. 1)
method: Workload characterisation of four VLA models (GR00T N1.6, pi0.5, OpenVLA-OFT, Cosmos-Policy): per-stage latency decomposition, roofline analysis, DVFS sweeps, and closed-loop asynchronous-overlap runs trading success against control period.
evaluation: Deadline: ~33 ms control period (30 Hz). RTX 4090, Jetson Thor, Jetson AGX Orin. Inference 117-396 ms (4090), 304-2603 ms (Orin); 43,200 LIBERO episodes; baselines eager vs compiled, default DVFS, overlap 10/25/50%.
contribution: Characterises where time goes when vision-language-action models run on edge GPUs, showing single inferences exceed the 33 ms control period by 4-80x and that asynchronous overlap trades task success for speed.
flag: timing is the contribution: yes (characterisation study, no new mechanism); application not safety-relevant (simulated manipulation, no safety metric). Check: no p99, jitter or deadline-miss rate is reported - the floor is met only by latency against the stated 33 ms period and per-episode worst-case RTT (RTT_max 126.7-2558.4 ms, averaged over episodes). The 1.5x margin and the SLO cut-offs in Sec. 5.4 are the authors' analysis choices. Authors state they "do not implement a scheduler". Closed loop is MuJoCo/LIBERO only; latency is measured on real hardware. Success drops 15-20 pp (robust models) and 31-49 pp (GR00T, Cosmos-Policy) from 10% to 50% overlap. Fetched via arXiv id for a DOI record; title matched.

title: RED: Adaptive Real-Time DAG Scheduling for Robotic Inference under Environmental Dynamics
venue: Digital Repository at the University of Maryland (University of Maryland College Park)
evidence: "The core of RED is a deadline-aware scheduler that assigns intermediate sub-deadlines, allowing it to accommodate evolving computation graphs and asynchronous inference induced by unpredictable conditions." (Abstract)
method: Real-time DAG scheduler for multi-task MIMONet DNN inference: proportional intermediate sub-deadlines recomputed online, EDF dispatch, encoder/decoder DAG refinement, on-demand synchronisation, and overload shedding of low-criticality tasks (ProactiveDrop).
evaluation: Platform-specific WCET-based end-to-end deadlines (Orin: 9815 and 3600 ms). Jetson Nano, TX2, AGX Xavier, AGX Orin, M-series MacBook; vs EDF and two ablations: miss rate -40.5%, mean latency -24.7%, QoE +34.8%; ROS 2: misses -67.3%.
contribution: Deadline-aware DAG scheduling for multi-task DNN inference on Jetson-class robots, re-assigning sub-deadlines online as the workload graph changes and cutting deadline misses by about 40% against EDF.
flag: timing is the contribution: yes (deadline-miss rate and response-time tails of DNN inference are the primary outcome); application robot/vehicle navigation perception, safety-relevant in framing but no safety metric. Check: arXiv preprint (v1, May 2026) that extends the authors' own conference paper [67] - possible duplicate of another record; text contains leftover reviewer-response wording ('prior-round reviewer concern'). Headline gains are relative percentages, absolute values mostly in figures; p99/p99.9 claim is read off a histogram, no table. Sec. 5.1 gives 'tight and loose deadlines' as 9815 ms and 3600 ms for Orin (order looks swapped). Sec. 6.3 prints miss rates as '0.99%'/'1.00%' that are probably fractions (99%/100%); Sec. 6.4 says both schedulers miss deadlines on Orin under bursts yet RED QoE is 1.00; end-to-end latencies there are 16-42 s. Timing 'guarantees' are propositions with proof sketches under a profiled-WCET assumption, not hard bounds. ROS 2 study uses a simulated camera. ProactiveDrop sheds inference jobs, not actions, so runtime_interceptor no. Read Secs 1-3 (part), 4.6, 5, 6.3-6.4; skimmed 4.1-4.5, 7-8.

title: Toward cooperative multi-agent video streaming perception
evidence: "we propose a virtual traffic shaper based on the mainstream 802.11 MAC protocol to ensure deterministic periodic video stream offloading in an uncertain wireless network" (English abstract, end of file; ligatures normalised)
method: MASSIVE: edge-assisted multi-device video analytics; a Pareto-improvement scheduler staggers periodic frame uploads across devices and a virtual traffic shaper over 802.11 polling makes offloading deterministic.
evaluation: Body in Chinese, not extracted. English abstract only: 122.7% accuracy and 1.8x capacity versus closest baseline on cooperative vision tasks in a wireless setting; no deadline, hardware or latency figures in the English part.
contribution: Edge-assisted cooperative multi-device video perception system that schedules periodic frame offloading to balance real-time accuracy, consistency and device capacity (paper in Chinese).
flag: timing is the contribution: partly (real-time accuracy under offloading delay and deterministic periodic uploads, but outcomes are accuracy, consistency and capacity, not deadlines or tails); application drone/vehicle/robot swarms, loosely safety-relevant. NOT IN ENGLISH: Scientia Sinica Informationis 53(1), body text is Chinese with only an English title, abstract and figure captions; the file is the right paper. Assessed from the English abstract only - the Chinese body was not read. '122.7% accuracy' is a ratio to baseline, not an absolute accuracy. If an English version exists it would need re-screening; on the abstract alone it leans E1 for Pillar 4.

title: Edge-intelligent safelink-V2X: A low-latency cooperative framework for real-time vulnerable road user protection
evidence: "By applying sensor fusion and machine learning-based conflict prediction, the system identifies potential collision points and issues real-time, context-aware warnings through vehicle HMIs and VRU devices" (Abstract)
method: V2X cooperative warning framework: fused vehicle, infrastructure and pedestrian-device data feed a temporal convolutional network that predicts vehicle-VRU collision risk at an edge node; a knapsack scheduler issues tiered driver and VRU alerts.
evaluation: INTERACTION dataset replayed with simulated V2X impairments, 1000 Monte Carlo runs, Intel i9. Three literature baselines. Collision probability 0.018 vs 0.210 best baseline; false alerts 4.2 vs 12.8; latency 9.7 vs 84.2 ms.
contribution: A simulated V2X warning framework that predicts vehicle-to-vulnerable-road-user conflicts with a temporal convolutional network at the edge and alerts both driver and pedestrian, reporting lower predicted collision probability than three baselines.
flag: Pillar 1 by route (c) only, and a weak include: multi-agent hazard detection is the primary claim and collision probability against baselines the primary outcome, so the criteria are met on paper, but the evidence quality is doubtful and the maintainer may reasonably exclude. It is NOT a runtime interceptor: the system only warns people; nothing is overridden or braked, and no driver or pedestrian reaction is modelled. Doubts: (1) 'collision probability' is the model's own risk estimate on dataset replays ('calculated by running the trained TCN on the test sequences ... and correlating its proactive risk ratings'), not collisions avoided in closed loop. (2) Numbers disagree: abstract says latency 30% lower, body says 'more than 94%' and Table 3 -88.5%; abstract says situational awareness +44%, Table 3 +24.6%, text 'more than 45%'; CP improvement 91.4% vs 'over 94%'. (3) False alert and missed detection deltas are both exactly -67.2%. (4) Baselines are three systems from other papers with no account of re-implementation. (5) Sec. 4.1 describes the INTERACTION trajectory dataset as 'audio recordings', one of several signs of careless or machine-assisted writing; the text also contains reviewer-response phrasing ('has been added', 'was included to increase the reliability'). (6) 9.7 ms is from a MATLAB/Simulink and Python simulation on a desktop i9, not edge hardware or a real V2X link; the stated requirement is 150 ms. (7) Table 2 has no units and no baseline. The 'situational awareness index' is a perception-coverage formula, not human situation awareness, so criterion (e) is not met.

title: Towards Real-Time Segmentation on the Edge
evidence: "We train an MLP latency model based on generated architecture configurations and their latency measured on mobile devices, so that we can predict the latency of subnets during search phase." (Abstract)
method: RTSeg: dual-branch segmentation supernet mixing lightweight convolutions and self-attention; block and width search with a latency regulariser driven by an MLP predictor of on-device latency; self-distillation boosters.
evaluation: Target latency used in the search loss but its value is never stated. Samsung Galaxy S21 (Snapdragon 888, Adreno 660 GPU): RTSeg-S/M/L 17.9/15.5/13.2 FPS at 73.1/74.4/75.3 mIoU on Cityscapes vs BiSeNetV2 5.0 FPS, 73.4 mIoU.
contribution: Latency-driven architecture search for semantic segmentation that reaches about 15 FPS and 74% mIoU on Cityscapes on a phone GPU.
flag: timing is the contribution: partly (latency-constrained NAS with a learned latency predictor, under 4% error claimed) but results are reported only as mean FPS and mIoU - no stated latency budget or deadline value, no tail, worst-case or jitter figures, no deadline-miss metric; application generic segmentation with autonomous driving as motivation only. Closest call in this batch: if the maintainer counts latency-constrained NAS as 'accuracy traded against a latency budget' it could be include, but the budget is never given numerically and 15 FPS is called 'semi-real-time' by the authors themselves. FPS measured with the authors' own compiler; several baselines have no FPS. Edge-deployment cell withheld because the paper is excluded as compression/architecture work, though measurements are on a real Galaxy S21.

title: EnViT: Enhancing the Performance of Early-Exit Vision Transformers via Exit-Aware Structured Dropout-Enabled Self-Distillation
evidence: "We adopt Multiply-Accumulate Operations (MACs) as the computational cost metric." (Sec. 4, Evaluation metrics)
method: EnViT: training scheme for early-exit ViTs using exit-aware structured layer dropout to create virtual sub-models that are self-distilled from the full model; confidence-threshold exits at inference.
evaluation: No deadline or latency budget stated. Five image datasets, ViT-B/16, six early-exit baselines plus ablation; accuracy 80.45-95.33% at 1.72-2.23x MAC speed-up. Trained and tested on Xeon server with 4 A40 GPUs; only latency figures are motivational (ViT-B 56 ms on Jetson Orin NX, Table 1).
contribution: Training method that raises early-exit accuracy in vision transformers without degrading late exits, reported as accuracy against a computed MAC speed-up ratio.
flag: timing is the contribution: no; application not safety-relevant (image classification). Speed-up is a computed MAC ratio, not measured latency; no deadline, budget, bound or tail analysis; no edge-hardware results for EnViT itself (Jetson figures in Table 1 are for plain ViTs). Proofs are in an appendix not in this file. Read in full.

title: Autonomous Realization of Safety- and Time-Critical Embedded Artificial Intelligence
venue: Design, Automation and Test in Europe
evidence: "This is an early project concept presentation of the FASTER-AI project" (Sec. I)
method: Project concept (FASTER-AI): pipeline of hardware-aware NAS with pruning/quantisation, MLIR-based code generation and an isolating runtime to co-deploy ML inference with safety- and time-critical logic on DSP/FPGA hardware.
evaluation: None. No experiments, no deadline or budget figure, no hardware measurements, no latency numbers, no baseline; avionics and telecom base-station use cases are described only qualitatively.
contribution: Four-page multi-partner project description of a planned end-to-end toolchain for putting neural inference on safety- and time-critical embedded hardware without violating real-time guarantees.
flag: timing is the contribution: partly (preserving real-time guarantees is a stated goal, but nothing is measured or proved); application safety-relevant (avionics, telecom). DATE Multi-Partner Project track concept paper: all claims are future tense (we intend, we plan), zero quantitative results, so it fails the evaluation floor. Read in full.

title: Server Selection and Inference Rate Optimization in AoI-Driven Distributed Systems
evidence: "The primary metric we consider is the age of information (AoI)" (Sec. I)
method: Queueing and game-theoretic analysis of how N sources choose between a local and a remote MEC inference server and their request rates to minimise average age of information; three policies Super-Best, Nash-Best, Nash-Nash.
evaluation: No deadline or budget; metric is mean AoI. Closed-form M/M/1 analysis plus C++ event simulator (M/M/c, M/D/c); 30 vehicles, mu1=1 req/ms, mu2=5-20 req/ms, remote RTT 15 ms. Mean AoI about 15-25 ms; price of anarchy below about 1.2, converging to 1.1. No hardware.
contribution: Shows by queueing analysis and simulation that selfish selection between edge inference servers costs only about 10% in average age of information if per-source request rates are coordinated.
flag: timing is the contribution: partly (freshness of inference results is the subject, but only AVERAGE AoI is optimised - no deadline, budget, bound or tail analysis); application framed as safety-relevant (assisted driving). No learned model anywhere: inference is an exponential or deterministic service time in a queue, so condition 2 fails too. Entirely analytical/simulated. Authors' earlier work [11] used deadline-completion probability - that one may fit better. PoA 15-20% figure read from text, curves not visible in the text file. Read in full.

title: Class-Aware Early-Exit Networks for Efficient and Secure Edge Deployment
evidence: "early-exit edge inference should optimize priority-weighted computational depth, not average computation alone" (Sec. 1.1 Thesis Statement)
method: PhD dissertation: class-aware early-exit networks (ClassyNet, RACENet runtime control vector, federated CAFED) that send high-priority classes to earlier exits, plus exit-suppression attacks (DDAS, ESPA) and a draft-acceptance guard.
evaluation: No deadline or budget stated. Jetson TX2 (plus split to workstation): HP-class mean inference e.g. 24 to 18 ms vs SDN (Table 14), up to 9.41x priority-class speed-up vs BranchyNet; DDAS +55% time, +128% power. Ch. 8 on dual RTX 3090: p95 11.0 s to 17.2 s under attack.
contribution: Dissertation showing early-exit networks can give designated urgent classes lower average inference latency on a Jetson TX2, and that adversarial inputs can erase early-exit speed-ups unless exit behaviour is monitored.
flag: timing is the contribution: partly; application partly safety-relevant (intrusion detection, HAR; mostly CIFAR-class benchmarks). BORDERLINE, likely to be overturned: chapters 3-6 reduce AVERAGE per-class latency with no stated deadline, budget or bound (hence E1), but Ch. 8 reports p95 latency of LayerSkip-Llama2-7B under attack with baselines and a guard that falls back to full depth, and Ch. 7 measures attack-induced slowdown - if tail analysis in one chapter suffices, this is an include with d. Ch. 8 testbed is dual RTX 3090 'near-edge', not an edge device. Unreviewed dissertation dated July 2026; chapters probably duplicate separately published papers (ClassyNet, RACENet, CAFED, DDAS) - check the queue. 503k chars: read abstract, Ch. 1, Ch. 3 edge results, Tables 13-14 and 27, Ch. 8 metrics and results; NOT read: Ch. 2, Ch. 4, most of Ch. 5-7 method text, Ch. 6 results, Ch. 9.

title: Industrial EdgeSign: NAS-Optimized Real-Time Hand Gesture Recognition for Operator Communication in Smart Factories
evidence: "we got results of 99th percentile latency = 72 ms" (Sec. 3.6 Edge Deployment Performance)
method: Industrial EdgeSign: hardware-aware NAS that prunes candidates above 100 ms latency, yielding a truncated-ResNet50, tubelet and local-Transformer gesture recogniser with VLM-distilled text pre-training, deployed with TensorRT on Jetson Nano.
evaluation: Deadline 100 ms (ISO 13849-1 PLd emergency response). Jetson Nano 4GB: 86 +/- 3.2 ms and 94.7% accuracy; emergency-stop p99 72 ms over 1000 runs; full-pipeline worst case 120.7 ms in 24-h stress test; Raspberry Pi 4 158 ms. Latency ablations (Tables 4-5: 48-124 ms); no baseline on latency.
contribution: NAS-derived gesture recogniser for factory operators that reports 99th-percentile and worst-case latency on a Jetson Nano against a 100 ms emergency-stop requirement, with accuracy-latency ablations.
flag: timing is the contribution: partly (a 100 ms deadline drives the NAS and p99/worst-case latency is reported, but most of the paper is gesture/sign translation accuracy); application safety-relevant (emergency-stop gestures). DOUBTS, could well be overturned: (1) latency figures are inconsistent - 86 ms inference (abstract, Tables 4, 5, 11) vs 41.5 ms full pipeline (Table 7), and Table 7 worst case 120.7 ms EXCEEDS the 100 ms deadline while stage worst cases do not sum to it; (2) the 72 ms p99 and 99.7% fail-safe figures come from an unnamed 'third-party verification' with no method detail; (3) reads like a repurposed sign-language-translation paper - model called STTSLT and 2DCNTSLT, BLEU/ROUGE on ML2HP (a hand-pose dataset), conclusion speaks of sign language translation, SHREC'17 described as industrial, a paragraph duplicated in the intro, reference numbers for baselines inconsistent; (4) timing baselines are only the paper's own ablations, plus an unspecified cloud baseline (TCT 2.8 s vs 1.2 s, 12 operators). Fail-safe mode (freeze output + alert) is fault-triggered, not a decision interceptor. Read in full except Sec. 2 method derivations (skimmed).

title: A 5G-MEC-Enabled, Digital-Twin-Trained Framework for Autonomous Mobile Robots on the ROSMASTER R2 Platform
evidence: "From the perspective of real-time control, low jitter is more valuable than low average latency, because it determines the worst-case end-to-end delay that the control loop must tolerate." (Sec 7.1)
method: Private 5G SA plus MEC offloading of a YOLO26 detector with a utility-based node selector (CPU, RAM, GPU, RTT); sim-trained LiDAR localizer and SAC fallback run on the robot.
evaluation: Real robot testbed, Wi-Fi 5 vs 5G SA vs onboard. Budgets: 100 ms RTT reference, 125 ms LiDAR period. Jetson Orin NX + RTX A4500 MEC. E2E 62 vs 67 ms (1 stream), 93 vs 79 ms (4); jitter std 14.8 vs 2.1 ms; P95 96 vs 76 ms; localizer 6 ms, P95 8.4 ms.
contribution: Measured comparison of onboard, Wi-Fi-MEC and private-5G-MEC detector offloading on a small robot shows 5G gives seven times lower jitter and a lower P95 than Wi-Fi despite higher mean latency.
flag: timing is the contribution: partly; application safety-relevant: weakly (lab mobile robot, authors call localization and line-keeping safety-critical). Integration/reference-design paper; latency, jitter and P95 are one of five evaluation axes beside energy and sim-to-real accuracy. No deadline-miss rate; the 100 ms figure is only an RTT normaliser in the node selector and the only explicit budget (125 ms) is for the onboard localizer, met by a wide margin. P95 values appear only in Table 8; no P99. Node selector shown on one 230 s trace with no baseline selector. Variance under thermal throttling is described but not quantified. Check whether a measurement study without a timing mechanism is in scope.

title: ML-NIC: accelerating machine learning inference using smart network interface cards
evidence: "ML-NIC can provide tighter guaranteed latency bounds in the presence of other network traffic with shorter tail latencies." (Abstract)
method: Compiles trained scikit-learn decision trees (up to 256 leaves) to Micro-C and maps feature evaluation in parallel across the microengines of a Netronome SmartNIC data plane.
evaluation: Four datasets on a Netronome Agilio CX 2x25GbE SmartNIC vs CPU and P4 (Xavier et al.) baselines under 0-99% link and CPU load. No deadline tested (50 ms cited in intro). Mine p50 18.0 vs 184.8 us CPU; p99.9 35.5 vs 71.3 (P4) vs 202.9; 99% CPU load p99.9 36.9 vs 7979 us.
contribution: ML-NIC compiles decision trees onto SmartNIC microengines, cutting median and 99.9th-percentile inference latency several-fold against CPU and P4 baselines and holding the tail flat under link and CPU load.
flag: timing is the contribution: yes (latency and p99/p99.9 tails under load are the main result, but as acceleration, not against any deadline); application safety-relevant: no (mine, Landsat, gas-sensor, CICIDS classification; safety uses only cited as motivation). Check: the learned model is a small decision tree, not a neural network; 'edge' means a NIC in a server testbed, not an embedded device, so edge deployment not credited; 'guaranteed latency bounds' is empirical percentiles over 1000 packets, no proved bound; latencies are microseconds. Two-column text extraction interleaved, tables read from Tables 4-5 only in part.

title: Super-Resolution Task Inference Acceleration for In-Vehicle Real-Time Video via Edge–End Collaboration
evidence: "the inference time of a single frame on end device j, the intermediate data transmission time, and the inference time on the edge server should all be less than the single-frame playback time." (Sec 3.2.2)
method: Dynamic device-edge partitioning of a super-resolution CNN for several terminals: min-max latency under a per-frame real-time constraint, solved as a potential-style game with periodic or threshold-triggered re-partitioning.
evaluation: FSRCNN x4 on REDS4, 1-5 terminals. Deadline: each stage under frame period 1/F (F not given numerically). Jetson Nano and PCs + Xeon/RTX2080Ti edge server over throttled LAN (30-90 Mbps), edge load 0-50%. Baselines terminal-only, edge-only, static split. Results only as plots; decision overhead under 1 ms (5 ms for 100 layers).
contribution: A game-theoretic dynamic model-partitioning scheme splits super-resolution inference between in-vehicle devices and an edge server so each frame stage stays within the playback period while minimising the worst terminal's latency.
flag: timing is the contribution: yes (per-frame deadline constraint and min-max latency are the formulation); application safety-relevant: weakly (train surveillance video enhancement, not a decision). title: ZTSafe: Safety-Certified Risk-Adaptive Scheduling for Zero-Trust Time-Sensitive Industrial Networks
evidence: "An independent runtime safety shield [8] checks every proposal against the contracts and the current conservative risk bounds; only proposals that pass are atomically committed inside a protection window." (Sec 1.2 Core Idea: Propose, Verify, Commit)

Check: (1) the acting system is a network scheduler, not an agent or robot policy; the maintainer should confirm that counts as an acting system; (2) plausibility of scale: 14,000 episodes of 60 s per method is about 9.7 days of testbed time each, and this is claimed for 6 end-to-end methods plus 7 ablation variants plus risk and executor baselines on physical plants (tank, BLDC motor, mobile robot) - months of continuous hardware runs; raw logs said to be 2.1 TB; nothing is public (data and code on application under a data-use agreement), so results are unverifiable; (3) all 126 residual violations fall in the four scenarios that attack the risk calibration (S3, S7, S8, S14), zero in the other 10,000 episodes, which is very clean; (4) scenarios were designed by the same group (the paper says so); (5) theorems are conditional on Assumption 1 and an uncompromised trusted base; shield is tested, not formally verified; (6) refs 9, 10 and 23 (spatial scattering modulation, RIS) are cited for unrelated claims - citation padding; (7) L3 scalability row is simulation only and exceeds the 10 ms budget; (8) safety cost is 1.8 pp on-time completion vs SA-TSN and a 4.6% fallback trigger rate. I read Sec 1, 5.5-5.6, 6.1-6.4, 6.7, 6.10-6.11, 7; Sec 3-4 contract synthesis, 5.2-5.4, Exp2, 3, 5, 6 and the appendices were only skimmed via headings.

evidence: "was still able to meet a deadline success rate of around 90 % at 250 % utilization" (Sec. 9.1.3; results in Sec. 7.6.3)
method: PhD thesis: time-triggered multi-version mode-change scheduler plus anytime neural networks - early exits added to backbones, online runtime estimation, checkpoints that pick an exit against a timing budget, anomaly detection that can abort inference.
evaluation: Deadline 1.5x mean network runtime; NVIDIA Jetson AGX Orin, ResNeXt-101, GoogleNet, YoloV11, GPUNet at 50-250% utilisation: deadlines met to 150%, ~90% success at 250%; checkpoint overhead 0.23-0.62 ms mean, 0.85-1.81 ms p99.
contribution: A checkpoint-based scheduler picks early exits of anytime neural networks against per-task timing budgets, keeping about 90% of deadlines at 250% utilisation on a Jetson AGX Orin, within a time-triggered mode-change framework.
flag: timing is the contribution: yes - deadline-constrained scheduling of early-exit networks with accuracy traded against a timing budget; application safety-relevant (automotive domain controllers, SOTIF). Check: this is a 300-page doctoral dissertation (KIT, 2026) - maintainer to decide if a thesis is an eligible record type or whether the underlying paper [Sta25b] should stand in; no external scheduler baseline for the ANN part (comparison is networks with vs without exits, release patterns, and ablations of the runtime estimator); deadline-success figures are in plots, only 'around 90 %' and 'up to 150 %' stated in prose; Sec. 7.6.3 says batched release performs best while Sec. 9.1.3 says batched is worst; boxed Finding 11 gives a 2.318 ms overhead figure that does not match Table 7.20. Interceptor 'yes' rests on the checkpoint aborting inference or forcing a mode change on anomaly; no safety metric, so (a) not claimed. READ: abstract, Sec. 7.5-7.6, 8.2 end, 9.1.3; skimmed ToC. NOT READ: chapters 1-6, 7.1-7.4, 8.1, 9.1.1-9.1.2, 9.2.

title: AI Digital Twins in Simulink: Safe RL for Hardware-in-the-Loop Control
venue: International Journal of Academic and Industrial Research Innovations(IJAIRI)
evidence: "Safety uses a shield that filters unsafe actions and a control barrier function h(x) with inequality constraints enforcing forward invariance. A scheduler enforces sampling periods and budgets" (Sec. 3 Methodology)
method: Simulink digital-twin framework: PPO policy filtered at runtime by a shield and CBF quadratic program that minimally adjusts the RL action, plus scheduler co-design to hold a latency budget.
evaluation: Synthetic HIL-style workloads with injected delay and jitter, 5 seeds; PID, PPO, PPO+shield, +CBF, +scheduler opt. Budget P95<=5 ms; P95 2.0/5.5/6.0/6.5/3.0 ms; violations per 10k 12.5/7.8/2.9/1.8/1.2. No hardware named.
contribution: Proposes a Simulink digital-twin pipeline in which a shield and control barrier function veto unsafe RL actions under a 5 ms P95 latency budget, reporting fewer violations than PPO and PID in synthetic tests.
flag: timing is the contribution: partly (safety shield and latency budget are co-primary); application safety-relevant (safety-critical embedded control, generic). Criteria are met only on paper - DOUBT THE EVIDENCE: 12-page single-author paper in the author's own organisation's journal (IJAIRI, National Education Services), reads as template or machine-generated; whole evaluation is one 5-row table with no plant, task, hardware, scheduler or RL details; data called synthetic and experiments HIL-style, no real hardware. Abstract claims deadline miss ratio, bounded worst-case latency, rate-monotonic scheduler and FMI co-simulation results, none of which appear in the body. Two of the safe variants (6.0 and 6.5 ms) exceed the stated 5 ms budget. References undated (n.d.) plus 12 self-citations, some dated 2021 on LLM topics. Maintainer may well prefer exclude-E2.

title: EDGE ARTIFICIAL INTELLIGENCE BASED AUTOMATION FOR ULTRA-LOW-LATENCY CONTROL IN INDUSTRIAL ROBOTIC SYSTEMS
venue: Review of Applied Science and Technology
evidence: "A structured questionnaire has been used to operationalize the study variables, and a five-point Likert scale has been applied to ensure consistent measurement of latent constructs across respondents." (Methods)
method: Cross-sectional questionnaire study: regression of practitioner-perceived ultra-low-latency control performance on perceived Edge AI automation maturity in industrial robotic cells. No system or mechanism is built.
evaluation: N=162 practitioners, 5-point Likert scales; r=0.61, beta=0.58, R2=0.46. No deadline or budget stated, no hardware, no measured latency in ms; no baseline system.
contribution: Survey of 162 industrial practitioners finding that perceived Edge AI automation maturity predicts perceived low-latency control performance; no latency is measured.
flag: timing is the contribution: no (latency is only a perceived, self-reported Likert construct); application safety-relevant only loosely (industrial robots). No learned model is run and no timing is measured, so it fails the evaluation floor; exclude-E1 would be equally defensible. 37-page file, read abstract, methods, results tables via grep and limitations; long literature review skimmed only.

title: Edge-Aware Hybrid-Action Reinforcement Learning for Latency-Sensitive Cooperative Bus Signal Priority in Vehicular Edge Networks
venue: Journal of Intelligent Computing and Networking
evidence: "Task completion rate is defined as the proportion of BSP decision tasks completed within a predefined system deadline of 100 ms" (Sec. 5.3.1); "a deadline-aware feasibility projection mechanism is introduced to filter or adjust candidate priority actions" (Sec. 1)
method: Multi-agent hybrid-action RL (CVAE latent actions, GAT neighbour aggregation, CTDE) for bus signal priority run on roadside edge nodes, with a feasibility projection that suppresses actions missing the control window.
evaluation: 15-intersection field corridor plus SUMO 102-intersection simulation; cloud vs edge, ablations. Deadline 100 ms: E2E 89.7 vs 24.6 ms, completion 94.3% vs 99.1%; valid-control 99.5% to 87.6% at 10-200 ms delay. Edge hardware unnamed.
contribution: Deadline-aware multi-agent RL for bus signal priority at roadside edge nodes: edge inference cut mean decision latency from 89.7 to 24.6 ms and raised 100 ms deadline completion from 94.3% to 99.1%.
flag: timing is the contribution: partly (deadline-aware edge execution is one of four contributions; most results are bus delay and traffic metrics); application safety-relevant only weakly (traffic signal control, signal-safety constraints). Check: only mean latency and completion rate are logged in the field, authors state p95/p99 are not available; valid-control, delay, packet-loss and workload results are simulation only (SUMO with Python edge emulation); ablation removing edge state or edge penalties changes bus delay by under 3 points and reports no deadline metric; edge node hardware never named so edge deployment cell not given; text refers to Table 10 for figures that are in Table 12. The projection filters or suppresses infeasible actions at execution time, hence interceptor yes, but criterion (a) not claimed since it is a feasibility mask not a safety monitor. Field result is an uncontrolled before-after comparison.

title: GOODBYE LATENCY: WHY FUTURE MEDICAL DEVICES NEED ARTIFICIAL BRAINS
evidence: "the SNN identified the anomaly onset within 0.2 milliseconds of the electrical event. The standard system consistently registered the event with a variance of 12 to 18 milliseconds, a jitter caused by the operating system's task scheduler and interrupt handling routines." (Results and Discussion)
method: Spiking neural network converted from a trained classifier and mapped to an Intel Loihi 2 neuromorphic chip for on-device ECG and EEG event detection, compared with a CNN on an ARM Cortex-M4.
evaluation: MIT-BIH and CHB-MIT streams, 1000 inference cycles; target sub-millisecond. Loihi 2 vs ARM Cortex-M4: latency 0.85 vs 14.20 ms, jitter 0.2 vs 12-18 ms, seizure trigger 3 vs 45 ms, phase-lock 98% vs about 70%, accuracy 96.4% vs 97.1%.
contribution: Benchmarks a spiking network on Intel Loihi 2 against a CNN on an ARM Cortex-M4 for closed-loop arrhythmia and seizure detection, reporting 0.85 ms versus 14.2 ms latency and far lower timing jitter.
flag: timing is the contribution: partly (latency and jitter of on-device inference are the headline, with energy co-primary; no hard deadline, only a sub-millisecond target stated as an aim, and no tail percentiles); application safety-relevant (implantable closed-loop medical devices). DOUBT: first and corresponding author is from a fine-arts faculty; method section is vague on how Loihi 2 was obtained and programmed (names both Lava and NengoDL) and calls the study a hardware-in-the-loop simulation, so real-hardware measurement is uncertain - edge deployment cell given on the paper's own claim only. Energy per inference is printed as 1.02 J vs 646.1 J, impossible in joules (micro prefix lost); phase-lock 70% is derived from 'ineffective in 30%'. Prose is promotional (definitively establish). If the maintainer reads the scope rule strictly (mean latency, no deadline) this becomes exclude-E1.

title: Concurrent Video-Stream Workload and Sustained Thermal Conditions Affect the Latency and Real-Time Performance of Object Detection on the NVIDIA Jetson Orin Nano
evidence: "Deadline performance was evaluated as the proportion of frames whose pipeline latency exceeded a 100 ms reference, taken from Sperling and Ernst (8) as the real-time perception target." (Methods, Data Analysis)
method: Measurement study of YOLO26s (TensorRT FP16) object-detection inference and pipeline latency on a Jetson Orin Nano under 1, 2 and 3 concurrent video streams and under low versus high GPU temperature.
evaluation: Jetson Orin Nano 8 GB, 25 W; 3x60 s trials per condition. Deadline 100 ms (also 150 ms): mean 83.9/101.1/129.7 ms, p99 105.2/137.9/195.3 ms, frames over 100 ms 1.50/43.75/81.30%; thermal effect 1.5 ms.
contribution: Shows on a Jetson Orin Nano that adding concurrent video streams pushes YOLO pipeline latency past a 100 ms deadline (1.5% to 81% of frames late, p99 105 to 195 ms) while sustained heat has little effect.
flag: timing is the contribution: yes (tail latency and deadline-miss rate of detector inference on real edge hardware); application safety-relevant (autonomous-vehicle perception, though no vehicle response measured). Check: published in American Journal of Student Research by a high-school author, so venue quality is low but the reporting is careful and code is public; comparison is across workload conditions (single stream as baseline), not against another method; only 3 trials per condition, thermal comparison is a single run each; prerecorded 4K video replayed on every stream; detection accuracy not measured, so no accuracy-latency trade-off; no mechanism proposed, purely a measurement study.

title: VLM-based high-level action planner for mobile robots
venue: UPCommons institutional repository (Universitat Politècnica de Catalunya)
evidence: "If no model output arrives for longer than a fixed timeout (STALE_TIMEOUT=8 s), the dispatcher forces a SLOW_DOWN" (Sec 3.1.3 Low-level control module)
method: Hierarchical ROS2 driving stack: VLM picks a discrete high-level action every 4-5 s; a control layer applies action whitelist, STOP override, commitment lock, speed ramp and an 8 s stale-output watchdog.
evaluation: CARLA Town10HD, 5 scenarios, Qwen3.5:2B local vs Claude Haiku 4.5 cloud; valid calls 91.5% vs 100%; latency median 5.0 vs 4.0 s; 8 s watchdog; RTX 5050 laptop; no safeguard ablation.
contribution: A master's thesis wrapping a slow VLM driving planner in a rule-based control layer whose 8 s stale-output watchdog and overrides keep a simulated vehicle viable between multi-second inferences.
flag: timing is the contribution: partly (latency is tolerated by a watchdog, not analysed or bounded); application safety-relevant (autonomous driving, simulated). Master's thesis (UPC ETSEIB), not peer reviewed. Latency is elapsed time between calls, which the thesis itself says is "an elapsed value rather than a measurement"; no tail figures, no deadline-miss rate beyond raw stale-event counts (0-5 per run), no ablation with safeguards off, single map and spawn point, no collision-rate table found. The safeguard layer does meet criterion (a) as an interceptor, but with no safety metric against a baseline it would be E2 on that route. Laptop GPU, not edge hardware. Read abstract, contributions, Sec 3.1.2.6, 3.1.3, 3.3, Table 12 and 15, limitations; skimmed state of the art and per-scenario narratives.

title: On-Device Preference Graph Reasoner for Personalized and Verifiable Home Automation
venue: National Journal of Ubiquitous Computing and Intelligent Environments
evidence: "Actions that do not conform with any constraint are not accepted and actions that have been verified are accepted for execution." (Sec 4.2 Verification and Safety Performance)
method: Heterogeneous preference graph with attention-based reasoning ranks home-automation actions on a gateway; multi-user conflict scoring; a constraint check (safety, privacy, energy, device state) rejects actions and substitutes a fallback.
evaluation: Unspecified dataset; 8 baselines on accuracy (98.6% vs GAT 97.3%). Verification: one funnel figure, 120 candidate actions, 32 rejected, 88 approved; no baseline. Latency 12.1 ms, 9.8 MB.
contribution: Describes an on-device graph reasoner for personalised smart-home automation with a constraint check that rejects unsafe actions before execution; the reported evidence is thin and unverifiable.
flag: neither - the verification gate fits criterion (a) on paper (Eq. 6-7 veto plus safe fallback), but its only evidence is a funnel figure (Fig. 3: 120 actions, 15 safety, 10 privacy, 5 energy, 2 device-state rejections, 88 approved) with no ground truth, no baseline and no ablation; the unsafe-action rejection rate, false acceptance, false rejection and constraint-checking latency named in the abstract and Sec 4.2 are never given as numbers. exclude-E1 is also defensible: the paper is about preference personalisation and the verifier is one module of six. Signs the work is unevaluated or templated: (1) Table 1 lists hardware as Raspberry Pi 5 or NVIDIA Jetson Orin Nano and the dataset as Simulated or Real Smart Home Dataset - neither is pinned down; number of households, users and samples never stated; (2) Sec 4.5 is titled Scalability and Ablation Results but contains no ablation; (3) Sec 4.4 reports conflict resolution, fairness and explanation fidelity only as high, with no values; (4) the abstract says the framework should enable, in the future tense; (5) platform is called Home Citizen in Sec 3.5 and Home Assistant in Table 1; (6) garbled sentences (lacked formal verification and would not be formally verified in the future; keeping prediction performance below a negligible level); (7) references are generic and partly irrelevant (U-Net, BERT, ReLU) and in-text citation numbers do not match their topics; (8) single author, low-profile journal (National Journal of Ubiquitous Computing and Intelligent Environment), submitted to accepted in two months. Likely machine-assisted text; I did not credit the edge deployment cell because the device is not identified. Whole paper read (8 pages).

title: Low-Overhead Scheduling for Real-Time AI Workloads on Multi-Core Edge Chips
venue: International Journal of Advance in Applied Science Research
evidence: "Lite Sched stayed very stable and reduced that worst case delay by about 35.7 percent" (Sec 5.3.1 Tail Latency and Determinism)
method: Lite Sched: offline per-layer profiling builds a memory-contention lookup table; a heuristic-pruned tabular Q-learning agent schedules DNN layers and control tasks across CPU/GPU/DLA under a hard-deadline constraint with low overhead.
evaluation: Jetson Orin Nano, PREEMPT_RT; YOLOv8 plus control-loop tasks; vs Linux CFS, EDF, DQN scheduler; p99 latency -35.7% vs CFS; scheduler overhead 1.5% vs 12% DQN; no deadline value or absolute ms given.
contribution: A lookup-table-guided lightweight scheduler for DNN and control workloads on a Jetson Orin Nano, reported to cut 99th-percentile latency by 35.7% against Linux CFS at 1.5% CPU overhead.
flag: timing is the contribution: yes (p99 latency of DNN workloads under memory contention); application framed as safety-critical (robots, vehicles) but generic synthetic workload. Weak evidence, check before accepting: results are relative percentages only - no absolute latency in ms, no numeric deadline, no deadline-miss rate, no task counts or run counts; D_hard appears only as a symbol in the formulation, so latency/jitter cell not claimed. The 35.7% is stated against CFS/greedy; EDF and DQN comparisons are qualitative or in figures not recoverable from text. Page header carries two journal names and ISSNs; single author; several citations are irrelevant to the sentence they support (climate projections, liquidity pricing, recommender systems), suggesting citation padding or machine-assisted text. Just clears the floor on a tail-latency-vs-baseline claim; E2 is defensible.

title: Real-Time Reachability for Neurosymbolic Reinforcement Learning-based Safe Autonomous Navigation
evidence: "Missed Deadline Ratio, which is the ratio of timesteps where the SG selection time exceeds TsgMax = 100 ms, out of a total of over 30K timesteps" (Sec 4.1 Experimental Setup, Metrics)
method: RusTReach: anytime real-time reachability in Rust rolls out the goal-conditioned RL policy inside the reach computation to pick safe subgoals between planner waypoints within a per-step runtime budget, safeguarding policy actions.
evaluation: Simulated quadcopter and car, 1000 episodes, run on Jetson Nano; 100 ms deadline; subgoal selection mean 8.4-40.1 ms, missed-deadline ratio 0.000 to <0.001; failure 0.066 vs MFNLC 0.163, WO 0.570 (dynamic).
contribution: Anytime reachability analysis over a learned RL policy selects safe subgoals within a 100 ms deadline on a Jetson Nano, cutting navigation failures against a neural-Lyapunov monitor with near-zero missed deadlines.
flag: timing is the contribution: yes (deadline-bounded anytime reachability, missed-deadline ratio reported); application safety-relevant (collision avoidance for UAV/ground vehicle). Check: vehicle and obstacles are simulated, only the computation runs on the Jetson Nano; single agent with moving obstacles, not multi-agent. Timing columns are reported only for the two RusTReach variants (RR FC ablation), not for MFNLC or waypoint-only baselines, so the deadline result has an ablation but no external timing baseline; only mean selection time, no tail or worst case. Deadline is on the reachability/subgoal step which embeds RL policy inference, not on NN inference alone. Abstract's 1.7x faster figure matches Table 1 (18.0-19.7 s vs 30.5-40.2 s). Failure ratio lumps collisions, timeouts and no-subgoal cases. PMLR v288 (NeuS 2025), peer reviewed.
